articles.title: FOMC Meeting Puts Fed Interest Rate Decision in Focus as Inflation Rises - Coinpedia
articles.summary: FOMC Meeting Puts Fed Interest Rate Decision in Focus as Inflation Rises  Coinpedia
articles.full_text:
The US Federal Reserve faces a difficult decision ahead of its October 28 meeting as rising inflation and higher energy prices coincide with concerns about economic growth. Markets expect the Fed to keep interest rates unchanged, but Chair Kevin Warsh’s comments will be closely watched for clues about future rate decisions.
US inflation accelerated in September, with the Consumer Price Index (CPI) rising 3.7% year over year. The Producer Price Index (PPI), which measures changes in prices received by businesses, increased 1.3% from August. Higher energy prices have added to inflation concerns, while the US-Iran conflict has raised further uncertainty over energy costs.
Inflation and Economic Weakness Complicate Fed Policy
The Fed aims to bring inflation down to its 2% target, but higher energy costs could slow that progress. At the same time, high borrowing costs are weighing on housing affordability, and job cuts have raised concerns about employment.
This leaves policymakers balancing two risks. Keeping interest rates high could help control inflation but put further pressure on economic activity. Cutting rates could support growth but risk keeping inflation elevated.
These conditions have raised concerns about stagflation, which occurs when high inflation coincides with weak economic growth. Whether the US economy faces a sustained period of stagflation will depend on how prices, employment, and economic output develop.
Expectations of another rate increase at the October meeting have declined after New York Fed President John Williams and Fed Vice Chair Philip Jefferson indicated that policymakers could take time to assess the economy following September’s rate increase.
Bloomberg Federal Reserve reporter Maria Luisa Capora said investors will focus on Warsh’s explanation for the expected pause and any indications about future policy.
Fed Guidance and Economic Data in Focus
Warsh’s comments could influence expectations for interest rates. A signal that rates may remain high for longer could put pressure on stocks, while indications of potential rate cuts could raise concerns about whether the Fed is doing enough to control inflation.
Investors will also watch the October 29 releases of US third-quarter GDP, Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) inflation, and initial jobless claims. These reports will provide further information about economic growth, price pressures, and labor-market conditions.
The Bank of Japan’s monetary policy meeting on October 29–30 and the US midterm elections on November 3 are also on the calendar.
The Fed’s decision will depend on how policymakers assess persistent inflation alongside economic risks. Investors will look to the policy statement and Warsh’s press conference for a clearer indication of the central bank’s next steps.

articles.title: Yen holds gains as BOJ rate hike expectations support currency - Economies.com
articles.summary: Yen holds gains as BOJ rate hike expectations support currency  Economies.com
articles.full_text:
The yen traded near 157 per dollar on Monday, October 26, as investors assessed prospects for further Bank of Japan interest rate increases ahead of a closely watched monetary policy meeting later this week.
The currency remained stronger than last week's levels, supported by declining US Treasury yields and speculation that Japanese authorities could intervene again to prevent excessive exchange rate volatility.
Price overview
USD/JPY traded around 156.70 yen in Monday's live intraday quotations, down approximately 0.08%.
The currency pair mostly moved between 156.67 and 157.22 yen during the session.
Bank of Japan outlook
The Bank of Japan is expected to maintain its benchmark interest rate at 1.25% at its meeting ending Friday, although policymakers could signal another increase before year-end.
Persistent inflation, rising wages and higher energy costs have strengthened expectations of further monetary tightening.
Investors are particularly focused on the possibility of a December rate increase to 1.5%, which would further narrow the interest rate differential between Japan and the United States.
Intervention speculation
The yen's recent recovery has also reflected concerns about possible intervention by Japanese authorities following substantial currency volatility.
Traders remain sensitive to official statements, particularly after speculation about coordinated action involving Tokyo and Washington.
US Treasury yields decline
The benchmark 10-year US Treasury yield slipped below 5%, reducing the dollar's advantage over the yen.
Investors expect the Federal Reserve to leave interest rates unchanged at its October meeting, although its guidance could influence currency movements.
Market outlook
The yen's near-term direction will depend on the Bank of Japan's policy signals and developments in US bond markets.
A decline in USD/JPY below 156.67 could encourage further yen buying, while resistance remains near 157.22.
Any indication of a December rate increase could provide additional support for the Japanese currency.

articles.title: Gold's $4,000 Line Holds the Market's Gaze as Margin Calls, Oil and a Hawkish Fed Pull in Different - ad-hoc-news.de
articles.summary: Gold's $4,000 Line Holds the Market's Gaze as Margin Calls, Oil and a Hawkish Fed Pull in Different  ad-hoc-news.de
articles.full_text:
Gold finished Friday at $3,997.48 an ounce, a weekly loss of 4.1% that says as much about forced selling as it does about sentiment. Behind that number sit two distinct pressures — a speculative retreat on the COMEX and a scramble for cash after a technology-stock rout — layered on top of an inflation-and-rates backdrop that has, for now, stripped the metal of its usual safe-haven bid.
Start with the futures market. CFTC positioning data as of Tuesday showed large speculators cutting their net long exposure, even as open interest initially rose 1.5%. The two moves together point to a market that wasn't uniformly walking away: small speculators were adding to longs while the big players trimmed. By Friday, open interest on COMEX had slipped to 400,538 contracts, down 0.2% week-on-week. That later decline may hint at a cooling in the unwinding, though it falls well short of proof that a floor is in place.
The liquidity story runs alongside it. Commerzbank analyst Carsten Fritsch points to gold sales aimed at covering equity losses and margin calls, with the selloff in technology and AI shares capable of triggering exactly such liquidations. Reuters reported the same dynamic. In this light, bullion is doing double duty — a hedge for some, a source of ready cash for others — and that second role explains part of the weakness without requiring any rethink of its long-term crisis credentials.
Why the Safe-Haven Trade Isn't Working
ING laid out the puzzle plainly on Friday: investors were fixated on expensive oil and what it might mean for inflation and central-bank policy. Gold therefore drew no benefit from lower US yields or from a flight to safety. The takeaway for holders is uncomfortable — geopolitical uncertainty on its own offers no dependable support right now. When higher energy costs entrench expectations of rates staying high for longer, that drag can outweigh the demand for protection.
CIBC Capital Markets, whose forecasts landed on Wednesday, still expects a recovery, just from a lower base and against less friendly monetary conditions than previously assumed. Analysts Anita Soni and Cosmos Chiu see gold at $4,500 an ounce in the fourth quarter of 2026 — above the latest close. They attribute their reduced projections to tighter policy, higher real yields and a firmer dollar. For 2027, the pair forecast an average price of $5,200; that annual figure should not be confused with the year-end target, nor read as a near-term call.
Official Buying and Indian Demand Offer a Counterweight
On the demand side, support hasn't vanished. The World Gold Council reports that China's central bank bought 23 tonnes in September, its largest monthly purchase since October 2023. That official demand offsets some of the selling pressure, though it is no guarantee of an imminent turn — the recent price action shows central-bank buying and falling quotes can coexist comfortably.
The physical picture elsewhere is mixed. Indian gold purchases and premiums both picked up, according to Reuters, while Chinese jewellery demand stayed subdued. No broad-based surge in demand is visible.
Saxo Bank identifies near-term support at $3,970 an ounce. Only a move back above $4,230, in its view, would confirm the correction is over. That framing captures the distinction investors now face: a bounce would not be a confirmed reversal. As long as speculative buyers keep reducing positions and others need liquidity, physical demand is squaring off against substantial selling pressure. Whether inflation and rate worries keep the upper hand is the question that decides what comes next.

articles.title: Federal Reserve to announce its latest interest rate move this week. Here's what economists expect. - CBS News
articles.summary: Federal Reserve to announce its latest interest rate move this week. Here's what economists expect.  CBS NewsWhy the Fed Is Expected to Hold Rates Steady Despite a Case for Raising Them  WSJWhy the Fed may hold off on another rate hike despite high inflation  USA TodayFederal Reserve is likely to hold interest rates steady in October. Here's what that means for consumers  CNBCWarsh Tells Traders to Watch the Data. They Still Follow the Fed  Bloom...
articles.full_text:
The Federal Reserve is scheduled to meet this week, when U.S. central bankers will decide whether to raise interest rates for the second time this year in a bid to subdue inflation.
Most economists and Wall Street analysts expect the Fed to leave its benchmark rate unchanged at 3.75% to 4% when officials release the latest policy statement on Wednesday.
Consumer prices have surged this year, with headline inflation across the U.S. rising at a in September as energy costs jumped. Core inflation, which excludes volatile energy and gas categories, rose 2.6% from a year ago amid signs inflation could be seeping into the broader economy. The Fed targets annual inflation of 2%.
Gasoline prices, which have hovered above $4 a gallon for the last three months, accounted for more than half the September increase in consumer prices, according to the Labor Department.
"Although the latest hot inflation readings and rise in inflation expectations will concern Fed officials, they still appear broadly intent on tightening policy at a measured pace," Thomas Ryan, senior North America economist at investor advisory firm Capital Economics, said in a recent research note.
In September, the Fed raised — what banks charge each other for overnight loans — by a quarter of a percentage point — its first hike in three years, thereby raising borrowing costs across the U.S. economy. The Fed is scheduled to announce its latest interest rate decision at 2 p.m. ET on Wednesday.
The meeting comes at a crucial time, as Americans head to the polls to cast their ballots in the midterm elections on Nov. 3. Many Americans have expressed frustration with the state of the economy as they contend with of gas, food, and other expenses.
Most economists and investors expect the Fed to raise rates one more time before year-end, likely at its last meeting of the year on Dec. 8-9.
According to CME Group's Fed Watch tool, which uses 30-day Fed funds futures prices to predict rate decisions, traders see an 88% probability that the Fed will hold rates steady in October and a 71% probability the Fed will raise rates in December (no meeting scheduled for November).
In quarterly projections last month, the Fed signaled that its rate-setting committee expected to raise rates later this year. At the same time, some Fed policymakers have signaled that the central bank is in no rush to lift borrowing costs.
"With the policy action we took at our September meeting, there is no need for urgency, and we have time to gather more information," New York Fed President John Williams said in a speech at the University at Buffalo following the Fed's rate hike in September.
Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh will give a press conference after this week's rate decision. Until then, investors are unlikely to get any clues from Warsh, who has argued against sharing forward guidance on rate decisions.

articles.title: Fed predictions for 2026: Will another rate hike happen by the end of the year? - Yahoo Finance
articles.summary: Fed predictions for 2026: Will another rate hike happen by the end of the year?  Yahoo Finance
articles.full_text:
At the beginning of 2026, the biggest question surrounding the Federal Reserve and interest rates was whether the Fed would cut its target rate at some point this year. However, it's become increasingly clear that a rate cut won't happen any time soon. In fact, the Fed raised its target rate for the first time in over three years in September, and it's possible that another rate hike will happen before the year is over.
Following the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC)'s most recent meeting in September, under the leadership of new Fed Chair Kevin Warsh, the committee announced its decision to raise the target range for the federal funds rate to 3.75%-4%.
In its statement, the committee noted that "Inflation remains elevated. Today's policy action will support a timelier return to the Committee's 2 percent goal."
With two more Fed meetings on the calendar for the remainder of 2026, consumers are wondering how potential rate changes could impact their bottom lines.
Here's what the experts have to say, and what you should do to prepare in the meantime.
Read more: How a Fed rate cut affects your bank accounts, loans, credit cards, and investments
What is the federal funds rate, and why does it matter?
The federal funds rate is the interest rate at which depository institutions charge each other for ultra-short-term loans, usually overnight. It's expressed as a range, and financial institutions negotiate a specific rate within that range.
The federal funds rate plays a key role in the Federal Reserve's management of inflation. When inflation is too high, the Fed typically raises its rate to reduce consumer spending and slow economic activity. Conversely, the Fed may lower its rate to stimulate economic activity and growth.
The federal funds rate doesn't directly affect the rates offered by individual banks, but it does have an influence. When the Fed's target rate increases or decreases, rates for high-yield savings accounts, certificates of deposit (CDs), money market accounts, credit cards, home loans, and other banking products generally follow suit.
That means when the Fed's rate is high, it can be a good time to deposit money in a bank account and earn more interest. When it's low, it's a good time to borrow money or refinance at a lower interest rate.
Read more: How do banks set their savings account interest rates?
How the federal funds rate has changed over time
After inflation peaked in June 2022, the Fed implemented a series of rate hikes in an effort to tame rising costs. By July 2023, the federal funds rate reached a target range of 5.25%-5.5% — the highest it had been since 2006.
The Fed then held rates steady until September 2024, at which point it made a 50-basis-point cut. The federal funds rate was reduced by another 25 bps in November, and again in December.
Three more cuts occurred in 2025 — in September, October, and December — dropping 25 bps each time. And after holding rates steady through most of 2026, it implemented a 25 basis point rate hike in September. Currently, the Fed's target range is 3.75%-4%.
Read more: A look at the federal funds rate over the past 50 years
Fed predictions for 2026
The Fed's job is to carefully monitor the economy and maintain stability. During each meeting, it may adjust the federal funds rate and overall monetary policy based on what the economy needs to continue running smoothly. However, it doesn't necessarily announce its plans ahead of time.
Economic experts monitor the economy's health closely and formulate their own ideas about the Fed's next move based on the data they have available.
For example, the Fed's latest dot plot indicated that a second rate hike is expected in 2026. However, CME's FedWatch tool predicts less than a 10% chance of a rate hike following the conclusion of this week's Fed meeting.
"Interest rate markets currently expect one or two rate increases," said Gary Pzegeo, CFA and chief investment officer at CIBC Private Wealth, a fee-based financial advisor firm headquartered in Chicago. "Energy prices cooled in June, but the escalation of hostilities in the Middle East have led to an increase in global crude oil prices and retail gasoline prices at home."
Pzegeo added, "it is difficult to predict how geopolitical events will play out, but the current trend would suggest the Fed will follow through with a rate hike to cool demand and offset the reduction in energy supply." He noted that if the Fed does raise rates, consumers should expect the cost of borrowing money to increase.
Read more: Jobs, inflation, and the Fed: How they're all related
Money moves you can make ahead of a potential rate increase
If the Fed raises interest rates, borrowing becomes more expensive while returns on deposit accounts often improve. Although no one can predict the Fed's next move with certainty, there are several steps you can take to protect — and even improve — your finances in anticipation of a rate increase.
- Pay down high-interest debt. Variable-rate debt, such as credit cards and lines of credit, often becomes more expensive following Fed rate hikes. Focus on paying down these balances now so your interest costs don't increase if the Fed raises rates.
- Refinance or lock in fixed rates if you plan to borrow. If you're considering a mortgage, auto loan, or personal loan, securing a fixed interest rate before borrowing costs rise can help you save money over the life of the loan.
- Boost your emergency fund. A larger cash cushion can help you avoid relying on high-interest credit cards if borrowing becomes more expensive during a period of higher rates.
- Shop around for better savings rates. Banks often increase yields on high-yield savings accounts, money market accounts, and CDs when the Fed increases its rate. So, it pays to shop around and ensure you're still earning the most competitive rate on your savings.
- Build a CD ladder. If you expect rates to continue rising, a CD ladder lets you take advantage of future rate increases while still earning competitive yields today.

articles.title: What is the FOMC blackout period and why do central banks have one - investingLive
articles.summary: What is the FOMC blackout period and why do central banks have one  investingLive
articles.full_text:
Summary
- Central banks impose blackout periods to prevent policymakers from influencing market expectations through public comments ahead of monetary policy decisions. During these periods, traders rely more on economic data and other market developments to assess the outlook for interest rates. The Fed, ECB, BoE and BoC all have similar communication restrictions, although the rules and timing vary.
Central banks influence financial markets through both interest rate decisions and communication. Speeches and interviews can change expectations for future monetary policy, affecting bonds, currencies, equities and so on. To limit these signals immediately before policy decisions, many central banks have a blackout period.
A blackout period is a predefined period during which policymakers are restricted from publicly discussing monetary policy or the upcoming decision. The rules vary across central banks, but the purpose is to ensure that official announcements remain the primary source of information about the committee's decision.
The Federal Reserve's FOMC blackout period begins at midnight eastern time on the second Saturday before a scheduled meeting and ends at 11:59 p.m. on the day after the meeting.
Other central banks follow similar practices. The ECB observes a quiet period beginning seven days before a monetary policy meeting. The Bank of England restricts Monetary Policy Committee members' communications for 8-9 days before the official rate announcement. The Bank of Canada restricts communications on monetary policy and the economic outlook during the week before the rate decision.
Before the blackout, policymakers' speeches can provide clues about their views on inflation, growth and upcoming interest rate decisions. For example, high ranking officials can correct a mispricing in the markets by signalling the most likely outcome of an upcoming meeting to avoid surprises that generally lead to high volatility.
However, the blackout period does not prevent markets from pricing in a different outcome. An unexpectedly hot inflation report or employment release can still significantly change interest rate expectations. For example, the higher than expected inflation expectations in the University of Michigan survey released during the blackout period, infamously led the Fed to hike by 75 bps in June 2022.
After the blackout ends, policymakers can resume public commentary. Their speeches may provide further insight into the decision and the outlook for future policy. The policy announcement, accompanying statement and press conference remain the main sources of information. Subsequent speeches can help clarify the committee's reaction to new economic developments.

articles.full_text:
Stock futures were little changed on Monday night following a winning session on Wall Street, with traders looking ahead to a slew of corporate earnings while the Federal Reserve gets set to begin its two-day policy meeting.
Dow Jones Industrial Average futures slipped 8 points, or less than 0.1%, while S&P 500 futures were marginally lower. Nasdaq-100 futures added 0.1%.
In Asia, Japan’s Nikkei 225 rose 1.7% while the Topix gained 0.4%. South Korea’s Kospi advanced 3.8% and the tech-focused, small-cap Kosdaq gained 2.9%. Australia’s benchmark S&P/ASX 200 was 0.32% lower.
Wall Street kicked off the week on a solid note. The Dow climbed 146.42 points, or 0.3%. The S&P 500 gained 0.7%, while the Nasdaq Composite advanced 0.8% as tech shares outperformed. The artificial intelligence trade got a boost after Anthropic filed to go public at the Nasdaq. This would mark another major tech IPO for 2026, following SpaceX’s blockbuster listing in June.
Tesla shares advanced more than 5%, while Nvidia climbed 2%. Microsoft and Amazon also rose on the day.
Those gains come as the artificial intelligence trade has faced pressure from investors worried companies in the space are borrowing too much cash to fund their AI build-outs.
On Tuesday, traders will pore through a deluge of third-quarter earnings reports. Coca-Cola, Robinhood and Boeing are among the companies set to post results. Tech giants Microsoft, Alphabet and Amazon are due out later in the week.
The Fed is also set to kick off its latest monetary policy meeting. While the central bank is expected to keep rates unchanged, traders will look for clues on whether another rate hike will take place before year-end.
“If, as expected, there is no change in rates, it will still be interesting to see what the vote is after the swings in the last two meetings,” wrote Thomas Block, Washington policy strategist at Fundstrat. “While the Fed views itself above partisan politics, it would be unlikely that the Fed would move rates a week before a national election.”
On the economic front, traders will be watching for durable orders, consumer confidence data and the new home sales report.

articles.title: Fed Cuts Rates While ECB Holds Steady: Analyzing J. Safra Sarasin's Insights Amid Labor Risks - elciudadano.com
articles.summary: Fed Cuts Rates While ECB Holds Steady: Analyzing J. Safra Sarasin's Insights Amid Labor Risks  elciudadano.com
articles.full_text:
Original article: La Fed recorta y el BCE se queda quieto: la prudencia que anticipó J. Safra Sarasin choca con el riesgo laboral
The Swiss bank deemed it unnecessary to rush changes in October, anticipating a pause from the ECB; little did they realize, the Fed cut rates while the ECB remained steady: the caution predicted by J. Safra Sarasin collides with labor risks as financial system adjustments continue while supply chain demand and supply remain influenced.
By Bruno Sommer
Central banks from the two largest advanced economies concluded the week with contrasting messages. The Federal Reserve trimmed interest rates by 25 basis points to a range of 3.75%–4.00%, while the European Central Bank kept all three of its benchmark rates unchanged for the third consecutive meeting. This U.S. decision stood in contrast to the cautious approach suggested by Karsten Junius, Chief Economist and Director of Economic Research at Bank J. Safra Sarasin, who believed neither central bank needed to hasten rate increases in October.
In a report leading up to the meetings, Junius argued that although inflation risks persisted, both the Fed and the ECB needed to weigh inflationary pressures stemming from energy prices and the impact of tightening financial conditions. According to him, this balance advised patience: the ECB would maintain rates, and the Fed could afford to wait. The Swiss bank even considered that the next move by the Fed could be an increase in December, targeting a terminal rate between 4.75%–5.00%.
However, the reality told a different story. The Fed implemented its second consecutive rate cut, justifying the decision by stating that while inflation «remains high,» downside risks to employment had increased. Unemployment was at 4.3%, and job growth had nearly stalled. The move was not unanimous: two members opposed it, one advocating for a 50 basis point cut and another in favor of maintaining rates. The U.S. CPI stood at 3.0% year-on-year, both overall and in the core reading, with gasoline prices rising 4.1% and energy index climbing 1.5%.
In contrast, the ECB adhered to the scenario anticipated by Junius. Keeping rates steady was consistent with an inflation rate in the Eurozone that dropped to 2.1% in October, near the target of 2%, influenced by a 1.0% decrease in energy prices. Additionally, spontaneous tightening of financial conditions in the Eurozone, due to fiscal concerns in France, raised sovereign debt yields and widened spreads for peripheral countries. This context diminished the urgency for further adjustments from Frankfurt.
This divergence sends a clear signal to markets: the Fed prioritized the nascent weakness in the labor market over inflation that still exceeds its target, while the ECB could afford a pause because inflation was nearing its goal and financial conditions were already tightening. Thus, the caution foretold by J. Safra Sarasin found its best expression in Frankfurt; in Washington, labor urgency took precedence.
Analysis | When Adjustment Comes from the Financial Core, Not Supply and Demand Balance
The divergence between the Fed and the ECB raises an uncomfortable question: to what extent does economic adjustment stem from a real rebalancing between supply and demand, and to what extent from conditions imposed by the financial system’s core? When interest rates, liquidity, risk premiums, and collateral move due to policy decisions or market stress, the cost of readjustment does not necessarily fall on those generating imbalances. It hits small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), indebted households, and long-term investment projects especially hard, while those with greater market power or privileged access to financing can better withstand and even expand their relative position.
The problem intensifies when supply and demand are already distorted by political interventions, military conflicts, or supply chain disruptions that favor certain actors over others. In this context, monetary policy can combat demand inflation, but it hardly resolves supply inflation. Raising rates does not unblock a port, replace an energy source, or diversify a supply chain; often, it just redistributes the cost of adjustment and may consolidate income for those in a better position.
This is not about attributing a generalized intent to every political or business decision, but rather highlighting a design risk: if adjustment is imposed from the financial core while supply and demand remain influenced, monetary policy gains in macroeconomic discipline but loses in distributional precision. The result could be more persistent inflation, higher credit costs for the productive economy, and greater market concentration. Thus, the critical reading does not invalidate the decisions made by the Fed and the ECB, but it does condition them: without fiscal, energy, competition, and supply diversification policies, financial adjustment risks replacing real adjustment rather than accompanying it.
By Bruno Sommer

articles.title: Gold's Slide to $3,997 Puts Fed, Margin Calls and Physical Buyers in the Same Frame - ad-hoc-news.de
articles.summary: Gold's Slide to $3,997 Puts Fed, Margin Calls and Physical Buyers in the Same Frame  ad-hoc-news.de
articles.full_text:
Gold finished Friday at $3,997.48 an ounce, a weekly loss of 4.1% that says as much about forced liquidation as it does about inflation. With the Federal Reserve's October 27–28 meeting now in view, the metal is caught between rising energy costs, a jump in Treasury yields and a wave of selling tied to losses elsewhere in portfolios.
The yield move was the day's clearest pressure point. The ten-year US Treasury yield climbed 4.8 basis points to 5.001% on Friday, sharpening the appeal of interest-bearing assets and making it harder for a metal that pays no coupon to find its footing. Reuters linked the latest gold selling to higher energy prices and the expectation of a longer stretch of elevated US rates. Margin calls after losses in technology shares added a second, separate motive: investors sold gold and silver to raise cash.
That distinction matters. Selling to meet margin obligations is not the same as a fresh verdict on gold's rate outlook, and the recent session shows the metal does not automatically act as a safe haven when markets turn strained. Inflation protection and short-term price action can pull in opposite directions.
Futures data show the speculative retreat
Positioning at the COMEX tells a similar story from a different angle. CFTC figures as of Tuesday showed large speculators cutting their net long positions, while open interest initially rose 1.5%. Small speculators, by contrast, added to their net longs — so the pullback was not a uniform exit by all participants. By Friday, open interest had fallen to 400,538 contracts, down 0.2% from the prior week. That later decline may hint at an easing in the unwinding, though it falls well short of proof that a floor has formed.
Commerzbank analyst Carsten Fritsch points to gold sales used to cover equity losses and margin calls, with the selloff in technology and AI shares capable of triggering such liquidations. In that situation gold serves not only as a hedge but as a source of ready cash — which explains part of the weakness without requiring any change in its long-run crisis-protection case. For a genuine stabilization, both fresh demand and an easing of margin-related selling would be needed; the positioning data so far do not confirm that process is complete.
Forecasters split on the path back
CIBC Capital Markets cut its fourth-quarter 2026 gold forecast to $4,500 an ounce, citing real yields and a strong dollar as near-term drags, according to a Wednesday report from analysts Anita Soni and Cosmos Chiu. The reduction is not a blanket bearish call: the bank still expects higher prices the following year and sees an average of $5,200 an ounce in 2027. DZ BANK, in a forecast dated October 16, put year-end gold at around $4,300 and tied any recovery to a final US rate hike toward the end of the year, pointing to sustained central bank buying as support. Both views share a common thread — the expected rebound is a projection, not a trend already visible in prices.
Central banks and the physical market
After the Fed, the European Central Bank decides on October 29, with unchanged rates widely expected in media reports. Remarks on energy prices could carry particular weight, since gold's direction hinges on whether policymakers treat the inflation pressure as grounds for a longer stretch of tight money.
Physical demand offers a partial counterweight. In India, business picked up around the festival and wedding season, with manufacturers reporting healthy order flows and dealers restocking; scrap gold exchange added domestic supply. China saw improved demand for jewellery, bars and coins around the early-October holidays, helped by earlier price declines. Reuters reported that Indian purchases and premiums both rose, while Chinese jewellery demand stayed subdued — so a broad demand surge is not yet evident.
Saxo Bank sees near-term support at $3,970 an ounce. Only a return above $4,230 would, in its view, confirm the correction is over. Until speculative buyers stop trimming positions and the need for liquidity fades, physical buying faces a heavy tide of selling.

articles.summary: Morgan Stanley declares the U.S. stock market correction is nearing its end! It maintains its year-end S&P 500 target of 8,000 points and identifies three key catalysts for a rebound.  Moomoo
articles.full_text:
As Morgan Stanley continues to maintain a bullish outlook on equities, recent market performance has precisely demonstrated the strong momentum behind the rebound in semiconductor-led technology stocks. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index rose by 0.44% on October 23 and further increased by 2.82% on October 26.
Zhitong Finance APP has learned that Michael Wilson, Chief U.S. Equity Strategist at Morgan Stanley, emphasized in his latest research report that the firm’s current assessment is that the internal correction in the U.S. stock market, which began in June, has entered its final tail-end phase. However, indices may still undergo one last downward probe. As the pressure from AI financing costs eases, the outlook for the midterm elections becomes clearer, and the Federal Reserve’s monetary liquidity policy clarifies, the market is expected to see a significant year-end rebound.
According to top strategists at Wall Street financial giants such as Morgan Stanley, the logic for contrarian accumulation and buying on dips is forming for global AI computing power themes and broader technology stocks, which have recently suffered heavy selling pressure. However, whether technology stocks can achieve a bottoming-out rebound and sustain an upward trend thereafter will depend on a dual verification period before year-end: the earnings disclosure season and the evolution of AI financing conditions.
Just as Morgan Stanley maintains its bullish stance on the stock market, recent market performance has precisely demonstrated the tension behind the major rebound in semiconductor-led technology stocks, alongside the fragmentation and divergence in funding conditions revealed by the corporate credit bond market.
The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index rose 0.44% on October 23 and further gained 2.82% on October 26, but its closing level of 11,083.5 points remains approximately 24.27% below the closing high recorded on June 22. The Nasdaq-100 Index, known as the "bellwether for tech stocks," and the broader Nasdaq Composite Index, which includes more technology constituents, rose 1.09% and approximately 0.83% respectively on October 26. They remain about 6.25% and 5.18% below their closing highs from October 6. While a short-term strong rebound has emerged in U.S. tech stocks, the deep corrections previously accumulated in the semiconductor sector, which accounts for a significant share of tech market capitalization, are far from being fully repaired.
The credit market reveals another side of negative constraints facing the AI computing power trade theme. The yield on CoreWeave’s bonds maturing in 2031 reached 15.76% in the secondary market on October 22, indicating that investors are demanding higher risk premiums and compensation for the financing dependence and debt repayment risks associated with its AI computing infrastructure.
During intraday trading on October 26, the five-year Credit Default Swap (CDS) spread for CoreWeave (CRWV.US)—the core stock target at the heart of the "AI computing power sell-off storm" and "AI bubble burst" narratives—was approximately 1,148 basis points. Assuming a 40% recovery rate, model estimates imply a cumulative five-year default probability of approximately 62%. It is important to note that this indicator includes a credit risk premium and cannot be directly equated to the company’s actual default probability over the next five years. During the same period, the five-year CDS spreads for Meta, Alphabet, and Microsoft were approximately 121, 83, and 55 basis points, respectively, up from 98, 73, and 52 basis points on September 25. This highlights a general rise in the risk compensation required by the credit market for corporate bonds, though the pressure borne by different companies varies significantly.
The five-year CDS for Japanese investment giant SoftBank, which has nearly fully bet on AI in recent years, rose to 432 basis points on October 20, reaching a four-year high. Its three tranches of U.S. dollar bonds issued in September carried coupons of 8.625%, 9.25%, and 9.75%, respectively. These data collectively indicate that whether the surge in demand for AI computing resources can translate into revenue across the industrial chain increasingly depends on customers' ability to secure continuous funding and whether project cash returns can cover financing costs. High-rated tech giants mainly face pressures from more expensive new financing and valuation discounting, while new cloud providers relying on external capital face direct constraints from narrowing financing channels.
Morgan Stanley's Wilson outlines three core catalysts for the year-end stock market rebound
Michael Wilson of Morgan Stanley stated that the bearish and negative sentiment adjustment in the U.S. stock market, which began in June, is entering its final concluding stage. The digestion of three key uncertainties—AI-related capital issues (AIQ, AIEQ), midterm election uncertainty, and changes in Federal Reserve liquidity—is expected to help form a market bottom, laying a significant foundation for the S&P 500 Index to rebound to near-record levels of around 8,000 points by year-end.
This transition of the economic cycle to the mid-cycle phase coincides with the peaking speed of change in the breadth of earnings forecast revisions. Previously, the "rolling recessions" experienced sequentially across various industries bottomed out around last year's "Liberation Day." The cycle transition has had a significant impact on individual stocks beneath the surface of the indices. As investors shift towards large-cap stocks with higher fundamental quality, early-cycle sectors such as new cloud providers, financials, cyclical consumer themes, and automobiles have clearly underperformed.
In a report released on Monday, Wilson wrote that since the onset of this rotation, approximately 60% of the constituents of the Russell 3000 Index (IWV.US), which focuses on small- and mid-cap stocks in the U.S. equity market, have declined by more than 20%. The semiconductor sector has been hit hardest, with 96% of its stocks experiencing drawdowns exceeding 20%.
The Quality Factor (QUAL) has continued to lead during this rotation and is currently breaking out. Wilson noted that although the S&P 500 Index has shown resilience and market breadth has begun to improve, indicating that index performance and internal market conditions are "converging toward the middle" as investors gradually digest the mid-cycle rotation.
Wilson stated that the tactical downside target remains at 7,100–7,200 points, implying that the index could dip slightly below its 200-day moving average. At the time of writing, the S&P 500 Index was trading around 7,688 points, less than 2% below the historical high reached in early October.
The strategist identified three catalysts that could signal the end of the correction. First, investor concerns and panic selling related to AI capital returns, cost and availability of funding, security issues, and NIMBYism (local community opposition to nearby data center construction) are expected to come to a head over the next three to four weeks.
Second, while midterm elections typically create initial headwinds for the market, strong returns often follow in the six to twelve months after the election concludes. Historically, the S&P 500 Index has averaged a gain of approximately 17% in the twelve months following midterm elections.
Third, and most critically, Wilson believes liquidity poses the greatest risk and serves as the primary catalyst for forming the market's final bottom. Federal Reserve Chair Walsh has slowed the pace of balance sheet expansion by about half, but interest rate policy remains behind the curve given that inflation is still above target. Financial conditions have tightened significantly, reaching levels comparable to those in 2018 and approaching those seen during the active tightening period in 2022.
The Morgan Stanley Composite Sentiment Indicator is currently at neutral levels, with third-quarter earnings projected to grow by 27% year-on-year. Based on this, Wilson maintains his view that attractive buying opportunities should emerge in the coming weeks as these key uncertainties gradually resolve.
Before the S&P 500 Index can break above 8,000 points, it must clear three hurdles: whether funding can be sustained, whether the election outcome will bring clarity, and whether liquidity conditions will shift.
Based on the S&P 500 Index closing at 7,676.77 points on October 26, the 7,100–7,200 point range implies a potential downside of approximately 6.2%–7.5%, while 8,000 points represents an upside potential of about 4.2%. If the index first retreats to this support zone and then recovers to 8,000 points, the gain would amount to approximately 11.1%–12.7%. This disparity suggests that the investment opportunity identified by Wilson is highly dependent on entry positioning and whether the earnings base remains stable after risks are released.
The first hurdle is whether the market can smoothly absorb the supply of AI financing. The Morgan Stanley analyst team, led by Wilson, has long monitored capital returns, the cost and availability of funding, as well as security controversies and community opposition to data center construction. In a media podcast on October 26, he further pointed out that additional financing needs to be absorbed by the market in the coming weeks; companies with weaker credentials may continue to face widening credit spreads and declining stock prices. He also expects the semiconductor index could decline another 10%–15% by mid-November. This indicates that his bullish year-end outlook still incorporates a difficult period of risk digestion.

Financial markets face a packed schedule of economic and corporate events this week, with a Federal Reserve interest rate decision, an expected 3.6% headline PCE inflation reading, earnings from major technology companies, and approximately $11 billion in Bitcoin options set to expire on Friday. The developments could put monetary policy, corporate performance and cryptocurrency derivatives markets in focus over several consecutive trading sessions.
Coin Bureau outlined the upcoming events in a post on X, describing the week as a major period for markets. The schedule includes the Federal Reserve's next policy decision on Wednesday, following an interest rate hike last month, as well as earnings reports from Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, Coinbase and Strategy.
Federal Reserve Decision and Inflation in Focus
The Federal Reserve is scheduled to make another monetary policy decision on Wednesday, according to Coin Bureau. The decision follows a rate hike last month, making the latest policy announcement an important event for investors monitoring the direction of US monetary policy.
The decision comes one day before headline personal consumption expenditures inflation, or PCE, is expected to reach 3.6%. That forecast is nearly double the Federal Reserve's 2% inflation target.
The timing places the Fed decision and the anticipated inflation report at the center of the week's economic calendar. The expected 3.6% reading is a forecast cited in Coin Bureau's post, rather than a confirmed inflation result. The available information does not specify the size of the previous rate increase or the outcome expected from Wednesday's decision.
Microsoft, Alphabet and Amazon Report Earnings
Corporate earnings will provide another major focus. Microsoft, Alphabet and Amazon are all scheduled to report results within a 30-hour period. Coin Bureau put their combined value at more than $10 trillion, underscoring the scale of the companies reporting during the same week.
The concentration of these reports creates a busy period for investors following the technology sector. All three companies are named in Coin Bureau's schedule, with their earnings announcements expected within the same 30-hour window.
Coinbase and Strategy are also scheduled to report earnings on Thursday. Their inclusion adds two companies closely associated with the cryptocurrency industry to a week already dominated by the Federal Reserve, inflation expectations and major technology earnings.
Bitcoin Options Worth $11 Billion Expire Friday
Cryptocurrency markets face another scheduled event on Friday, when approximately $11 billion in Bitcoin options are set to expire, according to Coin Bureau.
Options are derivatives contracts that give holders the right, but not the obligation, to buy or sell an underlying asset under specified terms. An expiration event involving a large notional value can draw attention from traders monitoring positioning in the Bitcoin derivatives market. However, the reported $11 billion figure alone does not establish whether the expiration will produce a particular price movement.
The Bitcoin options expiry follows Thursday's earnings reports from Coinbase and Strategy, placing several cryptocurrency-related events within the same weekly schedule.
Tuesday, October 27: Consumer Confidence, Israel's Election and Robinhood Earnings
The week's listed events begin on Tuesday, October 27, with a consumer confidence release scheduled for 10 a.m. Eastern Time. Coin Bureau also identified Israel's election and earnings from Robinhood Markets, whose stock ticker is HOOD, as events to watch that day.
Together, the scheduled events span economic data, political developments, corporate earnings and cryptocurrency derivatives. The Federal Reserve decision on Wednesday, the expected 3.6% headline PCE inflation reading, the technology earnings reports within 30 hours, Thursday's Coinbase and Strategy results, and Friday's approximately $11 billion Bitcoin options expiry form the central elements of the calendar outlined by Coin Bureau.

articles.full_text:
The Morning Bull - Australian Market Morning Update Monday, 26 Oct 2026
Australian shares are set for a cautious open, with sentiment anchored to stubborn US inflation expectations rather than local headlines. The tone leans guarded rather than bullish as investors weigh what that means for global interest rates.
The University of Michigan year ahead inflation outlook sits at 4.7% for October, well above typical central bank targets. Solid US services PMI readings point to ongoing demand. Taken together, those figures suggest that US policy makers may have limited room to ease settings quickly.
When inflation expectations hold near 5%, investors usually assume policy rates may need to stay restrictive for longer. That keeps global borrowing costs elevated, which can pressure equity valuations and complicate earnings planning for highly geared Australian businesses.
The key issue is whether upcoming US data on growth and spending confirms this sticky inflation picture or shows any cooling. If inflation readings soften, the current rate path narrative weakens. If they do not, equity risk premiums may need to adjust higher.
Stocks to Watch Before the Opening Bell
Ingenia Communities Group (INA)

articles.title: Stock Market Today: S&P 500, DJI Rise as Nvidia Rebounds, AI Debt Fears Persist Ahead of Fed Decision - Coinpaper
articles.summary: Stock Market Today: S&P 500, DJI Rise as Nvidia Rebounds, AI Debt Fears Persist Ahead of Fed Decision  Coinpaper
articles.full_text:
Key takeaways
- S&P 500 and Dow futures rise after Friday's losses
- Nvidia rebounds while AI infrastructure financing worries continue mounting
- Federal Reserve decision and Big Tech earnings dominate expectations
U.S. stock futures climbed Monday, October 26, as Nvidia and other semiconductor stocks rebounded from last week's selloff, although concerns about artificial intelligence financing continued to weigh on parts of the technology sector.
At 9:05 a.m. ET, Dow Jones Industrial Average (DJI) futures gained 0.4%, S&P 500 futures advanced 0.34%, and Nasdaq 100 futures rose 0.6%, according to Reuters. Nvidia, AMD and Intel each gained more than 1% in premarket trading.
The recovery followed Friday's losses, when the Dow dropped roughly 653 points, the S&P 500 declined 0.52%, and the Nasdaq Composite slipped 0.21%. Investors are now weighing renewed semiconductor demand against the AI financing concerns that have recently shaken technology stocks.
Nvidia Stock Rebounds, but AI Debt Concerns Remain
Nvidia recovered after a difficult stretch for semiconductor shares. The chipmaker traded near $213.40 shortly after Monday's opening bell, approximately 1.2% above Friday's $210.96 closing price.
The rebound follows a semiconductor selloff that erased approximately $2 trillion in market value over eight trading sessions. Investors have increasingly questioned whether the enormous infrastructure investments supporting AI demand can generate sufficient returns.
However, the pressure is particularly severe among companies financing expansion through borrowing.
Nvidia-backed CoreWeave fell approximately 3% in premarket trading, while Nebius and other AI infrastructure providers also faced selling pressure. CoreWeave and Nebius have each lost more than 30% of their market value this month.
The divergence highlights a financial distinction. Nvidia earns revenue selling processors, while infrastructure operators must fund expensive facilities and equipment before recovering their investment through customer contracts.
That vulnerability has become more visible as CoreWeave's borrowing costs rise and investors examine whether expected future revenue can support existing debt.
Fed Decision and Big Tech Earnings Could Determine Market Direction
The Federal Reserve's official calendar confirms that policymakers meet October 27-28, with an interest-rate decision scheduled Wednesday.
Markets largely expect the Fed to maintain its current 3.75%-4.00% target range. However, persistent inflation and elevated energy prices have kept the possibility of additional tightening later this year in focus.
Brent crude declined toward $110 per barrel Monday, providing some relief after oil's recent surge. Nevertheless, the earlier combination of rising Treasury yields and expensive energy has already challenged stock valuations.
Meanwhile, Alphabet and Microsoft are scheduled to report Wednesday, followed by Amazon on Thursday. Their results could reveal whether the massive AI spending boom is translating into sustainable revenue and profits.

articles.title: ECB Meeting: Five key questions on rates, inflation and Lagarde's exit - The Economic Times
articles.summary: ECB Meeting: Five key questions on rates, inflation and Lagarde's exit  The Economic Times
articles.full_text:
The ECB faces a challenging policy environment, with oil prices remaining above $100 a barrel and inflation risks elevated even as tighter financial conditions threaten to weigh on economic growth. Political instability in France and rising government borrowing costs have added to uncertainty surrounding the euro zone economy, the report stated.
Also Read |Global Market: China's yuan hits four-year high as dollar weakens ahead of policy meetings
ECB expected to keep rates unchanged
Economists polled by Reuters expect the central bank to raise rates by 25 basis points in December, reflecting concerns that inflation could remain elevated if energy costs continue to rise.
Eurozone inflation reached 3.8% in September, well above the ECB's 2% target. At the same time, rising government bond yields are tightening financial conditions and could constrain economic activity, complicating the central bank's efforts to balance price stability with growth.
Also Read |Global Market: South Korean shares fall over 1% as AI trade concerns weigh; won strengthens
Energy prices keep inflation risks elevated
The ECB is likely to remain alert to the possibility that higher energy costs could spread to other goods and services, eventually pushing up wages and broader inflation.
However, recent inflation data suggest that these second-round effects remain relatively contained. Core inflation, which excludes food and energy, edged up to 2.5% in September from 2.4% previously, indicating that higher energy costs have yet to trigger a more widespread acceleration in prices.
The report stated that comments from ECB officials, including Chief Economist Philip Lane, suggest policymakers are not yet overly concerned about an energy-driven inflation spiral.
Nevertheless, oil prices have risen sharply this year, while a survey released on Friday showed that euro zone consumers increased their inflation expectations for the next 12 months in September.
Markets are pricing in at least two additional rate increases by mid-2027. Further escalation of the Iran war or renewed pressure on energy prices could strengthen the case for additional tightening, even next year.
French bond selloff adds to ECB's challenges
The deterioration in France's public finances and political stability presents another challenge for the ECB as it prepares for its policy meeting.
French 10-year government bond yields have climbed above 5%, reaching their highest levels in 24 years, while political tensions and protests have complicated the government's efforts to address the country's fragile fiscal position.
The premium investors demand to hold French 10-year bonds over German government debt has widened to 167 basis points, compared with 92 basis points at the ECB's previous meeting.
The widening spread reflects growing investor concerns about France's fiscal outlook and the risk that political uncertainty could undermine efforts to control public debt.
However, the ECB is not expected to intervene immediately through its Transmission Protection Instrument (TPI), which allows it to purchase government bonds to counter unwarranted and disorderly tightening in financing conditions across euro zone member states.
ECB President Christine Lagarde has argued that France must address its debt problems through fiscal consolidation.
The central bank could, however, reconsider the pace of monetary tightening if financial instability in France threatens to significantly weaken economic growth. The report by Reuters stated that the ECB could also use its bond-buying mechanism to prevent a French crisis from spreading to other euro zone economies with stronger public finances, according to the report.
Lagarde's succession emerges as another focus
Investors are also likely to watch for developments concerning Lagarde's future and the succession process at the ECB.
Lagarde could be appointed as the next chair of the World Economic Forum as early as November, potentially bringing forward discussions about who might succeed her as ECB president.
Former central bank governors Klaas Knot of the Netherlands and Pablo Hernandez de Cos of Spain are considered leading candidates for the position.
Her departure would come amid broader changes to the ECB's leadership. The resignation of Executive Board member Isabel Schnabel has opened another vacancy, while Chief Economist Philip Lane is scheduled to step down in May.
Lagarde's current term is due to end in October next year. An earlier departure could allow European leaders to appoint a successor before France's spring presidential election, reducing the risk that domestic political developments could complicate the selection process.
A possible snap election in Spain could also influence the political dynamics surrounding the appointment.
Policy uncertainty likely to persist
The ECB's October meeting comes at a time when policymakers must navigate competing risks from persistent inflation, higher borrowing costs, geopolitical uncertainty and political instability in a major euro zone economy.
Although a pause in interest rates is widely anticipated, investors will scrutinise the central bank's assessment of energy prices, underlying inflation and financial conditions for clues about its next move.
The immediate decision may be straightforward, but the outlook for monetary policy remains uncertain, with the trajectory of the Iran war, oil prices and France's fiscal situation likely to shape the ECB's decisions in the coming months, according to the report.

articles.full_text:
U.S. Treasury yields were flat on the day Monday as investors looked ahead to the central bank’s interest rate decision and a flurry of economic data this week.
The benchmark 10-year Treasury yield was little changed at 4.986%, and the 30-year Treasury bond yield dipped nearly 2 basis points at 5.299%. The 2-year Treasury note yield rose 3 basis points higher to 4.716%.
One basis point is equal to 0.01%, and yields and prices move in opposite directions.
Investors are keenly anticipating the main event of the week, which will be the Federal Reserve’s interest rate decision on Wednesday. Traders are pricing in an over 90% chance that policymakers will hold interest rates steady at the current target range of 3.75% to 4%, per the CME FedWatch Tool.
Deutsche Bank analysts said they expect there to be more interest in Chairman Kevin Warsh’s comments following the decision, with focus on how the Fed “balances still-elevated inflation and solid growth against the recent tightening in financial conditions.”
“The broader message is still likely to be hawkish: our economists think recent inflation data support the case for further tightening over time, even if the Fed chooses to pause this week,” the analysts said in a Monday note.
They added that Warsh is expected to clarify that tight financial conditions are not a substitute for higher policy rates.
Investors will also closely monitor the personal consumption expenditures index, the Fed’s preferred inflation gauge, which will be released on Thursday.

articles.title: Federal Reserve, ECB and Bank of Japan Set for Back-to-Back Meetings This Week; All Three Seen Holding Rates - BigGo Finance
articles.summary: Federal Reserve, ECB and Bank of Japan Set for Back-to-Back Meetings This Week; All Three Seen Holding Rates  BigGo Finance
articles.full_text:
"Super Central Bank Week" Kicks Off: US, Europe and Japan Seen Holding Rates in Sync, December Hike Question in Focus
Global financial markets face a dense window of rate decisions this week. The Federal Reserve, the European Central Bank and the Bank of Japan will announce policy decisions in succession from October 28 to 30, with the Bank of Canada and the Reserve Bank of New Zealand also holding policy meetings in the same period. Markets broadly expect all three major central banks to hold off on rate hikes this time, but the hints in their post-meeting statements about the future policy path may carry more market influence than the rate decisions themselves.
With the Iran war pushing up energy prices and artificial intelligence-related investment supporting demand, global inflationary pressure has yet to dissipate, and the constraints facing each economy differ: the United States is focused on inflation resilience and the job market, Europe is hamstrung by turmoil in the French bond market, and Japan must weigh yen depreciation against the pace of monetary policy normalization.
Federal Reserve: Hold odds above 90%, December hike possible
The Fed will wrap up its two-day Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting on October 28 local time. In September the central bank raised the target range for the federal funds rate by 25 basis points to 3.75%-4.00%, its first hike since 2023. Market pricing shows the probability of keeping rates unchanged at this meeting has exceeded 90%.
The cooling of expectations is directly tied to cautious remarks by Fed Chair Kevin Warsh. Speaking on the sidelines of the International Monetary Fund and World Bank annual meetings on October 16, Warsh said the Fed is committed to price stability but will not prejudge policy decisions at future meetings. Derek Tang, an economist at Monetary Policy Analytics, said the remarks did not provide information sufficient to reinforce hawkish expectations.
Still, most institutions have not ruled out a December hike. A mid-October Reuters poll of 100 economists showed 94 expect a hold in October, but all respondents expect one more hike in December. Michael Pearce, chief US economist at Oxford Economics, noted the Fed may still need to keep raising rates in the near term, but recent comments from some officials suggest no rush to act at the October meeting.
David Mericle, chief US economist at Goldman Sachs, believes the Fed's recent policy signals are closer to a rhythm of "hiking every other meeting," making December the next key window. Anna Wong, chief US economist at Bloomberg Economics, said previous hikes need time to transmit to the real economy, and that financial conditions could tighten abruptly if AI-related assets correct.
Some warn that tightening could exceed expectations. According to Reuters, Alex Pelle, senior US economist at Mizuho Securities, believes holding in October would be a policy misjudgment and that the risk of a 50-basis-point hike in December outweighs that of 25 basis points. Michael Gapen, chief US economist at Morgan Stanley, also flagged that the Fed may need to tighten more than expected.
US third-quarter gross domestic product and the September personal consumption expenditures price index are due soon and will also shape market views on the path ahead.
European Central Bank: French bond market steals the show, hike option pushed to December
The ECB will announce its decision on October 29, with markets expecting it to keep its deposit facility rate at 2.50%. In September the central bank had just raised rates by 25 basis points, citing the Middle East conflict's push to inflation.
Eurozone inflation rose to 3.8% in September from 3.3% in August, a three-year high; core inflation, excluding energy and food, edged up to 2.5% from 2.4%. Energy prices were the main driver, but limited movement in core inflation leaves the ECB without a pressing need to act immediately.
More closely watched is the French government bond market. According to Agence France-Presse, political confrontation over next year's budget and concerns about fiscal sustainability pushed French government bond yields last week to their highest level since 2002. Markets are therefore debating whether the ECB will activate its Transmission Protection Instrument (TPI) — a mechanism that allows the central bank to buy a member state's bonds when yields show abnormal swings that impair monetary policy transmission.
But most analysts see a low probability of actual use. Andrew Kenningham, chief Europe economist at Capital Economics, said the France-Germany spread would need to widen substantially further for ECB intervention to be justified, and "this meeting will not produce a rescue measure for France." Carsten Brzeski, global head of macro at ING, noted that France's fiscal crisis actually reduces the likelihood of further ECB hikes, saying "the bond market is doing part of the ECB's tightening work for it."
Brzeski estimates that the rise in German government bond yields since September has an impact on growth and inflation roughly equivalent to a 25-basis-point hike, with the French effect closer to 50 basis points.
The focus of this meeting therefore lies more in how President Christine Lagarde assesses the persistence of energy prices and the hit to economic activity from rising financing costs. Lagarde stressed earlier this month that on the French government bond yield issue, "the first-best solution is in France, and it is fiscal policy." If inflationary pressure persists, a December hike could still return to the policy options.
Bank of Japan: Inflation forecasts may be revised up, December hike expectations build
The BOJ will announce its decision on October 30 and release its quarterly economic and price outlook report at the same time. In September the central bank raised its policy rate by 25 basis points to 1.25%, and markets broadly expect a hold this time.
Reuters, citing four people familiar with internal BOJ discussions, reported the central bank may slightly raise its core inflation forecast for fiscal 2027 to reflect prolonged price pressure from higher oil prices. The people also said the central bank does not see a need to act again immediately after the September hike.
BOJ Governor Kazuo Ueda said on October 16 that underlying inflation is near the 2% target and the central bank cannot tolerate prices rising at a steeper pace, with the policy goal having shifted to stabilizing inflation around 2%. The remarks are seen as a landmark turn in the policy focus from "stimulating inflation" to "anchoring inflation."
Naomi Muguruma, chief bond strategist at Mitsubishi UFJ Morgan Stanley Securities, said: "This is a historic moment for the BOJ, but now it has to press not just the accelerator but also the brake, which makes the task more challenging." She expects the central bank to decide whether to hike in December or January based on subsequent data and market moves.
A Reuters poll shows analysts expect the BOJ to raise rates to 1.50% in December and maintain a quarterly hiking pace. The current 1.25% policy rate has entered the 1.1%-2.5% neutral rate range estimated by central bank staff, and markets are focused on where the hiking cycle will end. The people said that with bank lending growth still strong, the central bank may stress at this meeting that financial conditions remain accommodative, leaving room for further hikes before rates approach neutral.
The yen exchange rate is another variable. If the yen weakens markedly again and pushes up import costs, inflationary pressure could accumulate further, reinforcing the case for a hike.
Market impact: Decisions secondary, forward guidance the star
For investors, a synchronized pause by the three central banks this week is already priced in, and the real trading clues come from differences in the wording of their statements. The direction of US Treasuries and the dollar depends on whether rates rise in December and whether that marks the end of the cycle; European asset prices are closely tied to France's fiscal situation and whether the ECB uses the TPI; and the yen and Japanese government bond yields are highly sensitive to the BOJ's upgraded inflation forecasts and Ueda's language.
Notably, the three central banks face the same external shock — energy costs driven up by the Iran war — yet have produced different policy responses. That divergence means volatility in global bond and currency markets could rise markedly after the decisions are announced, even with rates on hold.

articles.title: Indian Stock Markets Under Pressure as Oil Prices and Fed Decision Weigh on Investors - Bold News
articles.summary: Indian Stock Markets Under Pressure as Oil Prices and Fed Decision Weigh on Investors  Bold News
articles.full_text:
Rising crude costs, Middle East tensions and uncertainty over US monetary policy put Indian equities under pressure, while corporate earnings and foreign investment flows remain key market drivers.
MUMBAI, October 26: Indian equity markets faced renewed selling pressure on Monday as elevated crude oil prices, geopolitical tensions in the Middle East and uncertainty over the US Federal Reserve’s upcoming policy decision weighed on investor confidence.
The benchmark Nifty 50 declined 0.5 per cent to 22,485.65, while the BSE Sensex fell 0.46 per cent to 72,783.15, according to Reuters. Twelve of the 16 major sectoral indices recorded losses, reflecting the broad impact of concerns surrounding energy supplies, inflation and the global economic outlook.
Small-cap stocks declined 0.7 per cent, while the mid-cap index slipped 0.4 per cent. Information technology shares also remained under pressure, with the sector losing 1.1 per cent as investors assessed corporate earnings and the outlook for demand in overseas markets.
Infosys fell around 2 per cent after lowering its annual revenue growth forecast amid weakness in North America. The development added to concerns about the outlook for Indian technology companies, which depend significantly on international clients for a substantial portion of their business.
Other individual stocks moved in different directions. Shriram Finance declined 5 per cent after reducing its loan-growth forecast, while Kotak Mahindra Bank gained 2.3 per cent. Dr Reddy’s Laboratories advanced 3 per cent following stronger-than-expected quarterly profits.
The mixed performance highlighted how company-specific earnings developments continued to influence share prices even as broader market sentiment remained cautious.
Crude Oil Remains a Major Concern
Oil prices have become a central concern for investors because of escalating tensions involving Saudi Arabia and Yemen-based Houthi militants. Attacks on Saudi territory and energy infrastructure have raised fears of further disruption to supplies from a region that plays a crucial role in international energy markets.
Brent crude was trading around $114.50 per barrel on Monday, after retreating from a level near $117 reached amid growing supply concerns. The price remained elevated despite the decline, leaving energy-importing economies exposed to higher costs.
Oil prices had risen sharply towards the end of the previous week following attacks attributed to the Houthis. Saudi authorities reported intercepting additional missiles and drones, while the country’s main airport partially resumed operations after damage from earlier attacks.
The security situation has also raised concerns about maritime transportation through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a strategic passage connecting the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden. Disruption around this route could affect the movement of oil and other commodities, increasing shipping costs and complicating international trade.
For India, higher crude prices can create pressure on the import bill, the rupee and domestic inflation. The country purchases a substantial proportion of its crude oil requirements from overseas markets, making its economy sensitive to sustained increases in international energy prices.
More expensive oil can also affect transportation, manufacturing, aviation, logistics and other fuel-intensive industries. Companies may face higher operating costs, while consumers could experience additional pressure on household budgets if increased costs are passed on through prices.
Federal Reserve Decision in Focus
Investors are also preparing for the US Federal Reserve’s policy announcement scheduled for Wednesday, October 28.
Market expectations point towards the central bank keeping interest rates unchanged at its forthcoming meeting. However, investors will closely examine policymakers’ comments for clues about whether additional tightening could be considered later in the year.
The inflation outlook has become more complicated because of rising energy prices and continued uncertainty over the impact of international conflicts on supply chains. If inflation remains elevated, the Federal Reserve could find it difficult to ease monetary conditions.
Interest-rate decisions in the United States can influence international investment flows. Higher US yields can make American assets more attractive to global investors, potentially reducing demand for emerging-market equities and currencies.
For India, any strengthening of the US dollar could add pressure to the rupee and increase the cost of imports. A weaker currency may also complicate the outlook for businesses that rely on imported raw materials, machinery or energy.
Investors are therefore monitoring both the Fed’s immediate decision and its assessment of inflation, employment and economic growth.
Foreign Investment Flows Remain Important
Foreign portfolio investors have been another source of pressure on Indian equities. Data reported on Monday showed that overseas investors had withdrawn approximately Rs 48,056 crore from Indian equities during October up to that point.
The selling has reflected a combination of international and domestic concerns, including expensive crude oil, geopolitical uncertainty, inflation risks and questions surrounding corporate earnings.
Although foreign investor selling eased during the week ending October 23, with overseas investors turning net buyers on two trading days, the broader monthly outflow remained substantial.
Foreign portfolio investment can influence market liquidity, share valuations and currency movements. When overseas investors sell Indian shares and transfer funds abroad, the resulting demand for foreign currency can add to pressure on the rupee.
However, short-term investment flows can change direction as valuations, earnings expectations and global risk appetite evolve. Investors will therefore look for signs of sustained buying rather than interpreting a few sessions of improved activity as a definitive change in trend.
Domestic institutional investors and retail participants also remain important to the market’s performance, helping determine how much foreign selling translates into declines in benchmark indices.
Corporate Earnings Could Determine Stock Performance
The ongoing quarterly earnings season is providing another important test for the market.
Investors are assessing whether companies can maintain revenue growth and profitability despite higher input costs, uncertain overseas demand and changes in borrowing conditions.
The reduction in Infosys’ annual revenue growth forecast illustrates the importance of management guidance alongside reported profits. For technology businesses, demand from North American clients, discretionary spending by customers and the pace of new contracts can influence expectations for future growth.
Financial companies are being assessed on lending activity, asset quality, margins and credit demand. Shriram Finance’s lower loan-growth forecast has drawn attention to the outlook for credit expansion, while the gains in Kotak Mahindra Bank show that individual financial stocks can respond differently to company-specific developments.
Pharmaceutical companies may also experience different pressures from those affecting energy-intensive sectors. Dr Reddy’s Laboratories’ gains following better-than-expected quarterly profits demonstrated how positive earnings can support a stock even during a difficult broader market session.
The coming days are likely to bring additional company announcements, giving investors more information about the health of different industries.
Outlook Hinges on Energy, Policy and Earnings
Market participants face several interconnected developments as the week progresses: the trajectory of crude prices, the security situation in the Middle East, the Federal Reserve’s announcement and new corporate earnings figures.
A sustained rise in oil prices could increase inflationary pressure and weigh on the profitability of companies exposed to energy and transportation costs. Conversely, a durable improvement in supply conditions could ease some of these concerns, although the speed of any market recovery would also depend on earnings and investment flows.
Investors will also watch whether foreign portfolio flows stabilise and whether domestic economic indicators support expectations of continued growth.
For now, the combination of geopolitical uncertainty and elevated energy prices is encouraging caution across Indian financial markets. The immediate direction of equities is likely to depend on how these risks develop and whether corporate results provide sufficient support to offset concerns about costs and demand.
The market’s performance over the coming sessions will offer a clearer indication of whether the latest weakness represents a temporary reaction to global uncertainty or a more sustained reassessment of investment risks.

articles.title: Euro firms against dollar, yen ahead of central bank meetings - KELO-AM
articles.summary: Euro firms against dollar, yen ahead of central bank meetings  KELO-AM
articles.full_text:
By Stefano Rebaudo
Oct 26 (Reuters) – The euro edged higher on Monday as oil prices dropped and after Moody’s left France’s credit rating unchanged on Friday, with investors staying on the sidelines ahead of a week packed with central bank meetings.
The euro ended last week lower against the US dollar and the yen as a selloff in French government bonds drove the country’s debt risk premium to its highest level since the 2011 sovereign debt crisis, reigniting concerns about renewed financial stress across the euro zone.
However, French government bond (OAT) prices rose on Monday after Moody’s spared France a credit rating downgrade last week, easing pressure on a government struggling to shore up strained finances.
Brent crude futures eased after a Reuters report that Qatari mediators were in Tehran on Sunday as part of an effort to de-escalate regional tensions in coordination with the US, having surged to a six-month high last week. Higher oil prices weigh on import-dependent economies such as the euro zone and Japan.
The euro rose 0.10% to $1.1228 and 0.25% to 176.15 versus the yen.
According to Barclays’ strategists, “French stress is unlikely to go away ahead of the presidential election in April/May, and while the euro/dollar premium has now corrected to sub-3%, there is likely still some more unwind in store.”
France is bracing for more trouble this coming weekend related to student protests and broader anti-government demonstrations, said Interior Minister Laurent Nunez.
Last week, the US dollar came under selling pressure during a tech-led market selloff.
Corporate earnings reports from large cloud computing providers Alphabet, Microsoft and Amazon will also test the fragile AI-led market rally and broader risk appetite.
The dollar index, which measures the US currency against a basket of peers, was little changed at 101.80.
CENTRAL BANKS IN FOCUS
