Ether and XRP led losses among the majors as the AI trade took another hit in Asia, where Goldman Sachs cut its Kospi target by 25%.
- Bitcoin fell nearly 2% to about $79,800 as traders reduced risk before the Federal Reserve’s Wednesday meeting, while Ether, XRP and other major tokens also declined.
- Investors are watching for signals of a possible December rate increase, which could tighten liquidity and further pressure cryptocurrencies and stocks.
- A continuing sell-off in Asian technology shares weighed on sentiment, while Bitcoin must reclaim $82,500 to restore confidence among buyers.
Bitcoin fell nearly 2% to about $79,800 as of Monday Asian morning hours as traders cut risk ahead of this week’s Federal Reserve meeting and another leg down in the AI trade weighed on tech stocks across the region.
Selling hit almost every major token. Ether dropped nearly 3% to just above $2,300, and XRP lost about 3% to $1.28. SOL slid 2% and is barely holding $100. DOGE, ZEC, HYPE and BNB each fell 1% to 2%, while TRX was the only major in the green, up less than 1%, according to CoinDesk data.
“This week, all eyes are on the Fed meeting and it already seems like investors are de-risking as Bitcoin falls below the $80k mark. While the Fed probably won’t change rates this week, we’re watching how strongly the chair hints at a December hike — that’s what matters for crypto,” Jeff Mei, chief operating officer at crypto exchange BTSE, said in an email to CoinDesk.
“Given record high oil prices, the escalating US-Iran conflict, and inflation, the Fed could very well adopt an aggressive tone, which means higher rates and less liquidity for crypto and stocks,” he added.
The Fed announces its decision on Wednesday, and traders will be listening to Chair Kevin Warsh’s press conference for any hint that a hike is coming in December. Higher rates make borrowing more expensive and tend to pull money out of riskier assets like crypto.
In Asia, the AI selloff kept going. South Korea’s Kospi, which traders watch for AI sentiment because of how much weight chipmakers like Samsung Electronics carry in it, fell 1% after Goldman Sachs strategists cut their 12-month target for the index by 25%. Chip stocks were the biggest losers on Japan’s Nikkei, and Chinese AI model developers slumped. Nasdaq 100 futures slipped 0.1% as investors braced for earnings from the biggest U.S. tech companies this week.
The MSCI Asia Pacific Index fell 0.1%, and it’s struggling to recover from four straight weeks of losses, its longest losing run since April.
Oil gave markets a bit of relief. Brent crude fell 2% from a six-month high to about $114 a barrel after President Donald Trump said it’s “getting to be decision time” on whether to reach a deal with Iran or resume attacks. Treasuries rose.
Bitcoin needs to get back above $82,500, the floor it lost last Thursday, before buyers can call this week’s dip a pause.

Global markets face a pivotal week as the Federal Reserve, Bank of England, and Bank of Japan announce interest rate decisions. Investors are monitoring rising oil prices and persistent inflation against economic growth indicators, including U.S. Q2 GDP and PCE data. Concurrently, the tech sector enters a critical earnings phase, with Microsoft, Meta, Apple, and Amazon reporting results. Market participants will scrutinize these earnings for evidence of AI-driven capital expenditure returns. Additionally, Eurozone inflation and Chinese PMI data will offer further insights into global economic health, likely dictating volatility across equities, bonds, and currency markets.
TradingKey - In the coming week, global financial markets will face the most intensive window of central bank decisions and economic data in July. The Federal Reserve, the Bank of England, and the Bank of Japan will successively announce their interest rate decisions. As international oil prices broke back above $100 and pushed up inflation expectations, market concerns over further policy tightening by major central banks have clearly intensified.
On the macroeconomic front, the US will release a flurry of data, including preliminary second-quarter GDP, the June Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) price index, durable goods orders, consumer confidence, and the second-quarter Employment Cost Index. China will release its official manufacturing PMI for July, while the Eurozone will also publish its preliminary second-quarter GDP and July inflation data, providing investors with the latest indicators to assess global economic growth and inflation trends.
On the corporate front, the US stock market's second-quarter earnings season will enter its most critical phase. Microsoft ( MSFT ), Meta Platforms ( META ), Apple ( AAPL) and Amazon ( AMZN ), the four mega-cap tech giants, will report their earnings within a two-day span. Boeing ( BA ), Visa ( V ), Coca-Cola ( KO ), Ford Motor ( F ), United Parcel Service ( UPS ), Starbucks ( SBUX ), ExxonMobil ( XOM) and Chevron ( CVX) and other industrial, consumer, and energy leaders will also report their earnings in succession.
Federal Reserve Announces July Interest Rate Decision as Market Reassesses Rate Hike Risks
On Wednesday (July 29), the Federal Reserve will conclude its two-day monetary policy meeting and announce its latest interest rate decision, followed by a press conference held by the Fed Chair.
As Brent crude oil broke back above $100 per barrel, U.S. inflation expectations and Treasury yields rose significantly, fueling rapid market expectations for a Federal Reserve rate hike. As of July 23, interest rate futures showed that the probability of the Fed raising rates by 25 basis points at this meeting had risen to approximately 31.5%, a sharp increase from 12.8% a week earlier. However, holding rates steady remains the market's baseline expectation.
Investors will focus closely on how the Federal Reserve assesses rising energy prices, labor market resilience, and the risk of inflation reheating. If the policy statement or press conference signals a rate hike in September, the U.S. dollar and Treasury yields could continue to strengthen, while gold and high-valuation tech stocks could face pressure. Conversely, if the Fed views the oil price shock as primarily transitory, the market's tightening expectations may cool.
Bank of England Announces Interest Rate Decision, Focusing on Split Vote and Inflation Forecasts
On Thursday (July 30), the Bank of England will announce its latest interest rate decision and release its monetary policy meeting minutes alongside its quarterly Monetary Policy Report.
The Bank of England currently maintains its benchmark interest rate at 3.75%, and the market widely expects the central bank to hold rates steady at this meeting. The UK's inflation rate stood at 2.6% in June, remaining above the 2% policy target, while rising international oil prices could further push up energy, transportation, and food prices in the country.
The market will closely watch whether the number of votes within the Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) in favor of a rate hike increases, and whether the Bank of England raises its future inflation forecasts. If more committee members shift to supporting a hike, the British pound and gilt yields could strengthen; if the central bank continues to emphasize slowing economic growth, market expectations for a near-term rate hike may be constrained.
Bank of Japan Announces Interest Rate Decision, with Yen Trends and Timing of Next Rate Hike in Focus
On Friday (July 31), the Bank of Japan will announce its latest interest rate decision and release its quarterly economic outlook report.
The Bank of Japan raised its policy rate to 1% in June, the highest level in 31 years. The market expects the central bank to keep rates unchanged at this meeting, but it may continue to warn of inflation risks arising from a weak yen, rising imported energy costs, and wage growth.
Investors will focus on whether the Bank of Japan upwardly revises its economic growth or inflation forecasts, as well as Governor Kazuo Ueda's remarks regarding the timing of the next rate hike. If the BOJ signals another rate hike later this year, the yen could receive support; however, if its policy stance remains cautious, the U.S.-Japan interest rate differential and high oil prices may continue to pressure the currency.
U.S. GDP and Core PCE to Be Released on Same Day, Putting Economic Growth and Inflation to a Dual Test
On Thursday (July 30), the U.S. will simultaneously release the advance estimate for second-quarter GDP, along with personal income, personal spending, and the PCE price index for June.
Second-quarter GDP will reflect the overall performance of the U.S. economy against the backdrop of high interest rates, shifting trade policies, and the expansion of corporate investments in AI. The market will focus closely on consumer spending, business equipment investment, and inventory changes to assess whether the U.S. economy continues to expand.
The core PCE price index is the Federal Reserve's preferred inflation gauge. Following the rise in oil prices that pushed inflation expectations back up, whether core PCE remains above the Fed's 2% target will directly impact monetary policy expectations for September. If GDP remains strong and core PCE exceeds expectations, the market may ramp up bets on interest rate hikes; conversely, if growth slows significantly while inflation cools, U.S. equities and gold could receive some support.
Tech Giants' Earnings Reach Climax as Returns on AI Capital Expenditure Face Scrutiny
After the market close on Wednesday (July 29), Microsoft and Meta will release their latest earnings reports.
For Microsoft, the market will focus intensely on the growth rate of its Azure cloud computing business, AI capacity supply, the commercialization of Microsoft 365 Copilot, and data center capital expenditures. As concerns grow that tech companies are ramping up AI spending too quickly, whether Microsoft can demonstrate investment returns on AI through Azure and enterprise software revenue will be key to its stock performance.
For Meta, investors will look at advertising revenue growth, user engagement, advertising efficiency driven by AI recommendation systems, and cost changes following the company's substantial increases in data center and AI investments. Meta previously projected second-quarter revenue of $58 billion to $61 billion, while the scale of its 2026 AI-related capital expenditure has already become a central point of market attention.
After the market close on Thursday (July 30), Apple and Amazon will announce their financial results.
The focus of Apple's earnings report will include iPhone sales, services growth, performance in the Chinese market, product gross margins, and the commercialization progress of Apple Intelligence. For Amazon, the market will watch AWS cloud computing growth, generative AI orders, retail business margins, and full-year capital expenditure guidance. Amazon previously forecast second-quarter sales of $194 billion to $199 billion and operating income of $20 billion to $24 billion.

The US will release durable goods orders data for June. This data will reflect changes in demand for business equipment, machinery, aircraft, and other long-term assets, serving as an important indicator for tracking manufacturing investment and corporate capital expenditure.

articles.title: Rate hiked - The News Pakistan
articles.summary: Rate hiked  The News Pakistan
articles.full_text:
The Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) decided to increase the policy rate by 50 bps to 12 per cent in its meeting yesterday. The decision comes as Pakistan’s inflation rate remains well above the target range of 5-7 per cent, clocking in at 10.3 percent year-on-year in September. The MPC noted that this was higher than their expectations and highlighted how the intensification in the Middle East conflict, and low prospects of its near-term resolution, are keeping global energy prices at persistently elevated levels in its Monetary Policy Statement. Though the MPC believes that the impact of this global shock on the domestic economy has remained contained so far, with the external account and growth outlook broadly unchanged and amidst proactive monetary policy adjustment and continued fiscal discipline, geopolitical developments have worsened the inflation outlook as compared to the earlier assessment. As such, a 0.5 per cent hike in the policy rate seems appropriate at this stage but getting inflation back into the target range appears to depend not on domestic economic decisions but the geostrategic decisions of foreign countries. Sadly, while Pakistan’s economic outlook might depend heavily on the decisions others make, the impacts are local and they are becoming quite severe.
Flour prices have surged to as much Rs180 per kg in some parts of the country, LPG cylinders are reportedly being sold at more than twice the official price of Rs3,296 across the country just as winter and its associated gas woes begin to roll in and there appears to be no reprieve at the pump either. The MPC itself has noted that elevated prices of energy and wheat and its allied products contributed significantly to the headline inflation in September. This is what happens when a country is heavily dependent on fuel imports and that import bill surges by over 46 per cent in six months, as per the World Bank. The impact on growth might be contained so far, with the latest IMF forecast projecting 3.5 per cent growth, which is the lower bound of the SBP’s projection, one wonders how much longer this will be the case. More importantly, the overall picture that emerges is one of an economy moving in the opposite direction of where government policy has tried to guide it in recent years. Inflation is up, imports are still projected to be more than double exports over the ongoing fiscal year, investment remains tepid and the downward risks to growth only appear to be mounting.
It would be fair to note here that Pakistan is not the only country in this bind. The energy shock is roiling economies across the world, particularly net-fuel importers in Asia and the rest of the Global South. As the crisis unfolds, the IMF has warned developing countries that while they might be bearing the disproportionate impacts of the Middle East conflict, many have ‘no choice’ but to cut spending or potentially face debt restructuring. Climbing borrowing costs and rising inflation appear to have left little room for any alternative and developing countries cannot count an AI boom to paper over the cracks. But without more spending on essential services like health, education and infrastructure, how can countries like Pakistan ever be expected to get on a more sustainable growth path? All that being said, none of this excuses our own domestic shortcomings. Revenue collection appears to finally be getting on track, but the country’s tax system remains very unfair with the salaried regularly emerging as the top tax contributors despite enduring the most economic pain. The circular debt in both the power and gas sector continues to mount and unproductive SOEs continue to bleed the economy. Somehow, Pakistan has mastered the art of austerity, raising taxes, petroleum levies and policy rates, without mastering reforms. This is not an era for inefficiency, and the state has to get its own house in order before it tells people about tough decisions and global crises.

Oil surge raises India’s economic risks
Brent crude rose to $116.72 a barrel, compared with $96.24 a month earlier and $63.61 a year earlier, according to the report. The India crude basket reached $119.99 a barrel.
The increase threatens to raise India's import bill, intensify imported inflation and put additional pressure on the rupee. Higher energy costs could also squeeze corporate margins and household purchasing power.
Analyst assessment: The interaction between oil prices, currency weakness and inflation is the central macroeconomic challenge. If elevated energy prices persist, they could constrain monetary-policy flexibility while weakening consumption and business profitability.
Rupee pressure and capital flows
The dollar traded at Rs 94.94, compared with Rs 87.85 a year earlier, representing an approximately 8.1 per cent depreciation in the rupee against the dollar.
The report describes volatile foreign portfolio investment flows and Reserve Bank of India intervention in the currency market. Its charts also show sharp fluctuations in one-month and three-month rupee forward premiums, indicating changing conditions in the currency hedging market.
Also read: Gold paradox: Indians sell more but buy more too; a big question is lost in between
Cumulative foreign equity flows show substantial selling pressure over the year, although recent daily flows have been mixed. A few sessions of buying would not, by themselves, establish a sustained reversal.
The challenge is that currency weakness and equity outflows can reinforce each other, while higher oil prices increase demand for foreign currency.
Tight financial conditions
Indian government and corporate bond yields remain elevated. The report puts the 10-year government bond yield at 6.74 per cent, compared with 6.68 per cent a month earlier and 6.63 per cent a year earlier. The five-year overnight indexed swap rate climbed to 6.41 per cent from 6.04 per cent a month earlier.
The AAA-rated 10-year corporate bond yield rose to 7.61 per cent, from 7.44 per cent a month earlier.
Meanwhile, the report's liquidity charts show substantial fluctuations in RBI liquidity operations and domestic money-market conditions. Certificate-of-deposit yields have also increased across several maturities, suggesting higher funding costs for banks.
The report's US Treasury charts show the 10-year yield at 4.38 per cent, while the MOVE Index, a measure of Treasury-market volatility, rose to 108.84 from 68.03 a month earlier.
Also read: How US-Iran peace deal impacted oil prices, stock markets, gold and the rupee
The combination suggests that global risk aversion is supporting demand for safe-haven bonds, even as uncertainty remains elevated. Lower US yields do not automatically translate into lower Indian borrowing costs.
Gold retreats despite market uncertainty
Commodity charts show divergent performance. Gold fell to 3,996.10 in the report's quoted market-data units, from 4,343.43 a month earlier. Silver declined to 53.89 from 66.03.
Industrial metals also weakened: three-month aluminium on the London Metal Exchange fell to 3,043.50 from 3,267.00 a month earlier, while copper declined to 14,322.50 from 14,661.00.
The movements suggest that risk aversion has not benefited all commodities equally, while the sharp increase in crude oil prices remains the dominant concern for India.
Key highlights and challenges
Highlights
• Global equity markets have outperformed Indian benchmarks over the year
• US Treasury yields have eased amid risk aversion, although bond-market volatility has increased
• Indian government and corporate borrowing costs remain elevated
• Currency forwards and RBI liquidity operations reflect volatile domestic funding conditions
Challenges
• Higher crude prices threaten inflation, the current account and the rupee
• Foreign equity outflows risk prolonging domestic market underperformance
• Elevated bond yields could raise financing costs and pressure bond valuations
• Geopolitical uncertainty complicates global monetary-policy expectations
Central banks and oil in focus
Axis Bank identifies US Federal Reserve, European Central Bank and Bank of Japan decisions, alongside Indian fiscal and economic data, as important events for the week ahead.
The key market question is whether falling global yields can offset the pressure from expensive oil and fragile capital flows. A sustained decline in crude prices, stabilising foreign investment and stronger corporate earnings would improve the outlook. Without those developments, Indian equities, the rupee and domestic bonds could remain vulnerable to renewed volatility.

Financial markets face a series of major events this week, including interest rate decisions from three central banks, US economic data, quarterly earnings from leading technology companies and elections in several countries.
The Federal Reserve's monetary policy announcement on Wednesday will be a central focus, while investors will also assess the financial implications of artificial intelligence investment and developments in the Middle East conflict.
Political developments in Brazil, Serbia and Israel could provide additional considerations for international markets.
1. Federal Reserve, ECB and Bank of Japan Interest Rate Decisions
The Federal Reserve is widely expected to leave interest rates unchanged when it concludes its two-day policy meeting on Wednesday, following its first increase in borrowing costs since 2023 at the September meeting.
Federal Reserve officials have reiterated their commitment to returning inflation to the central bank's 2% target, although some policymakers have indicated that another immediate rate increase may not be necessary.
Investors will therefore focus on the accompanying policy statement and comments from Fed Chair Kevin Warsh for indications about the outlook for December.
Deutsche Bank analysts expect limited changes to the statement but believe the central bank could maintain a restrictive policy stance.
"Our economists expect only minor changes to the statement itself, although some policymakers could dissent from a decision to hold rates. The overall message is still likely to favour tighter monetary policy, as recent inflation figures support further increases over time, even if the Fed pauses this week," the analysts wrote.
According to CME's FedWatch Tool, financial markets were pricing in approximately a 73% probability of another rate increase at the Federal Open Market Committee's final meeting of the year in December.
The European Central Bank and the Bank of Japan are also scheduled to announce monetary policy decisions this week. Both institutions are expected to maintain their existing interest rates.
2. US GDP, Inflation and Labour Cost Data
Several US economic releases could influence expectations for the Federal Reserve's next policy decisions.
September durable goods orders are due on Tuesday, alongside the Conference Board's consumer confidence survey.
Deutsche Bank analysts expect durable goods demand to remain firm, supported by capital expenditure related to artificial intelligence and orders for aircraft.
Thursday's economic calendar includes September personal income and spending figures, the Federal Reserve's preferred inflation measure and an advance estimate of third-quarter US gross domestic product.

Global financial markets are entering a crucial week as five major central banks prepare to announce their latest interest rate decisions. With the US Federal Reserve, European Central Bank (ECB), Bank of Japan (BoJ), Bank of Canada (BoC) and Reserve Bank of New Zealand (RBNZ) all in focus, investors are preparing for potential volatility across currencies, commodities and global stock markets.
The central question is whether the US dollar can regain momentum while gold prices remain under pressure.
On Monday, 26 October, the US Dollar Index (DXY) traded around 101.64 as falling Treasury yields weighed on the greenback. Meanwhile, spot gold rebounded above US$4,000 per ounce after suffering a sharp decline in the previous week.
For Australian investors, the outlook is particularly important. With AUD/USD trading around US$0.7030 and Australian inflation figures due this week, the interaction between Federal Reserve policy and Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) expectations could create significant trading opportunities and risks.
Key Market Highlights: 26 October 2026
- US Dollar Index (DXY): Around 101.64, reflecting a softer US dollar ahead of the Federal Reserve decision.
- Gold price (XAU/USD): Around US$4,010 per ounce in early Monday trading, recovering modestly after a 4% weekly decline.
- AUD/USD: Trading near 0.7030, with Australian inflation data and US monetary policy in focus.
- US 10-year Treasury yield: Approximately 4.97%, hovering near a one-month low.
- Brent crude oil: Around US$114–115 per barrel, easing from recent highs but remaining elevated.
- Federal Reserve outlook: Markets largely expect rates to remain unchanged in October, while attention turns to the possibility of further tightening later this year.
- Key upcoming events: Australian CPI, the Fed decision, US GDP, PCE inflation and several other major central bank announcements.
These developments suggest that inflation expectations, interest rate differentials and geopolitical uncertainty will remain the primary drivers of financial markets.
Super Central Bank Week: Why the Fed Decision Matters
The Federal Reserve is scheduled to announce its October interest rate decision on Wednesday, 28 October, US time, corresponding to early Thursday morning in Sydney.
While markets widely anticipate that the Fed will leave interest rates unchanged, investors will pay particular attention to the accompanying policy statement and Federal Reserve Chair's comments.
The key issue is not simply whether the Fed raises rates this week, but whether policymakers signal that further tightening may be necessary.
Could persistent inflation force the Fed to remain hawkish?
The Federal Reserve continues to face a difficult policy environment.
Elevated energy prices are contributing to inflation concerns, while volatility in technology stocks and signs of slowing economic activity raise questions about the resilience of the US economy.
Higher oil prices can increase transportation, manufacturing and consumer costs, potentially making inflation more persistent.
At the same time, weaker financial markets may tighten financial conditions and reduce the need for aggressive monetary policy intervention.
This creates two competing forces:
Scenario 1: The Fed maintains a hawkish stance
If policymakers emphasise persistent inflation risks and suggest additional rate increases remain possible, US Treasury yields could rebound.
A rise in yields may support the US dollar while placing renewed pressure on non-yielding assets such as gold.
Scenario 2: The Fed adopts a more cautious tone
If the Fed highlights slowing growth, financial market instability or concerns about employment, investors may reduce expectations for further tightening.
This could weaken the US dollar and provide support for gold prices.
Consequently, the tone of the Fed's communication may matter more than the immediate interest rate decision.
US Dollar Forecast: Can DXY Resume Its Uptrend?
The US dollar entered the final week of October under pressure as Treasury yields declined and investors reassessed the outlook for US monetary policy.
On 26 October, the Dollar Index traded near 101.64, while the benchmark US 10-year Treasury yield hovered around 4.97%.
Falling yields have narrowed the interest rate advantage previously supporting the greenback.
However, several factors could still help the dollar recover.
1. US inflation remains a significant risk
Persistent inflation could encourage the Federal Reserve to maintain restrictive monetary policy for longer.
If upcoming PCE inflation data exceed market expectations, Treasury yields may rise, potentially strengthening the dollar.
2. Geopolitical uncertainty may increase safe-haven demand
The Middle East remains a major source of uncertainty.
Although diplomatic efforts involving Qatar have raised hopes of easing tensions between the United States and Iran, continued attacks and threats to energy infrastructure suggest that supply risks have not disappeared.
Escalating geopolitical tensions can increase demand for the US dollar, particularly during periods of market stress.
Nevertheless, the dollar's reaction is not guaranteed. If geopolitical developments lead to weaker US growth expectations and falling Treasury yields, the greenback may struggle to strengthen.
3. Central bank policy divergence could influence currency markets
This week's monetary policy decisions may reshape interest rate expectations across major economies.
If the Fed remains hawkish while other central banks signal a more accommodative outlook, the dollar could benefit from widening interest rate differentials.
Conversely, relatively hawkish guidance from overseas central banks could limit dollar gains.

The US Dollar Index is consolidating around 101.6 after retreating from recent highs.

Bullish scenario: A sustained move above 102.00 could indicate improving upward momentum and potentially open the way towards 103.00.
Bearish scenario: A failure to regain 102.00, followed by a decline below 101.00, could expose the 100.60 region.
A sustained break below 100.60 would weaken the case for an immediate dollar recovery.

Gold Price Forecast: Will XAU/USD Fall Below US$4,000 Again?
Gold prices experienced substantial selling pressure last week, with bullion declining approximately 4%, its largest weekly fall since June.
The precious metal briefly fell to its lowest level since mid-July before recovering towards US$4,010 on Monday.
The rebound followed a decline in oil prices, which temporarily reduced concerns about inflation and aggressive Federal Reserve tightening.
However, gold's near-term outlook remains uncertain.
Why has gold been under pressure?
Three major factors are influencing the precious metal.
Higher-for-longer interest rate expectations
Gold does not generate interest income. When investors expect US interest rates to remain elevated, interest-bearing assets can become relatively more attractive.
US dollar movements
Gold is internationally priced in US dollars. A stronger dollar can make gold more expensive for investors using other currencies, potentially weighing on demand.
Geopolitical developments
Gold often benefits from safe-haven demand during periods of geopolitical uncertainty.
However, this relationship can be complicated when geopolitical tensions push oil prices higher and increase inflation expectations.
In such circumstances, expectations of tighter monetary policy may offset some of gold's traditional safe-haven appeal.
Gold Technical Outlook: Key XAU/USD Levels
With gold trading near US$4,010 on 26 October, the US$4,000 level remains an important psychological reference.
Bullish gold scenario
If gold holds above US$4,000 and US Treasury yields continue declining, buyers may attempt to push prices towards US$4,050 and potentially US$4,100.
A more dovish-than-expected Fed statement could support this scenario.
Bearish gold scenario
If US inflation remains elevated and the Fed signals that further interest rate increases are possible, gold may face renewed selling pressure.
A sustained decline below US$4,000 could bring US$3,950 and US$3,900 into focus.
Importantly, a temporary recovery does not necessarily confirm the end of the broader correction.
Traders should monitor price action around these levels and remain alert to volatility surrounding major economic announcements.

For Australian investors, the Fed decision is especially relevant because of its potential impact on the Australian dollar.
AUD/USD traded around 0.7030 on Monday, 26 October, as investors awaited important inflation data from both Australia and the United States.
The Australian dollar is influenced by several factors, including:

- Global risk sentiment and demand for commodity-linked currencies.
- Australia's economic outlook and inflation trends.

Australian CPI could influence the RBA outlook

This may support the Australian dollar, particularly if the Fed adopts a more cautious stance.
Alternatively, weaker Australian inflation combined with a hawkish Fed could place downward pressure on AUD/USD.

articles.full_text:
The latest jump in oil prices has disturbed Indian equities, with both major indices starting the week with losses and 12 out of India’s 16 sectors booking losses, Reuters reported earlier in the day.
With Brent crude trading at over $114 per barrel, it is not hard to see why investor sentiment in the world’s third-largest importer of crude is not exactly optimistic, pushing Sensex down by 0.46 today, and Nifty 50 down by 0.5. IT stocks specifically shed 1.1%, the report said.
“Concerns over supply disruptions due to escalating Mideast tensions pushed crude oil prices higher,” Equinomic Research founder and head of research G Chokkalingam told Reuters.
“Domestic equities are likely to remain highly volatile, with a short-term downward bias and unless the Mideast conflict is resolved meaningfully, higher energy costs could reignite global inflation, restrain economic growth and darken the outlook for stock markets worldwide.”
Despite continued disruptions, India's imports of Middle Eastern crude climbed to 2.8 million barrels per day in September, lifting the region's share of total imports to 54%, up from 32% in August.
That increase was driven by Indian refiners buying a growing number of spot cargoes as the Gulf producers have managed to sneak out increasingly higher crude volumes through the Strait of Hormuz via ship-to-ship transfers in the Gulf of Oman.
Russia remained the single largest crude oil supplier to India in September, but the imports of Russian oil fell by 14% from August to 1.8 million bpd last month. The share of Russian oil in India’s oil imports also dropped to 33.5% from 46.6% in August.
The impact of the war on Indian investor sentiment will likely extend into next year as the U.S. and Iran remain as far apart on peace deal conditions as ever, with neither side willing to make concessions.

articles.title: How Taiwan’s Stock Market Got Too Big for Its Central Bank｜Industry｜2026-10-26｜web only - 天下雜誌
articles.summary: How Taiwan’s Stock Market Got Too Big for Its Central Bank｜Industry｜2026-10-26｜web only  天下雜誌
articles.full_text:
Source：Chien-Ying Chiu
Taiwan’s stock market has grown into one of the world’s largest, but the surge in foreign ownership is creating a new challenge: capital flows may now be too large for the Central Bank to manage. A record October sell-off exposed how quickly foreign investors can move money—and how vulnerable the Taiwan dollar could become when that tide reverses.
Views
How Taiwan’s Stock Market Got Too Big for Its Central Bank
By Eri Hsieh, Lisa Lin
web only
On Oct. 15th, foreign investors offloaded more than NT$302.5 billion in the Taiwan stock market (TAIEX), a record-shattering sell-off. More shockingly still, foreign investors moved the money out of Taiwan.
On the day of the sell-off, combined trading volume across the Taipei foreign exchanges totaled over $9.1 billion—an all-time single-day record.
“Nobody expected volume to explode like that in a single day,” says a senior currency trader. Even though the Central Bank intervened, the Taiwan dollar weakened by NT$0.192 against the U.S. dollar that day. In just October alone, the Taiwan dollar has depreciated 1.96%, making it the weakest among the Asian currencies.
All this goes to show that the Taiwan stock market has grown far larger than it once was.
Over 2026, TAIEX grew from under 30,000 to a whopping 50,000 points, overtaking France, Britain, Korea, Canada, and India to become the world’s fourth-largest stock market. Foreign investors held nearly half of the market’s capitalization, with a total value of nearly NT$80 trillion.
“Two years ago, when foreign investors moved 1% of their holdings, it amounted to NT$ 250 billion. Now, it’s NT$ 800 billion,” says a senior manager at a large financial firm. TAIEX also ranks the highest in terms of weight-by-country on the MSCI Emerging Markets Index—which means that whenever emerging-market funds face redemptions, Taiwan is hit first and hardest.
Two major reasons led to the exit of foreign capital. One, many funds close their fiscal year at the end of October and needed to lock in profits. Two, while the AI boom is driving up prices in the stock market, bond prices are falling. With equities now too heavy in their portfolios, foreign investors had to sell stocks and buy U.S. Treasuries.
This doesn’t mean that investors have lost confidence in AI. According to Jeff Chang (張錫), former chairman of Cathay Securities Investment Trust, “Foreign investors’ holdings grew by more than NT$ 20 trillion this year, so selling NT$ 2 trillion is nothing.”
Many in financial circles believe the Central Bank is comfortable with a weaker Taiwan dollar. But foreign money flows both ways. When foreign investors start buying Taiwanese stocks again, the Taiwan dollar will rapidly rebound in value.
The problem is, foreign investors hold the equivalent of $1.9 trillion in Taiwanese stocks and bonds, which is 3.21 times Taiwan’s $600 billion in foreign exchange reserves. A manager at a large financial firm warns that under extreme circumstances, even if the Central Bank were to exhaust its foreign exchange reserves to stabilize the currency, “it is no longer a question of willingness, but of capability.”
Foreign investors’ holdings of Taiwanese stocks and bonds have surged to more than three times Taiwan’s foreign exchange reserves, posing a new challenge for the Central Bank when it intervenes in the currency market. (Photo: Chien-Tong Wang)
Taiwan’s foreign exchange rate has long been under scrutiny by the U.S. Treasury. The Americans use three criteria to determine if a trading partner is a currency manipulator. Taiwan has met two of them for years; if it is found to be engaging in “persistent, one-sided intervention in the foreign exchange market,” it may face trade sanctions.
“Out of the world’s ten largest stock markets, only China, India, and Taiwan still manage their exchange rates,” says a foreign exchange expert at a private bank.
Because the Central Bank keeps Taiwan’s foreign exchange rate on a tight leash, companies and investors have gotten used to the invisible safety net and do not hedge seriously.
Take the life insurance industry. The new accounting rules allow foreign exchange gains and losses to be amortized over a number of years. One life insurer has parked over NT$30 billion in unamortized foreign exchange gains under other liabilities in the first half of this year. If the Taiwan dollar were to rise in value, these gains would become massive paper losses.
In 2025, Taiwan and the U.S. reached an agreement to disclose the Central Bank’s foreign exchange interventions on a quarterly basis. An economist opines there’s a good chance that Taiwan will move to monthly disclosure in the near future, like Korea, leaving the Central Bank less and less room to intervene.
The question Taiwanese enterprises and investors must ask themselves is this: are they ready to work with the Taiwan dollar once it’s deprived of its safety net?

Latest USD/CNY Central Parity Setting
On Monday, the People’s Bank of China (PBOC) set the central USD/CNY reference rate for the upcoming trading session at 6.7162. This compares with the previous trading day’s official fixing of 6.7180 and a 6.6691 estimate reported by Reuters.
| Fixing Reference | USD/CNY Level | 
|---|---|
| Monday PBOC central rate | 6.7162 | 
| Friday PBOC fix | 6.7180 | 
| Reuters estimate | 6.6691 | 
Mandate and Role of the People’s Bank of China
The primary monetary policy goals of the People’s Bank of China are described as safeguarding price stability – including exchange rate stability – and supporting economic growth. The central bank is also tasked with pushing forward financial sector reforms, such as the opening and development of China’s financial markets.
The PBOC is owned by the state of the People’s Republic of China and is not regarded as an independent institution. The Chinese Communist Party (CCP) Committee Secretary, who is nominated by the Chairman of the State Council, has significant influence over the central bank’s strategic direction and management, rather than the governor. However, Mr. Pan Gongsheng currently holds both of these posts.
PBOC Policy Instruments and Benchmark Rates
The PBOC employs a relatively broad toolkit to pursue its policy objectives. Key instruments include the seven-day Reverse Repo Rate, the Medium-term Lending Facility (MLF), foreign exchange operations, and the Reserve Requirement Ratio (RRR).
China’s benchmark lending reference is the Loan Prime Rate (LPR). Adjustments to the LPR directly affect borrowing costs on loans and mortgages, along with returns on savings in the domestic market. Through changes to the LPR, the central bank can also influence the external value of the Chinese renminbi.
Private Banking Presence in China
Private-sector banks are permitted to operate in China, although they represent a relatively small segment of the financial system. There are 19 private banks, with digital lenders WeBank and MYbank – backed by Tencent and Ant Group, respectively – cited as the largest. In 2014, authorities allowed domestically funded lenders fully capitalized by private capital to participate in the state-dominated banking sector.

articles.full_text:
- Benchmark three-month copper on the London Metal Exchange was down 0.56% at $14,242.5 a metric ton
SINGAPORE: Copper prices in London softened on Monday, weighed down by a buildup in warehouse stocks that eased supply worries and on concerns about high energy prices.
Benchmark three-month copper on the London Metal Exchange was down 0.56% at $14,242.5 a metric ton by 0300 GMT.
The most-traded copper contract on the Shanghai Futures Exchange rose 0.55% to 108,720 yuan ($16,299.36) a ton, tracking Friday’s overnight LME gains.
Copper stocks in LME warehouses surged last week to their highest levels since July, after a batch of deposits into LME-registered warehouses, mostly located in North America.
Expectations of a potential tariff on imports of refined copper into the US have pulled the metal into the country, thinning stocks elsewhere and pushing the metal on the LME to a record high of $14,875 a ton on September 11.
Macro fears and expectations of a shift in the draw of metal into the US are contributing to a bearish backdrop on copper, Alastair Munro, senior metals strategist at Marex, said in a note.
Meanwhile, oil prices started the week lower, but remained at elevated levels after a spree of attacks on Saudi Arabia by Yemen’s Houthis raised geopolitical risks.
Higher energy costs dampen global economic sentiment and have weighed on demand expectations for growth-dependent copper, which is used in electrification, construction, and consumer goods.
Providing some support, the Yangshan copper premium, a gauge of China’s appetite for imported copper, was at $168 a ton on Friday, its highest since 2014.
In China, the world’s biggest copper consumer, some smelters are in maintenance, with stocks in SHFE-monitored warehouses falling more than a quarter to 54,356 tons last week.
Among LME metals, aluminium lost 0.41%, zinc dipped 0.09%, lead shed 0.18%, nickel lost 1.19% and tin declined 0.24%.
Among SHFE metals, aluminium gained 0.89%, zinc was up 0.93%, lead dipped 0.12%, nickel dropped 2.06% and tin rose 0.98%.

On Tuesday (27 October, 9:25 AM, GMT+7, Bangkok time), most major indices in the Asia-Pacific increased, echoing gains seen on Wall Street. Investor sentiment received a lift following Anthropic’s official move towards a Nasdaq debut, which invigorated the technology sector. Market participants viewed the IPO as a significant addition to the roster of major tech listings in 2026, coming after SpaceX’s high-profile public offering earlier this year.
Anthropic, well known for its contributions to generative AI, revealed in a regulatory filing that it intends to be listed under the symbol “ANT” on the Nasdaq. The company, which initially submitted confidential documents to the SEC in June, has been preparing for its transition to public ownership by making its finances available for regulatory and investor review.
Broader market attention is also focused on upcoming company earnings announcements as well as the U.S. Federal Reserve’s two-day policy meeting that begins this week. Consensus among traders is that interest rates will remain unchanged following September’s increase, although they will be monitoring for any indication of a potential hike before the end of the year.
Geopolitical strains remain an influence on market dynamics. According to CNN, U.S. military forces stationed in the Middle East are on alert and prepared to initiate operations targeting Iran, pending directives from President Donald Trump.
Japan’s NIKKEI rose by 1.69% to 63,240.50. South Korea’s KOSPI surged 4.16% to 5,696.85, and Australia’s ASX 200 added 0.16% to 8,824.40.
Shanghai’s SSEC slid by 0.15% to 3,692.04. Shenzhen’s SZI climbed by 0.02% to 11,536.82, and Hong Kong’s HSI dropped by 0.33% to 23,135.28.
The U.S. stock markets edged up on Monday as the Dow Jones Industrial Average (DJIA) gained 0.28% to 52,361.58. NASDAQ advanced by 0.83% to 26,169.38, and S&P 500 grew by 0.70% to 7,676.77. VIX slumped by 5.45% to 18.39.
As for commodities, oil prices settled lower on Monday as expectations grew for easing tensions in the Middle East, although ongoing assaults targeting Saudi Arabian oil infrastructure and shipping routes continued to weigh on sentiment. Brent crude settled at $115.81 per barrel, declining by 91 cents, or 0.8%. U.S. West Texas Intermediate crude slipped $1.51, or 1.46%, to close at $101.76 a barrel.

articles.title: Five central banks set the tone for forex markets - IDNFinancials
articles.summary: Five central banks set the tone for forex markets  IDNFinancials
articles.full_text:
JAKARTA - Foreign exchange markets traded in a narrow range on Monday (26 October) ahead of monetary policy decisions by five major central banks and earnings reports from several major technology companies.
According to Reuters, US government bonds held on to most of their gains as investors sought safe-haven assets.
Concerns over the scale of investment in artificial intelligence (AI) triggered a sell-off in technology stocks, prompting investors to reduce their exposure to riskier assets.
The yield on 10-year US Treasury bonds stood at 4.967%, while the 30-year yield reached 5.299%. Both remained near their lowest levels in a month.
National Australia Bank Head of FX Strategy Ray Attrill said movements in US Treasury yields had become a key factor determining the dollar’s direction.
“For now, it appears that the US bond market is the main driver of broader dollar performance,” Attrill said.
“The market is responding to lower Treasury yields and narrowing yield differentials between the US and other major G10 economies. I think this has eased some of the upward pressure on the US dollar,” he added.
The US dollar index, which measures the currency against a basket of major currencies, was little changed at 101.65.
Meanwhile, the euro rose 0.15% against the US dollar to US$1.1218 after France avoided a credit rating downgrade by Moody’s despite ongoing social unrest.
Sterling gained 0.1% to US$1.3379. The Australian dollar was little changed at US$0.7031, while the New Zealand dollar rose 0.05% to US$0.5701. The Japanese yen was also broadly stable at 156.92 per US dollar.
Central Banks in Focus
Investors will closely monitor monetary policy decisions from five major central banks this week: the US Federal Reserve (Fed), European Central Bank (ECB), Bank of Japan (BOJ), Reserve Bank of New Zealand and Bank of Canada.
The Fed, ECB and BOJ are expected to keep interest rates unchanged, although inflationary pressures remain a concern. However, all three are expected to leave the door open to rate increases in December.
By contrast, the central banks of New Zealand and Canada are expected to raise interest rates this week.
Pepperstone Head of Research Chris Weston said central banks’ forward guidance following their rate decisions could have a greater influence on markets.
“Forward guidance could prove more important than the decisions themselves,” Weston said in a note.
“The decisions themselves may already be largely priced in. The real factor that could shift the near-term interest rate outlook is how policymakers shape expectations for their next meetings and whether markets need to reprice the forward rate curve,” he added.
Beyond central bank decisions, investors are also awaiting several US economic indicators, including October consumer confidence, the personal consumption expenditures (PCE) price index and weekly jobless claims.
AI Companies Put Markets to the Test
Global equity markets also face a test from earnings reports by major technology companies, particularly Alphabet, Microsoft and Amazon.
Investors will scrutinise the three companies’ results to assess the sustainability of the AI-driven stock market rally and broader risk appetite.
In commodity markets, spot gold edged up to US$4,014 per troy ounce. Meanwhile, cryptocurrency markets weakened. Bitcoin fell 0.3% to US$80,134.29, while ether declined 0.9% to US$2,323.34.
Currency and risk-asset movements this week will depend on central bank decisions, US economic data and investor reactions to earnings reports from major technology companies. (DH/LM)

articles.title: The Anthropic IPO by the numbers, from a possible valuation in the trillions to surging revenue - Barchart.com
articles.summary: The Anthropic IPO by the numbers, from a possible valuation in the trillions to surging revenue  Barchart.com
articles.full_text:
Anthropic has the chance to make history with what could be the biggest initial public offering of stock ever.
The artificial intelligence lab filed papers Monday setting up a Wall Street debut next month, ahead of its chief rival OpenAI and just months after SpaceX set records in June with an initial public offering that raised $86 billion.
In a 335-page prospectus, the company behind the Claude chatbot outlined rapid revenue growth, but an inability to turn a profit yet. The offering could bring in as much as $100 billion, according to reports, which would help to accelerate the expansion of the five-year-old startup.
The filing comes as Anthropic's competitors like OpenAI are holding off on going public until next year, and as fears rise that the technology could slip free of human control to carry out harmful actions. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei said the industry should slow its fast-moving development to give safety measures time to catch up.
But the company's massive spending and revenue point to strong momentum.
Here's a look at the key figures behind the lab's ambitions.
That's the reported valuation the company could reach once it goes public. This would surpass SpaceX's initial valuation of $1.77 trillion and make Anthropic one of the world's most valuable public companies. Nvidia, a maker of computer chips, leads that pack with a current valuation of more than $5 trillion.
Anthropic's final valuation and offering price have not been established.
Anthropic said in the filing it had this amount available as cash or cash-equivalents as of June 30. The company also said its plans to build out compute and infrastructure are “changing the cash flow profile of our business” and will mean high capital expenditures.
This is Anthropic's revenue in the first half of the year, which is about 14 times its revenue from the same period last year.
The amount of money Anthropic reported in net losses in the first half of the year. This included a one-time, $72.4 billion charge for an accounting adjustment related to financing agreements, according to the filing. It's not uncommon for tech companies going public to not yet have turned a profit.
This is how many pages Anthropic used to enumerate risk factors for investors. Public companies are required by the Securities and Exchange Commission to disclose risk factors in their prospectus, but the lengthy nature of those in Anthropic's is unusual.
Among the concerns were that advanced AI systems could pose “catastrophic or existential risks to humanity.”
The approximate number of customers Anthropic has that each account for $10 million or more of revenue in the past year. Anthropic did not disclose the names of its biggest customers in the filing, but it pointed to its top five customers representing approximately 25% of its revenue this year.
The voting power Amodei and six other co-founders of Anthropic will hold at the company after it goes public. The company will issue a single share of a Class F common stock to a limited liability company organized by its co-founders. Amodei's sister and Anthropic's president, Daniela Amodei, is among the former OpenAI employees who left the company to create Anthropic in 2021.

articles.title: Column: Quantum copper steals the show at LME Week - Mining.com.au
articles.summary: Column: Quantum copper steals the show at LME Week  Mining.com.au
articles.full_text:
The guest of honour at the London Metal Exchange (LME) Week was Doctor Copper, who spent last week defying the laws of physics, or at least London transport, by managing to be at every seminar, cocktail party and private meeting.
Maybe there were two of them at the annual gathering. Was Doctor Copper’s US double in attendance? After all, there are two very distinct copper markets right now.
Perhaps Doctor Copper was also using an AI-generated hologram, given the market’s fortunes seem increasingly tied to the massive global investment in next-generation data centres.
Despite copper being the hot topic of just about every conversation last week, no one seems any the wiser as to where the red metal, currently holding near record highs above US$14,000 ($19,930) per tonne, is headed.
This is because copper, ever the bellwether of global manufacturing, encapsulates the new metallic order, one in which demand, to quote Saad Rahim, chief economist at trade house Trafigura, is “everything, everywhere all at once,” but supply is fragmented by government policy.
Quantum copper
Copper remains the bull pick of the LME metals pack thanks to a compelling narrative of stellar demand prospects and structurally challenged supply.
Around three-quarters of those attending the LME Seminar on Monday picked it as the top performer over the next 12 months, although the share dropped to around half when the LME remembered it also trades tin and included the soldering metal in the follow-up poll.
But is the copper market currently oversupplied or undersupplied? The answer is both, depending on where you are.
At a global level, there is no shortage. The International Copper Study Group now expects a global supply surplus of 104,000 tonnes this year and a larger one of 368,000 tonnes next year.
Global exchange inventory is over 1.2 million tonnes, double year-ago levels.
But all the metal is sitting in the US thanks to the continued uncertainty as to whether President Donald Trump will impose import tariffs.
Everyone else is short of metal, particularly China, where Shanghai Futures Exchange inventory amounts to just 54,400 tonnes and the closely watched Yangshan import premium has surged to a 13-year high of US$168 per tonne over the LME price.
The Chinese copper market is currently the “tightest I’ve seen it in my career”, Nicholas Snowdon, head of research at commodity trader Mercuria, told the Financial Times Metals and Mining Summit.
The global copper market has fractured, and so too has pricing. “The reality is that one price fits all isn’t effective,” according to Jin Hennig, global head of metals at CME Group (NASDAQ:CME), which is rapidly listing new storage capacity to handle the flood of metal washing up in the US.
Copper has truly entered a quantum state, where reality depends on where you are observing the market.
Policy rules, OK?
It’s not just copper that is increasingly beholden to government policy.
Aluminium’s regional fragmentation, manifest in wildly divergent physical premiums, is also down to Trump’s 50% import tariffs.
Might Canada, traditionally the largest supplier of metal to the US market, get a tariff discount?
The mood music between the White House and the Canadian government doesn’t hold much promise, but according to Jorge Vazquez, founder of Harbor Aluminum, the chances of a tariff reset on Canadian metal are as high as 75%.
If it were to happen, US premiums would collapse and European premiums could almost double to over US$1,000 per tonne over the LME cash price, Vazquez told the LME Seminar.
Meanwhile, nickel’s short-term price prospects are totally dependent on what happens next in Indonesia, which over the last decade has grown to become the world’s dominant producer.
“The outlook now depends less on the scale of announced capacity and more on whether Indonesian policy continues to limit ore availability and prevents a return to persistent oversupply,” according to Nikhil Shah, head of nickel analysis at research house CRU.
Want to make sense of the cobalt market? You need to be tracking government policy in the Democratic Republic of Congo, the world’s largest supplier of the battery metal.
Those export controls are propping up the price but at the cost of a massive accumulation of in-country stocks, described by CRU’s Thomas Matthews as “a Pandora’s box” of uncertainty.
As metals become ever more strategic, government policy becomes ever more embedded in traditional supply-demand analysis.
Which is why everyone last week was talking about Doctor Copper. Or should that be Doctors Copper?
(The opinions expressed here are those of Andy Home, a columnist for Reuters.)
(Editing by Marguerita Choy)
Image: Codelco

articles.title: Anthropic files for potentially the biggest IPO ever as CEO warns of risk to humanity from AI - Barchart.com
articles.summary: Anthropic files for potentially the biggest IPO ever as CEO warns of risk to humanity from AI  Barchart.com
articles.full_text:
SAN FRANCISCO (AP) — Artificial intelligence giant Anthropic filed paperwork Monday for what could be the biggest initial public offering of stock ever, even as its top executive warns that advanced AI could pose an existential threat to humanity.
The filing sets up the San Francisco company for a Wall Street debut next month, potentially eclipsing the record $86 billion raised by SpaceX in its initial public offering in June. An Anthropic IPO would also put the company ahead of OpenAI in going public, setting the stage for a pair of blockbuster stock debuts by rival AI developers.
An IPO could give Anthropic enormous resources to accelerate its expansion. The amount the company ultimately raises remains uncertain, as do its final valuation and offering price. But even at lower estimates, it would turn the five-year-old startup into one of the world’s most valuable companies, potentially adding billions of dollars to the fortunes of CEO Dario Amodei and his sister and co-founder, Daniela.
The 335-page filing showed Anthropic’s revenue is growing rapidly, reaching more than $16 billion in the first half of the year — 14 times its revenue from the same period last year. But like many other tech companies going public, the company behind the Claude chatbot has yet to turn a profit.
Despite the losses, Anthropic, valued earlier this year at $965 billion by private investors, is reportedly set to see that value rise to $1.5 trillion or possibly $2 trillion, although its final valuation has not been established. At $1.5 trillion, Anthropic would rank among the world’s most valuable public companies, alongside Tesla.
As for money raised, the offering could bring in as much as $100 billion, according to reports, surpassing the record set by SpaceX.
In a regulatory filing, Anthropic said it will list its stock on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the ticker symbol "ANT."
In the filing, the company said it could use some of that money on acquiring other businesses and technology as well as investing in infrastructure to grow its business to take on rivals.
Formed in 2021 by former OpenAI leaders, Anthropic is locked in a fight for dominance with that company. But they have plenty of other competitors, including Google, newer startups in the U.S. and China and SpaceX, which has an AI business. Anthropic, OpenAI and SpaceX’s AI division have all been losing more money than they make because of the huge costs of resources in building AI, fueling concerns of a bubble.
The need for cash may explain why Anthropic is rushing to tap public markets this year, and not waiting until next year, as is OpenAI's plan. Adding to the pressure is the possibility demand for AI shares could drop, or even collapse. Investors have become jittery about the massive financing needs of the sector, and several tech companies have pulled IPO plans recently.
David Hsu, a management professor at the University of Pennsylvania, said he sees the filing more as a move to diversify the company’s financial base.
“Obviously, they feel great, or at least good enough, on the safety aspects relative to OpenAI, and so that puts them in a position to really stay on track now to go public (first),” Hsu said.
In addition to helping plug any cash shortfall, the IPO will shower extraordinary wealth on Anthropic’s seven founders, including Amodei and his sister. The filing didn't directly state their ownership stakes, but other figures disclosed suggest each will end up with 1.4% of the company, a windfall of as much as $28 billion a person should the company go public at the top expected value.
Dario, 43, and 39-year-old Daniela, who is Anthropic's president, are already worth $15.5 billion each, according to Forbes, which ranks them as the 176th and 177th richest in the world.
Anthropic reported a net loss of $80.7 billion in the first half of 2026, although that included a one-time, $72.4 billion charge for an accounting adjustment related to financing agreements, according to the filing. In the same period a year ago, Anthropic lost $13 billion.
The document includes some unusual provisions, including granting those two and their five other co-founders 50.1% of shareholder votes through a special class of shares. Anthropic also has appointed independent, financially disinterested members of a so-called Long-Term Benefit Trust, holding power to appoint directors, that is designed to ensure the company doesn’t put financial interests ahead of public safety.
Another unusual feature of the filing is its long list of “risk factors," a required disclosure for every public company but in this case one that runs nearly 100 pages — and makes for riveting reading.
Among the risks are the quotidian — the possibility it won't be able to retain key staff or navigate regulatory roadblocks — and the horrific. The latter includes the prospect of “malicious actors” using AI models to build chemical weapons, authoritarian rulers turning to the technology to crack down on their citizens and the possibility that its AI models could go rogue and “pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity.”
Anthropic and other leading companies have touted the technology's potential to cure diseases and speed economic growth. But it also threatens major disruptions to jobs by reducing the need for human labor.
A string of hacking incidents by rogue AI agents also has raised fears the technology will slip free of human control to carry out harmful, life-threatening tasks.
In September, Amodei said the AI industry should slow its fast-moving development to give safety measures time to catch up. Without such a slowdown, Amodei warned AI could be capable of letting loose a swarm of agents that could take over the entire internet within six to 12 months.
He offered a plan in a post on his website to increase checks on the industry, noting that Anthropic is already undertaking part of this on its own. As for other steps, though, he said that would require coordination across the industry and with governments around the world, including authoritarian ones.
Anthropic has tried to set itself apart from other AI companies as the “good guys,” focusing on safety and responsible development as opposed to growing at all costs. Some of this sentiment stems from the company’s dispute with the U.S. government, which broke out in February when the Trump administration accused Anthropic of endangering national security and designated the company a supply chain risk.
Anthropic sued the Pentagon in March for what it called an “unlawful campaign of retaliation” over its refusal to allow unrestricted military use of its technology. The legal challenge intensified a dispute over how AI can be used in warfare and mass surveillance.
ChatGPT maker OpenAI made its own deal to work with the Pentagon hours after the government punished Anthropic for its stance. Anthropic also filed a separate and narrower case involving a different rule the Pentagon is using to try to declare Anthropic a supply chain risk.
A California judge ruled in Anthropic’s favor in the first case and a Washington, D.C. judge sided with the government in the second. Both sides are appealing the decisions.
——
Bernard Condon reported from New York. Associated Press writer Kaitlyn Huamani contributed from Los Angeles.

articles.title: Gold holds above $4,000 as Hormuz diplomacy cools crude ahead of Fed decision - Kitco PM Report - Kitco
articles.summary: Gold holds above $4,000 as Hormuz diplomacy cools crude ahead of Fed decision - Kitco PM Report  Kitco
articles.full_text:
(Kitco NewsWire) - Spot gold and silver prices were higher in late U.S. trading Monday, recovering some of last week's steep losses as declining crude oil prices eased inflation concerns and encouraged renewed buying interest in precious metals ahead of this week's Federal Reserve monetary policy decision. Diplomatic efforts involving Iran and several regional powers helped reduce some of the immediate geopolitical premium in energy markets, while expectations for additional Fed tightening continued to limit bullion's recovery. Gold climbed back above $4,000.00 an ounce during the session, while silver held above $54.000 after testing lower levels last week. Both metals remained vulnerable to changes in Treasury yields, the dollar and the outlook for U.S. interest rates.
Market positioning remains focused on an October Federal Reserve pause, followed by the possibility of additional tightening before year-end. The Federal Reserve remains in its premeeting communications blackout, leaving Tuesday's economic releases and Wednesday's policy announcement as the principal catalysts for interest rate expectations. September durable goods orders are due Tuesday at 8:30 a.m. EDT, followed by October consumer confidence, September new-home sales and the Richmond Fed manufacturing survey at 10 a.m. EDT. The Federal Open Market Committee will announce its interest rate decision Wednesday at 2 p.m. EDT, followed by Fed Chair Kevin Warsh's news conference at 2:30 p.m. EDT. Thursday brings the advance third-quarter gross domestic product report, September personal consumption expenditures inflation data and weekly initial jobless claims at 8:30 a.m. EDT. Softer inflation figures and less restrictive Fed guidance could reduce December rate hike expectations and support gold through lower yields and a weaker dollar, while resilient economic activity or persistent price pressure would strengthen the case for further monetary tightening.
The Strait of Hormuz and U.S.-Iran situation remained a significant source of uncertainty Monday, although renewed diplomatic activity helped ease some immediate fears of another escalation in the Middle East. Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan have been working to revive talks with Iranian officials in Tehran, seeking to reduce the risk of further military confrontation and restore more normal commercial shipping conditions through the strategic waterway. Saudi officials emphasized the importance of reopening diplomatic channels, while the broader dispute between Washington and Tehran over sanctions, maritime access and regional security remains unresolved. Continuing Houthi attacks involving Saudi Arabia and persistent threats to Gulf energy infrastructure have complicated efforts to stabilize the region. Although alternative export routes have helped mitigate disruptions to petroleum shipments, tanker security concerns and the possibility of renewed hostilities continue to sustain a substantial geopolitical premium in crude oil prices.
Oil prices retreated Monday as diplomatic developments encouraged some reduction in the immediate supply-risk premium. Brent crude futures settled at $115.81 a barrel, down 0.8%, ending a three-session advance, although prices remained close to recent multimonth highs. WTI crude also declined, trading near $102.00 during the afternoon. For gold, the retreat in crude oil prices reduced some energy-driven inflation pressure, helping the metal recover despite lingering expectations for another Fed rate increase. However, the absence of a confirmed settlement between Washington and Tehran leaves the possibility of renewed disruption to Gulf energy supplies. Silver also benefited from the improved precious metals sentiment, although concerns about manufacturing activity and restrictive borrowing costs continue to limit its near-term recovery.
North American equity markets closed higher Monday as investors responded to lower crude oil prices and encouraging corporate earnings while positioning for a week of major central bank decisions. The Dow Jones Industrial Average gained 146.42 points, or 0.28%, to close at 52,361.58, while the S&P 500 advanced 53.09 points, or 0.70%, to finish at 7,676.77. The Nasdaq Composite rose 214.04 points, or 0.82%, to 26,169.38, with technology shares recovering after recent volatility. The Russell 2000 gained 10.52 points, or 0.38%, to close at 2,786.42. Canada's S&P/TSX Composite Index also advanced, finishing near 35,926 points, up approximately 0.39%, with gains in financial and selected technology shares supporting the broader market despite weakness in some energy-related stocks. Investors remain focused on quarterly earnings from major U.S. technology companies and the outlook for borrowing costs, particularly as elevated artificial intelligence investment spending continues to influence corporate valuations.
European equity markets also finished higher Monday as stronger corporate updates and improving business sentiment helped offset concerns about elevated energy prices and restrictive monetary policy. The pan-European Stoxx 600 advanced 0.77% to close at 640.66, recovering some of last week's losses. Germany's DAX gained approximately 0.9%, supported by better-than-expected corporate results and an improvement in German business confidence. British technology services provider Computacenter surged more than 13% after raising its annual profit outlook, while Danish biotechnology company Genmab gained approximately 12% following encouraging clinical trial results. articles.full_text:
Posted on 10/26/26 at 16:00
This week, Bitcoin faces interest rate decisions, economic reports, and cryptocurrency company earnings. Four major central banks will announce monetary policy decisions, while Coinbase, Robinhood, and Strategy are scheduled to release quarterly results. As of Monday morning, October 26, 2026, bitcoin was trading near $80,280, while ether was around $2,324, according to CoinGecko.
- On Wednesday, October 28, the Federal Reserve and Bank of Canada will announce their interest rate decisions. The European Central Bank (ECB) follows on Thursday, October 29, and the Bank of Japan is scheduled to announce its decision on Friday, October 30, in Tokyo.
- Robinhood will report earnings after the market closes Tuesday, October 27, while Coinbase and Strategy are scheduled to release their results after the close Thursday, October 29.
- Bitcoin fell to approximately $79,150 on Saturday, October 24, its lowest level in more than a month, according to FinancialMarkets.com.
Why it matters: Interest rates, inflation data, and earnings reports from major cryptocurrency companies can influence market sentiment. Bitcoin and other cryptocurrencies are highly volatile, with prices capable of moving sharply within hours. This guide outlines the week's main events and their scheduled times without recommending any particular investment.
Bitcoin Price Today: ETF Outflows and Key Levels to Watch
Bitcoin declined to around $79,150 on Saturday, October 24, according to FinancialMarkets.com. U.S. spot bitcoin exchange-traded funds (ETFs) recorded approximately $773.5 million in net outflows over two trading days: $635.6 million on October 22, the largest daily withdrawal since June, and a preliminary $137.9 million on October 23.
Coinbase's institutional research team estimates that the average purchase price for these ETF investors is approximately $81,300. On October 23, analysts warned that a sustained decline below the $80,000–$82,000 range could open the door to a further drop toward $73,000–$75,000. This represents a potential market scenario identified by analysts, not a guaranteed price movement.
Another bitcoin event to monitor this week is the expiration of approximately $10.9 billion in bitcoin options, representing 136,029 BTC, on Deribit on Friday, October 30. According to CryptoWatchDesk, the contracts account for roughly 35% of the platform's outstanding bitcoin options.
Fed, ECB, and Bank of Japan: Interest Rate Decisions This Week
According to CoinDesk, the Bank of Canada will announce its interest rate decision Wednesday, October 28, at 9:45 a.m. ET, with its previous policy rate at 2.25%. The Federal Reserve follows at 2:00 p.m. ET, with its previous target range at 3.75%–4.00%, and Fed Chair Kevin Warsh will hold a press conference at 2:30 p.m. ET. On Thursday, October 29, the ECB will announce its decision at 9:15 a.m. ET, with its previous deposit rate at 2.50%, followed by President Christine Lagarde's press conference at 9:45 a.m. ET. The Bank of Japan's decision is scheduled for Friday, October 30, in Tokyo, although the exact announcement time has not been confirmed. Its previous policy rate was 1.25%.
Vugar Usi Zade, CEO of cryptocurrency exchange MEXC, told CoinDesk that traders are paying more attention to what Warsh may say about the Federal Reserve's December meeting than to the upcoming rate decision itself. He argued that market expectations already reflect unchanged rates, making such an outcome less likely to trigger a major positive reaction. To understand the Fed's upcoming decision and its potential impact on household finances, read our guide to this week's Federal Reserve announcement.
Several important U.S. economic reports are also scheduled, according to CoinDesk. On Tuesday, October 27, the government will release September durable goods orders and new home sales data. On Thursday, October 29, at 8:30 a.m. ET, investors will receive the advance estimate of third-quarter gross domestic product (GDP), with annualized growth expected at 3.2%, compared with the previous 2.2% reading. September's Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) inflation report is also scheduled, following previous annual readings of 3.4% for headline inflation and 3.0% for core inflation. The Employment Cost Index will be released Friday, October 30.

Coinbase, Robinhood, and Strategy Earnings: What to Expect
According to CoinDesk, Galaxy Digital, PayPal, and SoFi are scheduled to report quarterly results before the market opens Tuesday, October 27, while Robinhood will report after the close. On Thursday, October 29, Mastercard will report before the opening bell, followed by Coinbase and Strategy after U.S. markets close.
Coinbase shares closed Friday, October 23, at $164.45, while Strategy ended the session at $146.01, according to FinancialMarkets.com. Strategy, one of the world's largest corporate holders of bitcoin, reported purchasing another 267 BTC on October 19 and has a special shareholders' meeting scheduled for Wednesday, October 28. Meanwhile, Coinbase's upcoming earnings cover a quarter that ended before October's cryptocurrency sell-off, meaning investors will also be watching for management's comments on more recent trading activity.
What Bitcoin Investors Should Know This Week
- Protect essential savings: Avoid investing money needed for rent, monthly bills, or emergencies.
- Expect volatility: Bitcoin and other cryptocurrencies can experience significant price swings within hours.
- Watch for scams: Be cautious of investment offers promising guaranteed returns.
- Review platform security: If you use Coinbase, Robinhood, or another trading platform, check its fees and enable two-factor authentication.

Fitch Ratings warns that broader price pressures threaten to keep U.S. inflation elevated for longer, presenting macro risks for global interest rates and cross-border portfolio flows.
Market snapshot: Rating agency Fitch Ratings has warned that broader price pressures across the U.S. economy are raising the risk of persistent inflation. The commentary signals potential constraints on monetary easing trajectories in global markets.
Data Snapshot
- Fitch Ratings expects U.S. real GDP growth to slow to 1.9% in 2026-27 while persistent price pressures and elevated fiscal deficits remain key macroeconomic risks.
Key Takeaways
- Broad-based U.S. price pressures heighten the risk of prolonged high monetary policy rates.
- U.S. economic growth moderating to 1.9% alongside sticky price trends complicates rate-cut timelines.
- Elevated U.S. Treasury yields could drive periodic volatility across global bond and currency markets.

Fitch's alert highlights that inflationary risks extend beyond temporary supply shocks into underlying broader prices. A prolonged inflationary stance in the U.S. limits central bank flexibility, keeping global cost of capital high and capping equity valuation expansions.

Persistent inflation in the U.S. maintains upward momentum on global benchmark bond yields. Emerging market equities and debt may experience foreign portfolio rebalancing if U.S. rates stay attractive relative to growth dynamics.

Global rating agencies remain cautious on structural inflation persistence, citing service-sector price dynamics, commodity fluctuations, and expansionary fiscal deficits as headwinds to central bank target convergence.

- Continued strength in the U.S. dollar elevating import costs for developing economies.
- Moderation in global trade volumes due to prolonged restrictive financing conditions.
Recent Developments
Fitch affirmed the U.S. sovereign credit rating at AA+ with a stable outlook, projecting real GDP growth to moderate to 1.9% in 2026-27 while citing inflation persistence and fiscal deficits as key ongoing vulnerabilities.

Persistent U.S. price pressures act as a key barometer for global liquidity, requiring market participants to maintain disciplined asset allocation in high-yield environments.

Corporate bonds are debt securities issued by companies to raise capital. When you buy a Citigroup Inc. 4.135% 26-OCT-2030 bond, you're lending money to Citigroup, Inc. in exchange for regular interest payments (coupons) and repayment of the full amount at maturity.
