Companies issue bonds to raise capital without giving up ownership, as they would by selling shares. By issuing bonds, a company borrows money and agrees to pay interest (coupons) and repay the principal at a fixed maturity date.
Businesses use bond financing to:
– Fund growth (expansion, acquisitions, new projects)
– Refinance existing debt at better rates
– Manage cash flow without issuing new shares
Compared to stocks, bonds allow Citigroup, Inc. to access large amounts of capital while maintaining full control of the business.
Bonds and stocks are two ways to invest in Citigroup, Inc., but they work very differently.
Here are the key differences:
– Ownership vs. lending: Stocks represent ownership in Citigroup, Inc., while bonds are a loan you give to the company
– Returns: Stocks may offer dividends and capital gains, while bonds pay fixed interest (coupon) and return principal at maturity
– Risk: Stocks are generally more volatile and can lose value, whereas bonds are considered lower risk
– Priority: Bondholders are paid before shareholders if the company goes bankrupt
The current coupon for Citigroup Inc. 4.135% 26-OCT-2030 bonds is 4.135%. This interest rate is variable, meaning it adjusts periodically, resulting in fluctuating regular payments to investors.

The US equity market futures indicate towards a positive opening on Monday, October 26, as investors focus on the sharp pullback in global crude oil prices, easing US Treasury yields, and the mixed cues from the Asian markets.
Dow Jones futures were trading 0.32% higher at around 52,567 points ahead of the opening bell on Monday’s market, as investors focus on rebound potential after last week’s lower close, according to Investing.com data.

articles.title: Euro-to-Dollar Week Ahead Forecast: Downtrend Risks Resuming - Pound Sterling Live
articles.summary: Euro-to-Dollar Week Ahead Forecast: Downtrend Risks Resuming  Pound Sterling Live
articles.full_text:
Image © Adobe Images
It's a big week for the euro and dollar, with a central bank decision apiece.
The Euro to Dollar exchange rate has worked off the oversold conditions that marked its early-October lows, and with that relief now spent, we see the risk of the broader downtrend resuming.
The picture is complicated by decisions from the Federal Reserve on Wednesday and the European Central Bank on Thursday, but the medium-term signals favour the next move being lower.
From a technical perspective, the momentum picture has reset: the RSI, shown beneath the price chart, is back at a more comfortable 38 after a spell below 30, though it has turned lower again:
EUR/USD daily chart. Image © Pound Sterling Live, chart created with TradingView.
EUR/USD trades at 1.1204 at the start of the week.
The RSI fell below 20 in early October, a deeply oversold reading, and the rebound that followed has since unwound it. With momentum reset and the gauge pointing down again, the pair has room to fall without becoming stretched.
The pair has also re-established contact with its 21-day moving average, drawn in blue, after trading well beneath it for most of September and early October. The average sits at 1.1234 and is still falling, and pushes towards it last week faded, the latest at 1.1256 on Thursday.
That leaves the 21-day acting as a lid, and below it the 14 October low at 1.1113 is the next level of note.
We favour a move back towards 1.1150 this week and, beyond that, a retest of 1.1113. A daily close above Thursday's 1.1256 high would change our near-term Euro to Dollar forecast.
Last week we called for a hold above 1.1150 and a modest rebound. The floor held, with no session trading below 1.1185, but the rebound stalled at the falling 21-day.
The Dollar Index Looks Ominous
The U.S. Dollar Index's rally has paused, but the setup looks ominous and we prefer the upside.
U.S. Dollar Index daily chart. Image © Pound Sterling Live, chart created with TradingView.
The index peaked near 103 in mid-October and has pulled back to 101.83, but it remains well above a rising 100-day moving average at 100.58, and its RSI has turned back up from the 50 midline.
A pause well above a rising 100-day reads as a correction within an uptrend. Buyers have stepped in long before the average was tested, and the trend that carried the index up from near 98.60 in early September remains in force.
Commonwealth Bank of Australia expects the dollar to recover some of last week's losses but sees 103 as a ceiling for now.
The Case For and Against the Euro
Our base case is for weakness, but the research we track is split, and the opposing case deserves a hearing.
On the bearish side, Jeremy Stretch at CIBC Capital Markets argues that extended euro short positions could build further: "Such a scenario advocates for a EUR/USD retreat towards 1.111, which marks the mid-point of the trading range witnessed since the start of 2025 (1.0141–1.20810.) Only should the cross retake the 2 October high at 1.1285, we peaked at 1.1269 last Friday, would test the view," he writes in a note of 23 October.
Bank of America's technical strategists put it more briefly in their weekly note of 23 October: "sell corrective rally in EUR/USD."
The bull case for the euro rests on those same short positions and on the AI-related stress in credit markets. Speculators hold their largest short euro position since October 2021, according to MUFG, which leaves room for a sharp squeeze, and the bank finds that the dollar has fallen against the euro in comparable episodes of tech credit stress.
"Following IG technology-credit widening regimes accompanied by falling Treasury yields, USD weakness has historically been concentrated against CHF and EUR. Over the subsequent six weeks, USD declined by an average 2.07% against CHF and 1.50% against EUR, while DXY fell 1.23%," says MUFG in its FX Weekly of 23 October.
French risks seem to have faded somewhat, but it is hard to see any tailwind emerging from that quarter. The French parliament debates the government's budget savings this week, and Budget Minister David Amiel has said amendments already approved would widen the deficit by €10bn, according to CBA.
ECB Decision Is Key for the Euro
The ECB announces its decision at 13:15 on Thursday, with consensus at an unchanged 2.50% deposit rate and a December hike around 75% priced, according to Brown Brothers Harriman.
A press conference that keeps December in play would support the euro, and anything that softens it would weigh. "We believe that the outcome of the ECB policy meeting could thus largely corroborate market rate hike expectations, in a boost to the EUR's relative rate appeal," writes Crédit Agricole CIB in a note dated 23 October.
Bank of America leans the other way, expecting the ECB on hold "leaning dovish as tighter financial conditions offset renewed energy-price risks," with some form of verbal intervention likely on French bond markets.
Eurozone GDP for the third quarter, where consensus is 0.2% growth on the quarter, and German October inflation, forecast at 3.1%, close the week on Friday. Above-consensus prints would support the euro.
The Fed's Hawkish Bias Underpins the Dollar
The Fed decides at 18:00 on Wednesday, with consensus looking for no change at 3.75% to 4.00%. A message that firms up a December hike would extend the dollar's advance, while any hint of patience would hand the euro some relief.
"The bar for pricing out a December Fed hike appears fairly high, which should prevent larger USD corrections for the moment," says ING in an FX note of 23 October.
Thursday's U.S. GDP and core PCE figures follow, with consensus at 3.0% and 0.3% month-on-month respectively, and prints above consensus would back the dollar.
With the dollar's uptrend intact, the 21-day capping the pair and few tailwinds for the euro, we favour the next move being lower, and our Euro to Dollar forecast looks for a drift towards 1.1150 this week.

articles.title: ‘We don’t have inflation’? Five charts show the US economic reality of Trump’s second term so far
articles.summary: As the US midterm elections approach, we take a look at data to see a true picture of the US economy under TrumpWith the midterm elections fast approaching, many Americans have the economy on their minds.US voters are exhausted by years of higher prices. Donald Trump won the presidency in 2024 on promises to lower inflation and undo the damage he said the Biden administration had inflicted on the economy. Continue reading...
articles.full_text:
US voters are exhausted by years of higher prices. Donald Trump won the presidency in 2024 on promises to lower inflation and undo the damage he said the Biden administration had inflicted on the economy.
In Trump’s view, his plan is working. At a recent rally in Montana, Trump boasted about the current economy, framing it as a booming time for Americans. “We’re richer now,” he said. “We don’t have inflation.”
Economic data paints a different picture. Inflation, especially gas prices, has soared over the last year. The job market has been in stasis, and higher interest rates have meant it’s more expensive for Americans to borrow money for loans and mortgages.
These fluctuations have a concrete impact on the lives of Americans. A recent Harris poll for the Guardian found that a majority of Americans, including some Republicans, disagree. Nearly two-thirds said they believe the country is experiencing a recession, and many said higher prices had been a pain point. Americans are reporting having trouble saving, and a third polled said one surprise bill could sink them financially.
Here’s what the data shows us about Trump’s second term so far.
Inflation
The rate of price increases has dramatically cooled since its peak in 2022, when the pandemic’s economic stimulus packages found their way into consumer prices. Inflation peaked at 9.1%, a 40-year high, in June 2022.
In January 2025, the month when Trump started his second term, inflation was down to 3%. By April 2025, it would be 2.3% – the lowest rate since 2021.
That’s when things start to get bumpy. After Trump placed tariffs on nearly everything that the US imports, inflation started to heat up again, climbing back up to 3% in September 2025. After many of his tariffs were paused and eventually found to be illegal, prices started going down again. In January and February 2026, inflation was back down to 2.4%.
The Iran war, specifically its impact on oil prices, has brought inflation back up to levels not seen since 2023. In May, inflation reached 4.2% and has hovered above 3.4% since.
It’s been nearly six years since Americans have seen inflation at a manageable 2% level. Price increases build up over time and can put a squeeze on budgets, which is why it’s such a sensitive point for voters during a crucial election.
Gas prices
In the Guardian’s recent poll with the Harris Poll, gas prices were the most common pain point for Americans, with 83% saying they are making a dent in their current finances.
Soon after the war in Iran began, the strait of Hormuz, a key route that a fifth of the world’s oil typically passes through, was blocked off. Its closure has pushed up prices all around the world. Though the US itself is a major oil producer, prices have still surged since the war. The average price of gas was $4.32 per gallon in mid-October, according to AAA, nearly $1.30 a gallon higher than a year ago.
Even for an oil-producing state like Texas, a gallon of gas is $3.81 compared with $2.64 a year ago. Meanwhile, drivers in California, a state that imports much of its gas from overseas, are paying $6.21 per gallon.
Monthly job figures
The labor market is another metric used to measure the health of the economy, and while the US job market has seen some growth since Trump took office again, figures have fluctuated over the last year. In 2025, altogether 181,000 new jobs were added to the economy, compared with 2.2m jobs in 2024.
Employers have been dealing with a mixed landscape for hiring: harsher immigration policies, uncertainty from tariffs and higher prices for supplies have all meant slow job growth. The unemployment rate has remained low, though, at just over 4%. Economists call this a “low-hire, low-fire” economy, in which employers are neither hiring nor dismissing workers.
S&P 500
Though many Americans report struggling in today’s economy, a small group have never been wealthier. The stock market has continued to soar since Trump took office, recovering from dips seen during his initial tariff announcement and the early days of the Iran war.
Economists largely see AI investment as the leading factor in the stock market’s acceleration. Tech companies are spending billions of dollars investing in datacenters and for chips that are needed to power AI.
While many Americans are invested in the stock market through their retirement and pension funds, this growth has really been a boon for the top 1% wealthiest Americans, who own nearly half of the stock market investments.
Economists say higher prices paired with an exuberant stock market have led to a K-shaped economy, where the wealthier have never felt richer while everyday Americans continue to deal with tightened budgets from high prices.
Interest rates
Interest rates are often not as noticeable to consumers as gas or grocery prices, which they come across every day. The impact that higher interest rates have on the economy takes longer to appear and runs deep. Interest rates shape how much Americans pay to borrow money – to run their businesses, pay off car loans and buy their homes.
For the Federal Reserve, shifting interest rates is the tool it uses to balance the economy. Raising rates can cool the economy, bringing prices down, though at the risk of hurting the job market. Lowering rates can stimulate the economy at the risk of leading to more inflation.
When Trump entered office in January 2025, the Fed was in the middle of a series of interest rate reductions. Officials said they were seeing inflation cooling and slower growth in the labor market. Interest rates were at a range of 4.25% to 4.5% – 1% lower than they were a year ago.
Uncertainty around Trump’s new tariffs would ultimately lead officials to pause the reduction, though the president was still demanding lower rates. As tariffs proved to have less of a long-term effect on prices, the Fed started lowering rates again in fall 2025.
For months, the Fed held off on changing rates as the economic impacts of the war of Iran bore out. But in September, the Fed hiked rates for the first time since 2023, by a quarter point. The Trump-appointed Fed chair, Kevin Warsh, said that “inflation is too high and has been for too long”.
Higher interest rates have already had an impact on mortgage rates, which had dipped down to below 6% (for a 30-year mortgage) for the first time since 2022, in February, but are now up past 7%.

articles.title: Finance Expert Weighs in on Fed’s Dilemma Days Before Midterm Elections | Newswise - Newswise
articles.summary: Finance Expert Weighs in on Fed’s Dilemma Days Before Midterm Elections | Newswise  Newswise
articles.full_text:
Newswise — Just days before the 2026 midterm election, the Federal Reserve will be faced with a high-stakes decision — raise interest rates to curb inflation or hold steady. According to Virginia Tech finance expert Brad Paye, politics are sure to be an elephant in the room when the Federal Open Market Committee meets Oct. 27-28.
“This Fed meeting boils down to an awkward situation,” Paye said. “Fundamentals suggest a rate increase may be needed, but the optics and political considerations five days before an election may lead the Fed to wait.”
However, the decision could impact consumers and their wallets.
“The financial impact on consumers depends entirely on the type of debt they carry,” Paye said. “It can be an immediate cost increase for variable-rate debt like credit cards and HELOCs. Long-term rates are driven by longer-term inflation and growth expectations. If a Fed rate hike convinces the market that inflation is being tackled, mortgage and car loan rates can actually stay relatively stable.”
According to Paye, if the Fed were perceived as a politically leaning institution, it could be a threat to the central bank’s viability. The Fed operates as an independent government agency under authority granted by Congress, meaning the decisions are intended to remain nonpartisan and free from influence by Congress or the president. This means that the institution should remain nonpartisan and decisions they make regarding the monetary policy of the United States are not impacted by the president or Congress.
"The Fed cares deeply about not leaning on the political scales,” Paye said. “If the public believes they’ve taken a political side, it poses a major threat to their autonomy and authority granted by Congress.”
He noted that this is not the first time the Fed has faced an interest rate decision close to an election. The central bank changed its rate target in the run-up to the 2022 midterm elections and 2024 Presidential election.
“In 2024, the Fed lowered rates shortly before the presidential election. Perhaps most comparably to the current scenario, the Fed raised the target in a decision close to the midterm elections in 2022,” Paye said. “In 2022, the inflation rate at that time was around 7% — much higher than the current rate — and arguably the Fed did not have the luxury of being able to defer a rate increase in that case.”
Paye added that Consumer Price Index data released on Wednesday, Oct. 14, will significantly influence the decision to raise rates or hold steady.
“The data came in a bit high, but perhaps not so high that an increase is now certain,” he said. “Textbook economics would suggest a rate hike. However, with the midterm election only five days after the decision, it could cause disagreement within the FOMC on whether to prioritize economic fundamentals or avoid political perception.”
For voters, however, the Fed decision might not be the most important factor when deciding who to vote for on Nov. 3.
“I'm not so sure the voters are going to change the way they vote depending on what the Fed does here,” Paye said. “I think many voters have already decided. For those still undecided, their choice will likely hinge on how much they believe the administration contributed to inflation.”
About Paye
Brad Paye is an associate professor in the Department of Finance, Insurance, and Business Law in the Pamplin College of Business. His research interests center on asset pricing and interactions between financial markets and macroeconomic conditions. His broader academic interests include volatility modeling, forecasting, econometrics, and the interdisciplinary field of neurofinance.
Interview availability
To schedule an interview with Brad Paye, email mediarelations@vt.edu.

articles.title: This is how the informal market closes in Cuba: the dollar rises and the euro loses ground - CiberCuba
articles.summary: This is how the informal market closes in Cuba: the dollar rises and the euro loses ground  CiberCuba
articles.full_text:
The informal currency market in Cuba closes this Monday with varying behavior among its main currencies: the dollar rises while the euro slips slightly, as the Cuban peso continues to lose ground against foreign currencies.
At 8:00 PM, local Cuban time, reports at the close of this Monday, October 26, 2026, a rising US dollar, a euro that declines slightly, and an MLC with a reference value that should be taken with caution. The day's balance confirms the sustained pressure on the Cuban peso, which continues to depreciate against the benchmark currencies.
The U.S. dollar is quoted at 843 Cuban pesos (CUP) at the close of this Monday. This represents an increase of 5 pesos compared to the previous day, when it was at 838 CUP. In a weekly perspective, the U.S. currency has accumulated a rise of 30 pesos from the 813 CUP it recorded seven days ago, which amounts to an increase of 3.7%. The comparison over 30 days shows a rise of 105 pesos since the 738 CUP recorded at the end of September, although it is worth noting that this variation may partly reflect methodological adjustments in the index. The dollar reaches its highest point in the last 30 days today, solidifying itself as the main reference currency in the Cuban informal market.
The euro is trading at 929 Cuban pesos (CUP) at the close of the day. This represents a decrease of 1 peso compared to the previous day, when it closed at 930 CUP. Despite this slight decline, the European currency maintains an upward trend for the week ahead: seven days ago, it was at 905 CUP, indicating a gain of 23.5 pesos over the week, a rise of 2.6%. In the last month, the euro has climbed 89 pesos from 840 CUP just 30 days ago, though this comparison should be approached with the same methodological caution. It surpasses the dollar by 86 pesos, solidifying its dominant position in the Cuban parallel market.
The MLC appears with an average value of 597 Cuban pesos (CUP) at the close of this Monday, although this is a rough reference that should be taken with caution given the low volume of transactions recorded during this time frame. Compared to the previous day, this figure represents an increase of 50 pesos from the 547 CUP on Sunday, and in the last week, it sits 4 pesos above the 593 CUP of seven days ago. Without physical existence, its use is limited to state-run stores that accept it, which restricts its circulation compared to cash currencies.
Exchange Rate Evolution
- Exchange rate of the dollar USD to CUP: 843 CUP.
- Exchange rate of the euro EUR to CUP: 929 CUP.
- Exchange rate from MLC to CUP: 597 CUP (indicative value, limited data).
The official exchange rate of the Central Bank of Cuba (Segment III), at 743 CUP per dollar and 832 CUP per euro, remains significantly below the rates that prevail in everyday practice in the informal currency market. The gap between the official and informal rates reflects the persistent scarcity of foreign currency in the state banking system and the high demand for dollars and euros among the population, whether for emigration, importing goods, protecting savings, or making purchases in the private sector.
Although Segment III was presented as a more flexible currency mechanism, its official rate remains far from that of the informal market and fails to meet the actual demand for foreign currency from the population. In a scenario of sustained inflation, low state wages, and increasing partial dollarization of the economy, every fluctuation in the informal market directly impacts internal prices and the purchasing power of Cubans.
The Exchange Rate of CiberCuba is an index of the informal Cuban market developed from the automated analysis of thousands of foreign exchange buying and selling posts in Telegram and Facebook groups. The calculation disregards atypical offers and spam messages, weighs each transaction according to its recency, and consolidates a representative value that is updated several times a day.

articles.title: UK shop price inflation ‘highest since 2024’ as retailers struggle to limit price rises - The Guardian
articles.summary: UK shop price inflation ‘highest since 2024’ as retailers struggle to limit price rises  The Guardian
articles.full_text:
Shop price inflation has risen to the highest level in two and a half years, according to the British Retail Consortium, which warned that “the dam is starting to break” when it comes to retailers trying to limit price rises for customers.
The lobby group said shop price inflation was 2.1% year on year in October, a sharp rise compared with 1.4% in September, and an indication that retailers were beginning to pass on the rising costs of energy and food ingredients since the Middle East conflict broke out.
It said food inflation, which has remained low during the past year, increased this month to 2.9% year on year – against a 2.5% rise in September – putting further pressure on the chancellor, John Healey, before his first budget on Wednesday.
Non-food inflation, which includes items such as clothing and footwear, more than doubled in October, from 0.8% to 1.7% year on year.
The price of Brent crude oil reached $117 a barrel in recent days, well above the $70 average in the months before the US and Israel attacked Iran in February. Gas prices have also risen sharply, pushing the UK consumer prices index to 3.5% last month.
Until this month, retailers had largely absorbed the higher costs of raw materials, mainly in response to weak demand from customers. In surveys, consumer confidence has declined sharply since the summer, when it became clearer the conflict in the Middle East was unlikely to end swiftly.
Bank of England officials are expected to raise interest rates next week from 3.75% to 4%. If the rise in retail prices persists, it is likely to persuade many of the Bank’s nine-member monetary policy committee to raise rates still further in December or the new year.
Helen Dickinson, the chief executive of the BRC, said: “The dam is starting to break on the huge wave of costs retailers have absorbed over the last two years.”
She said that while there was heavy discounting to attract shoppers ahead of Halloween celebrations, supermarkets could no longer keep the prices of tins and packets on their shelves from going up.
The chancellor is expected to come under intense pressure from his own backbenchers concerned that the high cost of living is harming many of their constituents.
The impact of cost of living pressures on low-income families is the subject of a report by Ruth Patrick, a professor in social and public policy at the University of Glasgow.
Based on a long-term study, it shows that high petrol and diesel prices are hitting families who need to transport disabled children to and from school and health appointments, and workers who use a car to travel to and from their jobs.
Petrol prices above £1.75 a litre in many places and diesel often above £2 a litre can mean that work doesn’t pay, according to Patrick, who leads Changing Realities, an online project tracking 100 low-income families.
She said that in the last month almost three-quarters (73%) of participants in the project had shopped in the reduced-items aisle, while 62% had changed the food they buy and 63% had left the heating off even when cold.
One respondent, Rosie L, who lives in rural Scotland, said: “It’s getting to a point where I don’t know how we are going to keep managing to run our car.” She added: “Public transport is not accessible or reliable where we are [and] not having access to a car would affect every single aspect of our lives. Particularly as my children are disabled.”
The report involves in-depth interviews with 70 participants, of which 67 shared strategies they had taken to reduce costs over the previous month.
Patrick said the help provided by governments and local authorities so far did not match the scale of the problem. “The budget provides an opportunity to make good on Andy Burnham’s pledge that his will be a ‘cost of living government’,” she argued.
“Taking sustainable and long-term steps to secure the adequacy of social security would be a vital step here, and there is particular scope in restoring the real value of child benefit, traditionally a vital source of support with the additional costs that come with children.”

articles.title: Goldman Says Yen Becoming Better Hedge Against AI Market Shock - Yahoo Finance
articles.summary: Goldman Says Yen Becoming Better Hedge Against AI Market Shock  Yahoo Finance
articles.full_text:
(Bloomberg) -- The yen is becoming a more effective hedge against an artificial intelligence-driven market shock as changes in Japan's policy backdrop reduce the risk of the currency weakening sharply when global yields rise, according to Goldman Sachs.
Most Read from Bloomberg
- Trump Prepares for Iran Escalation After US, Israeli Polls
- Apollo's Slok Says AI Has Delivered Zero Payoff Outside of Tech
- Bitcoin Billionaires Are Racing to Ride a 3,000% Crypto Boom
- Trump Says Decision Nearing on Iran: Deal or 'Finish It Off'
- Sinking Profits Turn China's $3.5 Trillion Stock Rout Into Trap
"The yen now looks like a more attractive hedge for procyclical portfolios than it has been over recent years, despite the global backdrop still arguing for further JPY weakness," strategists including Kamakshya Trivedi wrote in a note dated Oct. 23.
The call comes after the yen showed renewed signs of its traditional haven characteristics during last week's global tech stock rout. It surged 0.9% against the dollar Thursday and briefly reached its strongest level in more than a month Friday as concerns over the AI investment boom drove equities lower and sparked a sharp Treasury rally. The currency subsequently pared some of those gains as US yields stabilized.
Goldman argues that the AI boom has left both US equities and the dollar particularly exposed to a deterioration in the growth outlook. A shock that pushes stocks and bond yields lower at the same time would create the type of market environment that has historically been most favorable for the yen.
There are also early signs that the currency is becoming less vulnerable when global yields move higher, according to Goldman. Yen weakness in response to rising yields has been more limited recently than over the past six to seven years, which the strategists said likely reflects reduced depreciation pressure from Japan's domestic policy settings.
That marks a contrast with 2022, when the Bank of Japan maintained yield-curve control as global borrowing costs surged. The changing relationship means the yen "should be a less painful hedge to hold, even if carry remains negative," Goldman said.
A more constructive domestic policy backdrop, the yen's cheap valuation and elevated risk of currency intervention are also helping limit the potential upside in dollar-yen, improving the asymmetry of holding the Japanese currency as a hedge.
In the near term, Goldman continues to favor selling the euro against the yen, saying there is little obvious domestic catalyst for significant yen appreciation and a high bar for the BOJ to surprise markets with a hawkish message at its Oct. 30 policy decision announcement.

articles.title: El Nino's Ripple Effect: How a weather phenomenon could impact UK inflation and interest rates - EdexLive
articles.summary: El Nino's Ripple Effect: How a weather phenomenon could impact UK inflation and interest rates  EdexLive
articles.full_text:
Exeter (UK) (The Conversation): This year's El Nino, the natural weather phenomenon that drives variations in temperature and winds across the Pacific, has prompted the UK government to pledge GBP 15 million to help vulnerable countries such as Malawi, Kenya and Zambia prepare for droughts, floods and food shortages.
But the UK's economic response will go beyond international aid. The Bank of England has identified El Nino as one of the key factors that could increase food inflation in 2027.
This connection between a climate pattern in the Pacific Ocean and supermarket prices (and possibly interest rates) in the UK is a clear demonstration of how extreme weather is an economic issue as well as an environmental one.
Environmentally speaking, the effects of El Nino can be devastating, bringing severe drought to some regions and severe flooding to others. And a stronger El Nino has a larger influence on global weather patterns than a weaker one.
This year's event, already the strongest on record, is expected to peak later this year, and could cause global economic problems if it has a negative effect on major agricultural producers or transport routes.
Poor harvests can cause international agricultural prices to rise. Higher energy costs can simultaneously make fertiliser, processing and transportation more expensive.
The UK is particularly exposed to climate-related disruptions because of the international nature of its food supply (about 42 per cent of its food is imported).
But these effects are rarely immediate. Many food manufacturers and retailers use risk management techniques to limit their exposure to sudden changes in prices, which can initially shield consumers from international shocks.
The Bank of England made this point explicitly, saying the potential effects of El Nino are likely to emerge gradually, rather than causing widespread food shortages or dramatic price rises.
And the central bank of Spain found that the effect of El Nino varies according to commodity, time period and agricultural policy.
For the most part, disasters with regard to food supply can be avoided with the right kind of human intervention. Businesses adapt. Farmers change production decisions. Trade shifts towards alternative suppliers. Governments intervene.
El Nino should therefore be viewed as a potential source of risk and volatility, rather than as a confident prediction that UK food prices must rise.
Everything everywhere
But what happens when several external shocks occur together?
The Bank of England has considered this possibility too, warning that a strong El Nino alongside renewed energy disruption could put much greater pressure on UK food prices.
If extreme weather also affects major shipping routes, the effects on import prices could become stronger still. This is where a climate event potentially becomes a monetary policy problem, as central banks treat El Nino as a factor that may cause them to raise interest rates.
In a recent meeting, the Bank of England's monetary policy committee identified severe El Nino conditions as one possible source of additional pressure on agricultural prices, alongside energy markets and other global supply risks.
And this perhaps explains the thinking behind the UK government's plan to help countries prepare for El Nino. The GBP 15 million pledge announced in September 2026 is based on the idea of "anticipatory action": releasing money before a predictable emergency rather than waiting until the economic damage has occurred.
The government says around 35 per cent of humanitarian shocks can be predicted in advance, while less than 1 per cent of global humanitarian funding currently goes towards anticipatory action.
Weather or not
There is a broader financial principle at work here.
If climate forecasts contain economically useful information, financial decisions can respond before losses actually occur.
So food importers can reconsider commodity and currency strategies to guard against shocks. Banks can incorporate weather-related supply disruption into their financial evaluations, and companies can stress-test supply chains against simultaneous commodity, energy and transportation shocks.
Governments can connect climate forecasting more closely with food security and planning for economic resilience.
And while they may not be able to predict exactly what El Nino will do to the price of a shopping basket, they can certainly act in a way that recognises the fact that information about future weather has financial value.
The UK government has shown that it is using weather forecasts to release humanitarian finance before disasters happen overseas. Those forecasts no longer provide key information just for meteorologists, farmers and fishing boats.
Increasingly, they contain vital financial data.
This report was published from a wire feed. Apart from the headline, the EdexLive Desk has not edited the copy.

articles.title: Federal Reserve survey: Commodity, diesel prices hamper ag outlook - Agri News

articles.full_text:
CHICAGO — Agricultural conditions across the Federal Reserve districts in the Corn Belt continued to be described as subdued due volatile commodity prices and a surge in diesel prices.
A summary of commentary on current economic conditions was published Oct. 14 in the Federal Reserve District’s Beige Book, reflecting activity since early September based on information collected on or before Oct. 5.
Each Federal Reserve Bank gathers information on current economic conditions in its 12 districts through reports from bank and branch directors, plus interviews and online questionnaires completed by businesses, community organizations, economists, market experts and other sources.
Here are what the Corn Belt districts reported in the survey regarding the agricultural conditions.
Chicago
Expectations for 2026 Seventh District farm income edged down over the reporting period, which included the start of harvest.
Heavy rains in much of the district slowed the harvest and were expected to lower yields for corn and, especially, soybeans. Farmers also were expected to spend more on fuel to dry bushels, compounding the effect of high energy prices on the costs of harvest.
“Corn and soybean prices again moved higher, with reports of premiums for current deliveries. Wheat and egg prices were higher, while cattle, hog and most dairy prices declined,” the report noted of the conditions as of Oct. 5.
“In parts of the district, crop insurance wasn’t expected to make up for lost income. Even so, some contacts expected farmers to replace equipment after holding off doing so in recent years.”
The Seventh District of Chicago includes the northern two-thirds of Illinois and Indiana, all of Iowa, the southern two-thirds of Wisconsin and Michigan’s Lower Peninsula.
St. Louis
Agriculture conditions in the Eighth District have not changed since the September report.
“A contact in Tennessee noted that the 2026 crop should range from profitable to break-even, depending on yields and support from higher commodity prices,” the report stated.
“Grower sentiment is cautiously optimistic and less focused on immediate financial risk.”
In Arkansas, many acres previously planted with rice were replaced by soybeans or corn.
Dry conditions allowed several farmers to complete the harvest early without delays from storage or shipping.
Contacts reported strong yields for cotton, soybeans, rice and corn in Arkansas, while in Mississippi drought and high fuel costs reduced hay production.
Forestry contacts in Mississippi continued to report challenges stemming from high fuel and insurance costs, limited market access and difficulty thinning stands.
The St. Louis Federal Reserve District includes the southern parts of Illinois and Indiana and eastern half of Missouri, as well as parts of Tennessee, Arkansas, Kentucky and Mississippi.
Minneapolis
Ninth District agricultural conditions were unchanged since the previous report.
Early indications pointed to a significant decrease in corn production and quality in some areas compared with last year, due to impacts of summer heat and drought. Soybean and wheat production was also expected to decrease in the Ninth District. However, a recent rally in crop prices was welcome news to farmers.
Contacts were unsure what the net effect of higher prices and lower production would mean for incomes.
The Minneapolis-based Ninth District includes all of Minnesota, the Dakotas and Montana, the northern one-third of Wisconsin and Michigan’s Upper Peninsula.
Kansas City
Agricultural economic conditions in the 10th District were subdued alongside volatile commodity prices and increased input costs.
Crop prices rose notably in early September and stayed above year-ago levels, but market conditions were volatile, and a surge in diesel prices and severe drought in some areas raised concerns about costs and revenue.
A food manufacturer also cited diesel costs as a concern, with higher freight expenses expected to meaningfully affect operations and profitability.
Agricultural credit conditions deteriorated gradually. While high cattle prices provided support in some areas, many lenders noted that weakness in the crop sector had a modest negative effect on broader economic conditions.
The Kansas City district includes the western part of Missouri, Kansas, Nebraska, Oklahoma, Wyoming, Colorado and the northern New Mexico.

articles.title: Fed signals leave traders guessing ahead of rate decision - Los Angeles Times
articles.summary: Fed signals leave traders guessing ahead of rate decision  Los Angeles Times
articles.full_text:
Early on Oct. 14, just hours before the release of a much-anticipated report on U.S. inflation, TD Securities’ Gennadiy Goldberg recommended that clients bet against a Federal Reserve interest-rate hike later in the month. The logic was that inflation would likely be benign enough to justify a hold. Equally important, a slew of Fed officials had spent days pushing back against expectations for an imminent move.
Then the data came in hot. Traders quickly ramped up bets on an October hike, at one point putting the odds at roughly 50-50, up from about 20% before the report — and Goldberg and his team began debating whether to abandon their brand-new trade. But almost as quickly as the market moved against them, it started swinging back. By the end of the day, most of that move had been erased. “We didn’t even have a chance to take the trade off,” said Goldberg, head of U.S. interest-rate strategy.
Several market cross-currents were at play that day to stoke the roundtrip, including a stock selloff, AI jitters and increasing tensions in France. For many, though, it came down to the stream of Fedspeak signaling a pause in October. The seemingly explicit language stood out at a time when Chairman Kevin Warsh has said he wants to wean markets off such “forward guidance.”
Caught in the middle, traders fell back on the familiar and took their cue from what policymakers were saying. But they also acknowledge that on its own, the inflation data might have spurred them to wager on an October hike. All of this leaves investors in a precarious position heading into this week’s policy meeting, still somewhat guessing and prone to a jolt if their read of the situation turns out to be wrong.
“There’s a disconnect between what Warsh has said and what the others have signaled,” said Neil Dutta, head of economics at Renaissance Macro Research. “When you have this sort of development or condition, there’s always a risk that the market can get whipsawed at any given meeting.”
To be sure, recent market developments make the chance of such a whipsaw less likely. With AI shares continuing to slide and concerns starting to build around U.S. growth prospects should the artificial intelligence boom falter, traders now have even less conviction that the Fed will raise rates this week — or even this year. Odds of an October move now stand at less than 15%, based on interest-rate swaps. But it was a different picture just a few weeks ago, when the series of speeches began.
The backdrop was a brutal bond selloff that had sent U.S. yields sharply higher. The Fed had raised rates in September for the first time in three years, and expectations were building for an October hike and possibly another in December, all in the name of cooling an inflation rate that has persistently run ahead of the central bank’s target.
Tapping the brakes
This was the vibe when, on Sept. 29, Federal Reserve Bank of New York President John Williams said one more interest-rate hike “late this year” may be appropriate. That speech prompted traders to ratchet back the probability of an October hike slump to about 50% from 70%, based on federal funds futures contracts.
Williams was followed two days later on Oct. 1 by Vice Chair Philip Jefferson, who suggested policymakers should take more time before deciding whether additional hikes are needed, views that sent market bets tumbling further toward 25%. A speech by Gov. Christopher Waller on Oct. 8 that said officials don’t need to tighten at consecutive meetings was enough to cement the outlook.
“I think they were looking at the bond market and saying, ‘Whoa, they’re pricing in a lot more aggressive rate hikes than we are expecting,’” said Nationwide Chief Economist Kathy Bostjancic, referring to the Fed speakers. “So I think that unnerved them and they said ‘Well, let’s just slow things down.’”
By the time the inflation data came out showing the fastest growth in five months, investors already had their minds made up for them, with most anticipating a hold on rates. Bostjancic says the odds for a hike should be closer to 50-50, and others have even stronger views.
“The data is consistent with a hike,” said Ed Al-Hussainy, portfolio manager at Columbia Threadneedle. “The only thing that is standing between a hike and a hold is this Fed language.”
Warsh himself used an appearance in Bangkok on Oct. 16 to emphasize he isn’t pre-judging the outcome of any meeting. “I don’t believe in saying now what I might do at the meetings that we have in the balance in this year,” he said in a moderated discussion at the International Monetary Fund’s annual meetings. “It’s a new chapter at the Fed, and we’re not in that business anymore.”
Even so, traders focused on the fact that the Fed chairman did nothing to dispel market expectations for no move this week — even after the inflation data — other than reiterate a commitment to deliver “price stability.”
Big picture
Matthew Luzzetti, chief U.S. economist at Deutsche Bank AG said the Fed speeches before the inflation data were an example of traditional Fed communications during a period when officials feel there’s a disconnect between market pricing and what policymakers are anticipating. Without it, the market might be even more volatile.
“You can actually still fit it within the framework that Chair Warsh has outlined and other officials have outlined, which is that ‘We’re not data-point dependent, what we are is looking at the trends in the data,’” Luzzetti said, who expects additional rate hikes in the months ahead.
As for those trends — and critically for policymakers — inflation expectations remain anchored, which signals households and businesses remain confident that the central bank will curb prices in the months ahead.
There is support for Warsh’s views on trimming forward guidance both from fellow central bankers and private sector economists who say it can paint policymakers into a corner. There’s a case, too, for refreshing how the central bank communicates its policy outlook to businesses and households.
This time around, officials seemed to have felt signaling was necessary. But it’s left investors confused by the inconsistent messaging: Either there is forward guidance or there isn’t.
“The market needs to know the rules, and right now we don’t,” said Jamie Patton, co-head of global rates at the TCW Group.
Curran, Xie and Swezey write for Bloomberg.

articles.title: Federal Reserve is likely to hold interest rates steady in October. Here's what that means for consumers - CNBC
articles.summary: Federal Reserve is likely to hold interest rates steady in October. Here's what that means for consumers  CNBC
articles.full_text:
The Federal Reserve is expected to leave interest rates unchanged at its upcoming October meeting — even as higher energy costs complicate the inflation outlook and put additional pressure on household budgets.
The consumer price index, a broad measure of inflation, rose again in September, bringing the annual inflation rate up to 3.7%. Surging oil prices stemming from the U.S. war with Iran also helped drive September’s producer price index higher. On Friday, Brent crude oil was trading at a five-month high before falling slightly.
The Fed raised rates by 25 basis points to a range of 3.75% to 4% last month, its first hike since 2023. But fed funds futures last priced in less than a 10% chance the central bank will raise rates by another quarter point at its meeting this week, according to the CME Group’s FedWatch tool. Nearly 75% expect at least one hike by year-end.
“Inflation is still the No. 1 problem in the U.S. economy, and there are a lot of signs it is getting more broad-based,” said Heather Long, chief economist at Navy Federal Credit Union. “For consumers, it means really high borrowing costs for the foreseeable future.”
However, “given that it’s right before an election,” she added, “they won’t hike in October.”
The central bank’s upcoming meeting comes just days before the midterm elections and marks the final word on the pace of inflation in the U.S. before voters head to the polls, which could impact how much power each political party has in Washington.
In previous election cycles, the Fed has mostly maintained its charted course, research shows. The four times the Fed raised rates near a midterm — 1978, 1982, 2018 and 2022 — were all tied to rising inflation, according to Mark Shore, director and economist at CME Group.
Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh has expressed a commitment to bringing inflation down to the Fed’s 2% target. “If the Fed holds, markets could question the Fed’s inflation-fighting credibility,” said Bank of America economist Aditya Bhave in a research note on Oct. 23.
The Fed’s benchmark interest rate determines what banks charge one another for overnight loans. That rate then influences a wide range of consumer borrowing and savings rates. However, while higher interest rates can help ease inflationary pressures, they also raise borrowing costs in the near term, adding to the affordability crunch many households already face.
Shorter-term rates are closely tied to the prime rate, which is typically 3 percentage points above the federal funds rate. Longer-term borrowing costs, meanwhile, are driven more by inflation expectations and broader economic conditions.
“Higher longer-term rates are doing more damage to consumer wallets, as they’ve risen more than short-term rates, and are weighing heavily on refinancing activity, homebuying and vehicle sales,” said Mark Zandi, chief economist at Moody’s. “Higher short-term rates also hurt, but mostly by raising rates on credit cards, consumer finance loans and home equity lines.”
Most credit cards carry variable rates that move closely with the Fed’s benchmark rate. As a result, if the Fed leaves rates unchanged, credit card APRs are likely to remain near current levels. The average interest rate on a new credit card offer is now 23.96%, according to LendingTree.
Mortgage rates, by contrast, are influenced more by Treasury yields and the economic outlook. The yield on the 10-year U.S. Treasury, which serves as a benchmark for many long-term loans, has been near 5%, helping keep the average rate on a 30-year fixed mortgage close to 7.4%, according to Mortgage News Daily.
Auto loan rates are shaped by several factors, including the Fed’s benchmark rate. With financing costs still elevated, many car buyers are taking on larger loans and extending repayment terms to cope with affordability challenges, according to Edmunds.
Federal student loan rates are fixed for the life of the loan, but rates for new borrowers are already higher in the current academic year based on the results of the 10-year Treasury note auction held in May.
Savings rates tend to track changes in the federal funds rate, which is a rare upside to the higher-for-longer rate outlook. Because the Fed has kept rates elevated, savers continue to benefit from relatively attractive yields on high-yield savings accounts and other deposit products.

articles.title: Trump promised to stop inflation. Now Republicans may pay the price in the midterm elections - PBS
articles.summary: Trump promised to stop inflation. Now Republicans may pay the price in the midterm elections  PBS‘We don’t have inflation’? Five charts show the US economic reality of Trump’s second term so far  The GuardianAffordability Is Splintering the Voter Coalition Trump Built With Midterms at Stake  Bloomberg.comLive Q&A: Ask Us Your Questions About Midterms and the Economy  WSJTrump failed to stop inflation. Now Republicans may pay the price in the midterm el...
articles.full_text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump would prefer that voters not worry about inflation. But it's hard for them to ignore.
Filling up a basic Ford F-150 truck now costs about $100, up $30 from a year ago. Mortgage rates have jumped to levels that have depressed home sales. And for the past 12 months, consumer prices have risen faster than paychecks, making the average family poorer.
One week before midterm elections that will serve as a referendum on his second term, Trump is struggling to deliver on his campaign promise to bring down costs, even as he insists the country has entered an economic "golden age." The same frustration that powered his comeback two years ago could now cost Republicans control of Congress.
"Our nation is doing better now than ever before," Trump insists while campaigning, vowing that interest rates and oil prices will plunge once the war with Iran — which he started — comes to an end.
The word "affordability," he says, is nothing but "a con job by the Democrats," adding that "it doesn't mean anything to anybody."
Trump's rosy rhetoric meets voters' reality
That rhetoric comes as voters say they're struggling to afford basics like fuel and groceries and as they blame Trump for higher costs, pointing to the Republican president's aggressive tariff policies and the ongoing, unpopular war with Iran.
Record-high diesel prices, in particular, have driven up shipping and farming costs, creating trouble for Republicans in typically conservative states such as Iowa, Kansas, Ohio and Texas, where Democrats appear uniquely competitive in races that will shape Trump's final two years in office.
"The costs of things are absolutely the first thing people talk about, but also it's their pay not keeping up with the cost," said AFL-CIO President Liz Shuler. "It's a double whammy."
Prices at the pump have become a preeminent issue for voters.
"People hate paying more money for gas, and the prices have gone up a lot," said Stephen Moore, who has previously advised the president on the economy. "It's frustrating because Trump's done so many good things for the economy. But with the Iran situation, that's really had a big effect on the economy, and Republicans may pay a high price for that."
Misty Reeder, 48, said she considers herself "in the middle" politically but picked all Democrats on her ballot in Easley, South Carolina.
"I've noticed that things have been getting a lot harder," said Reeder, who receives disability payments. "You hear about it everywhere you go."
In the six years that she and her husband have been renting their home, Reeder said their rent had increased by hundreds of dollars.
"Something's gotta give," she said. "It's like a dam — the pressure's too much, and it's going to break."
Sandra Capell, 69, said she wants "to see some change" when it comes to the economy even though she voted Republican in Easley, which is part of South Carolina's conservative Upstate region.
"I think everybody is kind of suffering when it comes to groceries, gas, everything really," she said. "I'm looking at the Republican Party to jump on the wagon, get in the saddle and let's bring it back."
Beti Rosales, 47, said higher prices have taken a toll on her family's Mexican restaurant in Allentown, Pennsylvania, part of the Lehigh Valley that has seesawed between the parties in recent years. Limes and avocados cost more than before. So does the plumber who's occasionally needed.
Two years ago, Rosales decided to give Trump and Republicans a chance, hoping for relief from inflation.
"The reality now is that it actually didn't get better," she said. "It actually got worse. The prices of everything have increased."
Rosales is now considering voting Democratic in the midterms.
"Maybe fresh new faces might make a difference?" she said.
Trump promised he'd bring prices down
While running in 2024, Trump hammered President Joe Biden and Vice President Kamala Harris, his Democratic opponent in the election, for high inflation, which climbed as high as 9.1% in June 2022. He promised voters he would lower gasoline prices and unlock roaring growth.
"With your vote in this election, I will end inflation," he vowed.
In less than two years, Trump has aggressively remodeled the U.S. economy. He's slapped double-digit tariffs on many trading partners — including the European Union, India, Japan, Canada and Mexico — and sparked trade wars with allies. The U.S. government now holds stakes in several dozen private companies. He's signed broad income tax cuts into law.
But the persistent challenge of inflation has continued, overshadowing the positives of continued economic growth and a low unemployment rate. Inflation was 3% when Trump took office and reached 3.7% last month.
The president has played down the intensity of inflation, claiming that it is under 2% and "under control."
Democrats have seized on the discontent, using the same high cost of living that sank them before to pressure vulnerable Republicans and put congressional districts Trump won by even double digits in play.
"Now remember, they promised to lower prices on Day One. Instead, under the failed President Donald J. Trump, it costs more than ever in American history to fill up your truck, stock your fridge, visit the doctor or power your home," said Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff, a Democrat running for reelection, at a recent rally in Atlanta.
"You work harder and harder, but the treadmill gets faster and steeper and the bills get higher and higher," he told the crowd.
Cait Conley, a Democrat running in New York against Republican Rep. Mike Lawler, one of his party's most vulnerable incumbents, harkened back to his tweet from the last midterm elections, when Biden was president. Lawler had advised voters to "fill up your tank and go grocery shopping — it will inform your decision."
In a new ad, Conley said voters should follow that advice this year "and then tell me if the system's working for you."
"You deserve better. It shouldn't be this hard," she says.
Democrats turn Trump's attacks back on him
Conley and other candidates have pounded on a theme that Democrats believe will be especially effective this cycle: accusing Trump and other Republicans of compounding voters' economic pain by corruptly pursuing policies that help their billionaire donors at the expense of everyday Americans.
"I know you're frustrated. Washington politicians get rich while you get hurt. Corporations make huge profits while your costs go up," North Carolina Senate candidate Roy Cooper says in an ad airing in the competitive state.
That has included a particular focus on the war with Iran.
"Trump's war abroad costs taxpayers a billion dollars a day on a war we have no business fighting. Our schools crumble, our factories shutter, our gas prices skyrocket. But when they want war, billion-dollar blank checks," says Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed in another spot.
The president "thinks that the economy is doing well because he and his family have enriched themselves to the tune of several billion dollars," said Amy Richards, 56, a onetime Republican who has voted Democratic since Trump became his party's 2016 nominee.
"He has zero idea what it is like to receive a paycheck and have to feed yourself and your family," said Richards, standing outside a polling place in her town of Round Rock, Texas, on Friday, "and he doesn't care."
Republicans, meanwhile, have tried to cast Democrats as extreme, pointing to an ascendant populist wing that includes a number of Democratic socialists.
Moore, who advised Trump's campaigns, said he wished Republicans would spend more time talking about the economy's strengths, including rising median incomes and a record-setting stock market, even as he acknowledged those numbers might not resonate with voters.
"What matters is how people feel, and clearly people are feeling stressed out financially," he said.
Some Trump supporters remain satisfied. Renee Blood, 57, an executive assistant in Round Rock, feels the economy has "improved quite well."
"Of course we see gas prices up and down, but things are much more affordable," she said.
She plans to vote Republican because she worries things will get worse if Democrats return to power.
Trump's golden age might not have arrived, she said, but "we are still working on it."
Colvin reported from New York. Associated Press writer Meg Kinnard in Easley, S.C.; Mike Catalini in Allentown, Pa.; and Jesse Bedayn in Round Rock, Texas, contributed to this report.

articles.title: How many times will the BoE increase interest rates? - Investors' Chronicle
articles.summary: How many times will the BoE increase interest rates?  Investors' Chronicle
articles.full_text:
As far as markets are concerned, a rate hike next Thursday is a done deal. Traders see a near-96 per cent chance that the Bank of England’s (BoE) Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) will raise rates by a quarter of a percentage point on 5 November. This would take the base rate back to 4 per cent, bringing an end to an 11-month rate plateau, as the chart below shows.
Since the BoE last adjusted rates in December, a lot has happened. After conflict in the Middle East erupted this spring, oil prices surged from $60 a barrel to around $100. As an energy importer, the UK is particularly badly placed, but inflation has refused to return to target in other major economies too. The ECB, Bank of Japan and the US Federal Reserve have all hiked interest rates since the unrest began. The surprise is not that UK rates are set to rise again, but that the MPC has waited this long.
Why raise interest rates now?
After energy prices started rising in the spring, many of us felt a horrible sense of déjà vu. We know from bitter experience that rising energy costs can fuel inflation – but they don’t necessarily lead to a sustained rise in the price level. It depends on whether so-called ‘second-round effects’ bed in.
These occur when workers respond to higher prices by demanding bigger pay rises, while firms raise their own prices to compensate for rising costs. After the pandemic, second-round effects were strong: workers had considerable bargaining power while firms benefited from a wave of pent-up demand. This year, conditions have been far less conducive to a repeat.
Read more from Investors’ Chronicle
Unemployment unexpectedly fell in the three months to August, but total pay growth also dipped to 3.7 per cent – its lowest rate since late 2020. Inflation, meanwhile, is rising and remains above target at 3.5 per cent, driven by fuel costs. Still, food prices actually fell month on month, and these are one of the first places that you might expect to see an energy price shock feeding through. Looking at September’s data, James Smith, developed markets economist at ING, said that “second-round effects are so far non-existent”. There is no smoking gun in the economic data.
Ask Investors' Chronicle
- How do Federal Reserve interest rate decisions affect the Bank of England?
- How do interest rate changes affect my monthly mortgage repayments?
- Why do Bank of England economists and financial markets disagree on rates?
- What makes the current interest rate cycle different from previous ones?
These insights do not constitute advice and should not be relied upon by users in making any specific investment or other decisions.
BETA feature — this feature is still being tested and developed
As a result, analysts expect the MPC to frame next week’s hike as a ‘risk management’ move. At September’s meeting, governor Andrew Bailey warned that “it is likely policy may have to tighten” if the conflict in the Middle East persists. Three other MPC members who voted to hold also signalled in the minutes that they would support a rise if the war goes on. Analysts expect them to flip their vote next week, and many predict a 7-2 vote in favour of a hike.
There is another reason why now might be a good time to act. Since the start of the year, markets have priced in several hikes, with investors assuming that higher energy prices would force the BoE to act. These expectations have tightened financial conditions, pushing up mortgage rates and corporate borrowing costs, even though the BoE has kept its own policy rate unchanged all year. In effect, financial markets have done some of the BoE’s work for it. But the MPC can’t rely on markets to keep borrowing costs high indefinitely. Meeting minutes suggest that some hawks are increasingly uneasy about leaving the job to investors.
How high will they go?
It’s very unlikely that rates will regain their recent peak of 5.25 per cent (see chart). At the time of writing, markets were pricing in four rate hikes over the next 12 months, implying a high of around 4.75 per cent. Traders have, however, consistently overestimated the scale of policy tightening this year, and few analysts think that all of these hikes will actually materialise.
Analysts at BNP Paribas say that “we do not think that raising rates will be either a decision that the MPC takes lightly or the start of a prolonged or aggressive tightening cycle”. Berenberg economists agree, arguing after the last meeting that “one hike should suffice”. They expect a weak labour market and tight financial conditions to keep a lid on second-round effects, particularly on wages. “If we are right, it is unlikely that the central bank will have to follow through with more than one of the three or four hikes investors currently price in”, they said.

articles.summary: Anthropic files for IPO as revenue jumps 14-fold to $16.3 billion in H1  The HinduAnthropic, PBC - S-1 (Q2)  SEC.govAnthropic's blockbuster share listing - 5 surprising things we now know  BBCInside Anthropic's massive — and wild — IPO prospectus  Yahoo FinanceFrom Wall Street to Silicon Valley, Anthropic IPO poised to have massive 'trickle-down effect'  CNBC
articles.full_text:
Anthropic, the artificial intelligence company behind Claude, has filed to go public in the United States, disclosing rapid revenue growth, expanding enterprise spending and the high cost of developing and running advanced AI models.
The company filed a registration statement with the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) on October 26. It intends to list its Class A common stock on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the ticker symbol “ANT”. The number of shares to be offered and the price range have not yet been determined.
The public filing follows Anthropic’s confidential submission of a draft registration statement to the SEC on June 1, 2026. The proposed IPO remains subject to regulatory review.
One of the key disclosures is that revenue from a group of existing customers was about nine times higher in the three months ended September 30, 2026, than in the same period a year earlier. The calculation includes customers who generated at least $1 in revenue in the earlier period but excludes subscribers to Anthropic’s Claude Pro and Max plans.
The company reported more than 11,900 customers generating at least $100,000 in revenue over the preceding 12 months as of September 30, up from more than 950 a year earlier. More than 1,900 customers generated at least $1 million, while approximately 250 generated at least $10 million.
For the six months ended June 30, 2026, Anthropic reported revenue of $16.3 billion, up from $1.16 billion in the corresponding period a year earlier. Its net loss widened to $80.7 billion from $13 billion, largely because of accounting expenses arising from changes in the estimated value of certain financing instruments as the company’s valuation rose.
Anthropic reported an operating loss of $693 million in the first half of 2026, compared with $2.14 billion a year earlier. However, using its own adjusted measure, which excludes certain expenses, the company reported operating income of $1.6 billion, with a margin of about 10%.
It reported $8.95 billion in computing and infrastructure expenses in the first half of 2026, reflecting the costs of developing and running advanced AI models. As of June 30, the company held $131.7 billion in cash, cash equivalents and short-term investments, according to the filing.
The prospectus flags risks including dependence on computing infrastructure providers, competition and the cost of developing increasingly capable AI models. Major cloud providers supply Anthropic with computing capacity and help distribute its products, while also developing competing AI services.
The filing also outlines a governance structure intended to protect Anthropic’s long-term public-benefit mission. An entity formed by its seven co-founders will hold a special share carrying 50.1% of general voting power, while the company’s Long-Term Benefit Trust will have the right to appoint a majority of the board. This would limit the ability of ordinary shareholders to influence corporate governance, even after the company lists publicly.
Anthropic has not yet disclosed the number of shares to be offered or the proposed price range. The timing and terms of the IPO will depend on the regulatory process and market conditions.
