articles.title: Interest Rate Forecast for Tomorrow: Fed Expected to Hold Rates at 3.75%–4.00% - Norada Real Estate Investments
articles.summary: Interest Rate Forecast for Tomorrow: Fed Expected to Hold Rates at 3.75%–4.00%  Norada Real Estate Investments
articles.full_text:
If you've been waiting to hear what the Fed will do with interest rates, here's my forecast for tomorrow in one line: expect a hold. Policymakers sit down on Tuesday, October 27, and on Wednesday, October 28, at 2 p.m. Eastern Time they're very likely to leave the federal funds rate right where it is, at 3.75% to 4.00%. Fed funds futures now give a hold about a 90% chance. A quarter-point hike sits near 10%, and a cut is basically off the table.
That doesn't mean Wednesday is a dull day for your wallet. The real news will be in what the Fed hints about December. A Reuters poll of 100 economists, taken October 16–20, found 94 expect a pause this week, and every one of them sees a hike at the December 8–9 meeting. So if you're hoping for cheaper loans soon, I'd lower your hopes. If you're a saver, you're still in a good spot.
Interest Rate Forecast for Tomorrow: What to Expect When the Fed Meeting Opens
Picture a flight that's almost sure to leave on time. Nobody on board is worried about the takeoff. What they're listening for is the pilot's update about the weather up ahead. Wednesday's decision is the takeoff. The chair's words about the months ahead are the weather report, and that's what can move your mortgage, card, and savings rates.
Your Two-Day Fed Calendar
Here's how the next two days should unfold, so you know when to pay attention:
- Tuesday, October 27: Day one. Officials meet behind closed doors. No announcement comes out, so there's nothing to react to yet.
- Wednesday, October 28, 2 p.m. ET: The Fed releases its rate decision and its statement.
- Shortly after: Chair Kevin Warsh holds his press conference. Listen for any clue about December.
- November 10: The next inflation report comes out. That number will shape the December call.
Where the Odds Stand on Monday
Traders have grown more sure of a pause. One week ago, on October 20, CME FedWatch showed about an 83% chance of a hold and a 17% chance of a hike. By Monday morning, October 26, fed funds futures tracked by Investing.com's Fed Rate Monitor had the hold near 90% and the hike near 10%. The odds of a cut stayed at about zero the whole time.
Look further out, and the picture flips. Those same futures show roughly a 78% chance of at least one hike by the December 9 decision. Economists in the Reuters poll were unanimous on a December move. So the debate isn't really about Wednesday. It's about how soon the next increase arrives.
Why I Expect the Fed to Stand Pat This Week
The short answer is that prices are rising too fast to cut, but not broadly enough yet to force a quick second hike.
According to the Bureau of Labor Statistics, consumer prices climbed 0.6% in September and 3.7% from a year earlier. August's yearly pace was 3.4%. Either way, that's well above the Fed's 2% goal.
Most of that jump came from the gas pump. Gasoline rose 9.1% in one month and is 34.2% higher than a year ago. Energy as a whole is up 20.4% in 12 months.
Strip out food and energy, though, and so-called core prices were up 2.6% from a year ago, up from 2.4% in August. That gap matters. It tells officials the problem is mostly fuel for now. They'd like to see whether it starts leaking into rent and everyday services before they act again. Waiting a few more weeks gives them that chance.
Clues From Warsh and the Fed's Own Paperwork
Don't expect the chair to tip his hand early. In Bangkok on October 16, at the yearly IMF and World Bank meetings, Warsh told reporters, “I don't prejudge meetings,” Reuters reported. He wouldn't say what he plans for either of the year's last two meetings. He did note the Fed “removed a dose of accommodation about a month ago.” That's Fed-speak for September's rate hike.
The written record says more than he did:
- The September minutes (released October 7): Most officials said one more increase “would likely be appropriate by year end.” Several described today's rate as “not restrictive or only mildly restrictive,” meaning it may not be high enough to cool prices.
- The September projections: The middle forecast among officials has the federal funds rate ending 2026 at 4.1%. In June, it was 3.8%. A 4.1% finish fits one more quarter-point step, to 4.00% to 4.25%.
How a Hold Fits the Last 12 Months
A quick look back shows why this week feels like a pause between steps. The Fed trimmed rates three times in late 2025, in September, October, and December, landing at 3.50% to 3.75%. It then stayed put for most of this year. At the September 15–16 meeting, with inflation climbing again, it raised the range a quarter point to today's 3.75% to 4.00%. That was the first hike in three years, and it took effect September 17.
Your Mortgage Rate After Wednesday
Many buyers assume the Fed sets home loan rates. It doesn't. Mortgage rates track the bond market, mainly the 10-year Treasury yield. That yield moves with inflation and with investors' guesses about where Fed policy goes in the coming years.
There's been a little relief lately. The U.S. Treasury shows the 10-year yield at 5.00% on October 23, down from 5.15% on October 19. Freddie Mac put the average 30-year fixed at 7.32% for the week of October 22, down from 7.40%. The 15-year averaged 6.68%. This time last year, the 30-year was 6.19%.
Since a hold is already baked in, Wednesday's decision alone probably won't push mortgage rates lower. The tone could. A calm-sounding Warsh might let rates drift down a bit. A worried one could nudge them higher, even with no hike.
Here's what that looks like in dollars on a $350,000, 30-year loan (principal and interest only):
- At 7.32%: about $2,404 a month.
- At 7.57% (a quarter point higher): about $2,464 a month, or roughly $60 more each month and $720 more each year.
- At last year's 6.19%: about $2,141 a month. Today's buyer pays around $263 more every month for the same loan.
Cash, Credit Cards, and HELOCs
If You're Saving
A Fed that holds, or hikes later, keeps yields healthy on high-yield savings, money market funds, CDs, and Treasury bills. The 3-month T-bill paid 4.22% on October 23. That beats the 3.7% inflation rate, so parked cash can still outpace rising prices for now.
If You're Borrowing
Credit cards, home equity lines, and many personal loans are priced off the prime rate, and prime rises and falls with Fed policy. A hold means no relief on those balances. A December hike would raise them soon after. Wiping out a card balance now is one of the best returns you'll get. If your HELOC has a variable rate, budget for the payment to hold steady or climb.
My Call: Wednesday and the December Meeting
Based on everything above, here's where I land:
- A hold at 3.75% to 4.00% (my base case): Officials want more data, and nothing from the chair points to a surprise.
- A surprise hike (about 1 in 10): Only a big jolt between now and Wednesday afternoon would change that. I agree with the market's roughly 10% odds.
- A cut (no realistic chance): Easing isn't on the menu while inflation sits at 3.7% and is still climbing.
Looking to December, I expect one more quarter-point increase, to 4.00% to 4.25%. That's in line with the Fed's median projection, the futures market, and the Reuters poll. I don't see any cuts this year. For 30-year mortgage rates, I think the 7% to 7.5% range is the most likely home through year-end. A cooler gas market and a softer November inflation report could pull rates lower. Price increases spreading past energy could push them up.
A Simple Game Plan Before 2 p.m. Wednesday
- Buying soon? Get quotes from a few lenders and ask for a rate lock that runs past your closing date. Don't count on the Fed to lower your rate.
- Holding cash? Make sure it's earning a competitive yield while rates are high.
- Carrying debt? Pay down variable-rate balances before a possible December hike.
Nobody can perfectly time rates, and waiting for a perfect moment can cost you. Pick the move that fits your budget today. If borrowing costs ease later, you can look at your options again then.

articles.title: Are Bonds Pricing In a Fed Policy Mistake? - Advisor Perspectives
articles.summary: Are Bonds Pricing In a Fed Policy Mistake?  Advisor Perspectives
articles.full_text:
Advisor Perspectives welcomes guest contributions. The views presented here do not necessarily represent those of Advisor Perspectives.
Imagine someone looking into a crystal ball on October 1 and telling you what was about to happen: September CPI data would come in higher than expected, PPI would rise 1.3% (well above the 0.5% forecast), and crude oil would climb $10 in the next two weeks alone.
Based on that, where would you guess the 10-year Treasury yield was headed? On October 1, it was flirting with 5.25%. Given that barrage of hot inflation news, most professional bond traders would have bet on 5.50% or higher.
On October 14, the 10-year Treasury yield surged after the CPI report, hitting 5.33% minutes after the release. A few days later, it fell to 5.03%. The 30-year yield fell by a similar amount. Bonds rallied into the teeth of the bad inflation data.
Mohamed El-Erian, former CEO of PIMCO and a renowned bond expert, asked the obvious question on X: “Why are U.S. government bond yields falling despite hotter-than-expected CPI and PPI inflation prints?”
He offered two valid rationalizations. In this article, I walk through his AI-related explanations and add two of my own. Importantly, I emphasize the one I think matters most: The bond market may be starting to price in the risk that the Fed is being pushed into a policy mistake.
Explanation 1: A Flight to Quality out of Tech
El-Erian's first driver is a flight to quality "out of formerly high-flying tech stocks that are now coming under pressure."
Many semiconductor stocks have been under pressure. The SOX semiconductor index fell almost 20% between October 1 and the PPI release on October 15.
The Nasdaq, with a large semiconductor weighting, fell in sympathy. Foreign markets, including the tech-heavy Korea's KOSPI and Japan’s Nikkei, were also down sharply.
As I show below, healthcare (XLV), consumer staples (XLP), and other beaten-up value sectors have rallied since October 1, while technology (XLK) moved in the opposite direction. This rotation was primarily a flight to quality within the equity market, but El-Erian thinks it may have also sparked some bond buying.
Additionally, El-Erian notes that there are "emerging pockets of credit stress in the most vulnerable segments." To his point, CoreWeave, a large data center provider, saw yields on its debt rise from 9% to 15%. Because investors are demanding such high yields for CoreWeave’s debt and that of some of its competitors, there is a growing concern that CoreWeave might be the AI trade's canary in the coal mine.
Credit-related issues, such as those noted, often lead to a flight to quality from corporate bonds to U.S. Treasuries.
Explanation 2: Is Tech Still a Growth Engine?
El-Erian's second driver carries broader macroeconomic implications. AI-related capital spending has been a primary engine of economic growth. If investors are less willing to fund the AI build-out, and if firms can't afford to fund it, does the economic growth outlook dim?
Saxo's Charu Chanana noted: “Investors are becoming less willing to finance AI infrastructure growth at any cost.”
With 10-year yields above 5% and some AI-related credit spreads at junk bond levels, the cost of financing data centers has risen sharply. Less AI capex means less GDP growth, and lower expected growth argues for lower inflation, which results in lower long-term yields.
Explanation 3: Short Covering & Signs of Significant Demand
My first addition to El-Erian’s list is short covering. The bond market entered October leaning heavily toward higher yields.
To wit, CFTC data showed that asset managers added more than 100,000 contracts to their short 10-year Treasury futures exposure in the week ending September 22, one of the largest weekly additions since 2023, according to Bloomberg.
Furthermore, open interest in 10-year futures rose in 13 of 14 sessions through late September, and in five-year futures in 11 of 12 sessions. Those changes are consistent with new short positions being added as yields rose.
The 10- and 30-year Treasury auctions on October 7 and October 8 appear to have foreshadowed the reversal. Many investors expected weak demand for the new supply of debt. They got the opposite. Per the RIA Advisors team’s commentary piece, “ Bond Auctions: You Never Hear About The Good Ones”:The 10-year note auction on Wednesday sold $39 billion at a 5.300% high yield. It stopped 1.7 basis points through the when-issued level, meaning it cleared much better than the market expected. Thursday’s 30-year $22.5 billion bond auction was similar.
[Primary] dealers took a mere 2.5% of the 10-year, their lowest share on record for the tenor, and 6.8% of the 30-year. Indirect bidders, largely foreign central banks and domestic institutions, took 80.3% and 72.3%, both far above their averages.
When dealers are left buying little at Treasury auctions, as we saw, it means real- money buyers are absorbing supply at these yields. While the bond market didn’t rally on the strong auctions, it certainly put short sellers on notice that demand was robust at yields above 5%.
The rising demand may have prompted Treasury-bond buying to cover short positions. Given how offside the market was, the buying created a circular effect, forcing more short sellers to cover.
Explanation 4: The Bond Market Smells a Policy Mistake
The bond market may be beginning to believe that this month's hot inflation data will force the Fed’s hand toward more, not fewer, rate hikes, ultimately resulting in a policy error.
The yield curve's changing shape over the past two weeks supports our view. The 2-year and 10-year yield curve was 57 basis points on October 7th. Following the CPI and PPI reports, it flattened to 32 basis points. That's a relatively large 25-basis-point decline in two weeks, with most of it occurring on the days of the inflation data.
When all yields decline but long-end yields fall more than short-term yields, it is called a bull flattener. A market that expects the Fed to tighten into a weakening economy buys long bonds and flattens the curve. A market fearing runaway inflation should produce a bear-steepener reaction.
The front end of the yield curve prices the odds of Fed rate hikes. The long end is pricing the consequences.
Reasons to Fret About a Policy Mistake
There are a few reasons I think the bond market should worry about the Fed.
First, the recent increase in inflation is largely a supply shock. Gasoline and diesel prices are rising because of the conflict with Iran, not because consumers are overheating. The Fed can’t produce oil, but it can reduce demand for everything else.
Second, the labor market is weak. September payrolls rose just 29,000 and prior months were revised down by 60,000. Furthermore, the unemployment rate ticked up to 4.2% and real earnings are flat to slightly negative, leaving little evidence of an inflationary wage-price spiral.
Consumers are being squeezed. The most recent retail sales beat estimates at 0.8%, but gasoline sales drove most of the gain. For example, the Control Group, which the BEA uses in its GDP calculation, rose only 0.1. Essentially, higher gas prices are crowding out other spending.
Fed policy is already restrictive by the Fed's own math. The September rate hike raised Fed Funds to 3.75% to 4.00%, above the Fed’s own estimate of the longer-run neutral rate at 3.20%. The median dot plots in the latest Fed Economic Projections (SEP), along with commentary from some Fed members, suggest another rate hike or two is quite possible.
Financial conditions are tightening. The 10-year yield above 5%, 30-year mortgage rates near 7.50%, an 18-month high in the dollar, and widening credit spreads are all doing the Fed's work. Fed Funds rate hikes make financial conditions even more restrictive.
The Hawks’ Case
To be fair, Fed hawks have a rational case for raising rates further. The recent CPI report showed broader price increases across many goods and services, core PCE running near 3%, and, probably more importantly, inflation has been above the Fed's target for more than five years. The Fed is rightly concerned about inflation expectations becoming unanchored.
But the bond market is not voting on whether inflation is too high or what it has been. It is voting on where inflation will be and whether the Fed’s inflation cure will not only heal the patient of its inflation problem but also bring on recessionary side effects.
Summary
Falling bond yields amid hot inflation data are not a paradox. They reflect a flight to quality out of tech, doubts about AI as a growth engine, the unwinding of crowded short positions, and strong demand.
Most importantly, in my view, they signal concern that the Fed is responding to an energy-driven inflation shock and that inflation has been too high for too long, tightening into a slowing economy. The shape of the yield curve and the direction of long-end yields offer a good road map for what may happen next.

articles.title: What To Expect From This Week’s Federal Reserve Meeting - Investopedia
articles.summary: What To Expect From This Week’s Federal Reserve Meeting  Investopedia
articles.full_text:
Key Takeaways
- The Federal Reserve’s policy committee is likely to keep its key interest rate flat when it meets to set monetary policy on Wednesday.
- Economists expect the Fed to raise interest rates at future meetings to combat high inflation, but say there is no rush to raise them for a second consecutive meeting following September’s rate hike.
- Higher interest rates push up borrowing costs on all kinds of loans and can dampen inflation but risk slowing down the economy.
Federal Reserve officials are widely expected to leave the central bank’s key interest rate unchanged when they meet on Wednesday, signaling patience in their fight against inflation.
Financial markets were pricing in a one-in-ten chance that policymakers on the Federal Open Market Committee will vote to raise the fed funds rate by a quarter-point when they meet Wednesday, according to the CME Group’s FedWatch tool, which forecasts rate movements based on fed funds futures trading data.1
In recent weeks, Fed officials have publicly discussed whether to follow up on September’s quarter-point rate hike to counter higher-than-expected inflation. Although some Fed officials have voiced concerns, others have advocated a wait-and-see approach.
A higher fed funds rate means higher borrowing costs on all kinds of loans, which could discourage spending and subdue inflation. But it could also drag on the job market and the economy overall.
The Fed is balancing its dual mandate from Congress to keep inflation low and employment high. With inflation running above the Fed’s inflation goal for a fifth year and unemployment hovering near historic lows, most experts expect the Fed to raise interest rates again in December even if they forego an October hike.
“All signs are that the Federal Reserve will need to continue lifting interest rates in the near term, yet comments from a few key officials suggest they’re unlikely to do so at the October policy meeting,” Michael Pearce, chief U.S. economist at Oxford Economics, wrote in a commentary.
What This Means For The Economy
If the Fed pauses its rate hike campaign in October, it would allow officials more time to assess how much the Iran war’s fuel price hikes are pushing up inflation before taking action again.
Recent comments from two key FOMC members—Fed Governor Michelle Bowman and John C. Williams, president of the Federal Reserve Bank of New York—suggested they didn’t favor rate hikes at back-to-back meetings.
The recent Fed remarks indicated that most officials will support hiking rates by a quarter point at every other meeting, which would mean the next two rate hikes will take place in December and March, David Mericle, chief U.S. economist at Goldman Sachs, wrote in a commentary.
Related Education
Aside from the interest rate decision, the main point of interest from the Fed meeting Wednesday will be Chair Kevin Warsh’s press conference. If he sticks to form, however, he will avoid giving hints about future monetary policy decisions. Unlike previous Fed chairs, Warsh has stuck to a policy of not giving “forward guidance” to financial markets.
Still, Warsh’s words, however cryptic, could offer some clues.
“Chair Warsh is unlikely to offer any direct forward guidance in his press conference, but we expect he will implicitly endorse a December rate hike,” Ruchir Sharma, an economist at Nomura, wrote in a commentary. “His characterization of recent inflation data and market financial conditions could provide some clues around the threshold for additional tightening in 2027.”

articles.title: Wall Street Warning: The AI Trading "Canary" Is Crying Foul! CoreWeave Could Drag Down the U.S. Stock Market - Moomoo
articles.summary: Wall Street Warning: The AI Trading "Canary" Is Crying Foul! CoreWeave Could Drag Down the U.S. Stock Market  Moomoo
articles.full_text:
Wall Street strategists warn that the decline in shares of AI and cloud-computing providers could spread to other segments of the tech sector, potentially dragging U.S. equities down to their June lows.
Zhitong Finance APP has learned that Wall Street strategists are warning: the decline in the stock prices of AI cloud computing service providers could spill over into other segments of tech trading and potentially drag the U.S. stock market all the way back to its June lows.
At the eye of the storm is CoreWeave (CRWV.US). After its bonds fell to distressed levels this month, the company's stock has plunged 41% since October 6—the day major U.S. equity indices hit all-time highs. Over the same period, other "neocloud" players—companies that rent computing power to firms building and running AI models—have also posted double-digit declines: Iren Ltd. (IREN.US) is down 40%, and Nebius Group NV (NBIS.US) is down 36%.
Bonds rang the bell first, not stocks.
It was debt that ran into trouble first. On October 14, a CoreWeave bond maturing in 2032 with a coupon rate of 9.625% saw its secondary-market yield briefly climb to 15%; venture capitalist Chamath Palihapitiya posted this yield curve on social media, and Musk replied with a single word: "Yikes." At the same time, CoreWeave's five-year credit default swap (CDS) spread surged past 1,000 basis points—by comparison, SoftBank Group's stood at about 424 basis points, and Oracle's at roughly 288 basis points; the implied probability of default embedded in the five-year CDS rose to around 60%.
Behind the numbers lies the shape of this business: CoreWeave buys GPUs in bulk, builds data centers, and then rents out computing power by the hour to AI companies, with expansion almost entirely financed through debt. Its total debt has surged from roughly $15 billion a year ago to about $52 billion as of the end of June; interest expenses for the second quarter reached $640 million, compared with $267 million in the same period last year; quarterly revenue more than doubled to $2.58 billion, yet the company still posted a net loss of $626 million. One analyst put it bluntly: if the company borrows at a 9% cost while these investments can generate at best a 5% return, then every step of expansion is eroding corporate value.
Wall Street has dubbed it the "canary in the coal mine" of AI‑driven trading. The reason isn't its size, but rather that it's one of the few segments in the AI capital‑expenditure chain with frequent, publicly available credit pricing: bonds price cash flows, while equities price narratives, so the warning signs invariably emerge first in the bond market.
It's not just the secondary-market valve that's being tightened. In mid-October, South Korean AI computing power provider Elice plunged 32% on its Seoul stock market debut; Australia's Firmus Grid abandoned its plans for a public listing; and Britain's Nscale ran into headwinds at its targeted IPO valuation. In an internal memo, CoreWeave CEO Mike Intrator also acknowledged that "weakness and delays surrounding competitors' IPOs and debt financing" are seeping into CoreWeave's narrative, while describing market performance as "irrational."
From "Micro" to "Macro"
Investors' concerns extend beyond how much they've already borrowed to how much they'll need to borrow after earnings season. Last week, credit risk indicators for several major tech companies with hefty AI spending surged to new highs.
On that grueling Thursday, October 22, the Nasdaq-100 index fell nearly 3%, the S&P 500 posted its worst single-day performance since late July, and the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index plunged 6.72% in one day. Prior to this, the semiconductor sector had already declined for eight consecutive trading days—the longest losing streak since the 2008 financial crisis.
"It's now shifting from a micro‑event to a macro‑event," said Brian Reynolds, chief market strategist at Reynolds Strategy LLC, referring to the sell-off in tech stocks. "In other words, it's not just hitting tech—it's rippling through the entire credit market and then spilling over into equities."
Reynolds expects further selling, which could push the S&P 500 back to its early-June lows—implying a 4.7% drop from the index's Friday close. Based on the S&P 500's October 23 close of 7,623.68 and its June 10 low of 7,265.99, this decline would be roughly 4.7%, in line with his estimate. He also noted that the S&P 500 fell below its 50-day moving average on Thursday, potentially heading all the way back to the June low—precisely the level at which he'd be willing to buy. "I'm staying defensive over the next few weeks," Reynolds said. "I'd really like to step in at that lower level around 7,200."
How are financing costs passed on to chips?
Xinyun Company relies heavily on bond issuance to fund its expenditures. As U.S. Treasury yields rise and inflation remains stubbornly high, financing costs are climbing.
Luis Alvarado, co-head of global fixed-income strategy at Wells Fargo & Co.'s investment research institute, put it more bluntly: the wave of easy financing experienced in the first nine months of this year is beginning to recede. "Now, every new dollar of capital—especially marginal new capital—is subject to much closer scrutiny," he said, adding that investors will carefully assess how much additional yield issuers are willing to offer as compensation.
CoreWeave is also seeking cheaper funding—according to reports, the company is working to secure investment-grade ratings for more chip-backed debt in order to tap into insurance institutions' capital pools; co-founder Brannin McBee says that insurance-sector capital "is limitless" and stresses that he does not view this type of debt as "terrifying."
Ohsung Kwon, chief equity strategist at Wells Fargo & Co, pointed out that if New Cloud cuts its future capital expenditure plans to reassure investors, it would become a major headwind for the semiconductor sector—whose revenues come directly from data center developers who pay hefty sums for chips.
"If they start to perceive risks on the financing side, and the market becomes far more reluctant to support their capital expenditures than it is today, then any cuts in capital spending next year would pose a risk to the semiconductor industry," Kwon said in an interview.
This concern has weighed on the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index, which has fallen 15% since October.
More Than Technology: A "Reality Check"
It's not just tech stocks. Several Wall Street strategists warn that the collapse of the "new‑cloud" sector is delivering a "reality check" to the broader market—just as investors are already anxious about an AI bubble.
"If the AI bubble is set to burst, it will likely begin with a credit event: defaults on new‑cloud and high‑risk AI‑related debt, triggering a cascade of valuation write-downs, spending cuts, and contraction—both valuation multiples and growth rates will shrink," wrote Tom Essaye, founder of the Sevens Report, in a report last week. He added that he continues to monitor for warning signs in the credit markets.
Barclays' strategist team, led by Venu Krishna, noted that new‑economy stocks are currently responding to credit pressures in an "asymmetric" manner: "Widening yield spreads have triggered disproportionately sharp declines, while the relief from narrowing spreads has been quite limited, underscoring market skepticism about the durability of these companies' business models," they wrote in a report last week.
However, Krishna also noted that while he is watching for "signs of contagion" in the equity market, there is currently no evidence that the concerns have spread beyond tech and growth stocks. Investors have been rotating out of high‑flying tech shares into defensive sectors, a move that appears more reflective of uncertainty around AI‑driven trading than a broad, indiscriminate sell‑off affecting all asset classes.
However, once the sector with the largest weighting is sold off, it drags the index lower. Also on Thursday, the S&P 500 fell by more than 1%, even though the number of advancing stocks actually exceeded the number of decliners that day.
"Does the tail wag the dog, or is it the wolf that's crying 'Wolf!'?"
The market remains divided on how to interpret this warning. One view holds that CoreWeave, with its limited scale and high leverage, occupies a minor link in the supply chain; its recent disruption of trillion-dollar AI transactions is a classic case of "the tail wagging the dog"—a genuine localized credit event has been overly extrapolated into a reversal of the entire AI market. Another perspective emphasizes that the pressure has spread from the bond market to the stock market, with industry giants such as NVIDIA and Meta also caught up in the sell-off.
The earnings season has been intriguing: Meta's revenue exceeded expectations, yet it plunged due to hefty capital expenditures and cash-flow pressures; Super Micro Computer reported strong preliminary revenue figures, but still failed to allay concerns; Tesla cut its capital-expenditure plan, sparking worries about insufficient AI investment. Even Western Digital's stellar financial results couldn't win over investors. Investing.com - U.S. Treasury yields held close to multi-week lows on Monday, as fixed-income desks balanced safe-haven demand against a temporary reprieve in French sovereign debt and elevated energy-driven inflation risks ahead of key central bank policy decisions.
The benchmark 10-year Treasury yield hovered near its lowest level in more than a month, trading at 5.003% after touching over three-week lows late last week.
At the front of the curve, the policy-sensitive two-year Treasury yield - which closely tracks Federal Reserve interest rate expectations - similarly hovered near its lowest level in nearly two months at 4.712%, cementing institutional expectations that the Federal Open Market Committee will refrain from adjusting its benchmark interest rate at this week's policy meeting.
Moody's reprieve in france eases extreme European contagion
The consolidation across U.S. Treasuries follows an easing of acute selling pressure in European sovereign debt bourses. Sovereign credit rating agency Moody's affirmed France's Aa3 rating on Friday, providing immediate breathing room to European debt bourses and pulling the French 10-year OAT yield back below 5.00% to trade around 4.973%.
While the reprieve tempered fears of an immediate cross-border liquidity shock, the underlying fiscal realities across the Atlantic remain a critical focal point for U.S. fixed-income desks.
Market participants continue to monitor French President Emmanuel Macron's administration as it struggles to pass spending cuts through a fractured National Assembly to rein in a 5.4% GDP deficit amid ongoing nationwide demonstrations.
The persistent European fiscal friction and volatile spreads over German Bunds have maintained a consistent structural floor under liquid, high-quality U.S. sovereign duration.
Fed meets under shadow of elevated energy prices
Attention across American fixed-income desks is centered on the Federal Reserve's policy announcement on Wednesday, alongside parallel rate verdicts from the European Central Bank and the Bank of Japan later this week.
Policymakers gather against a complex macroeconomic backdrop shaped by persistent Middle Eastern geopolitical tensions, with crude prices hovering above $100 a barrel following coordinated military disruptions in the Persian Gulf.
Although Qatari mediation efforts in Tehran provided a modest pullback in crude on Monday, elevated energy benchmarks continue to inject stubborn headline inflation risks into sovereign bond curves.
Money markets widely assume the Federal Reserve will hold the federal funds rate steady at its current 3.75% to 4.00% target range this week. However, interest-rate futures continue to price in an approximately 80% probability that the Fed could resume tightening with a 25-basis-point rate hike in December should second-round inflation pressures fail to abate.

articles.full_text:
- XRP withdrawal transactions reached 55.75% on Binance and 54.85% across centralized exchanges, approaching their August highs.
- Binance's whale-versus-retail spread climbed to 49.5%, compared with 29.7% across centralized exchanges, highlighting a stronger relative concentration of whale-related activity.
- The Federal Reserve's October 28 policy decision could influence XRP's next move as traders look for signs of improving market momentum.
XRP is showing potentially bullish signals in exchange activity ahead of the Federal Reserve’s October 28 interest-rate decision. Withdrawal transactions are approaching their August highs, while deposit shares are nearing previous lows, indicating that withdrawals account for a growing proportion of exchange transactions.
XRP Withdrawals Approach August Highs as Exchange Deposits Decline
XRP’s exchange transaction mix is shifting toward withdrawals, providing a potentially encouraging signal for the token’s supply dynamics. On October 25, withdrawals accounted for 55.75% of XRP deposit and withdrawal transactions on Binance, approaching the August 18 high of 56.75%. Across centralized exchanges, the withdrawal share reached 54.85%, close to its previous peak of 55.4%.
Meanwhile, Binance’s deposit share declined to 44.25%, nearing its August low of 43.25%. Across all centralized exchanges, deposits accounted for 45.15%, compared with the previous low of 44.5%. This shift suggests that withdrawals are accounting for a larger share of XRP’s exchange transactions. If the trend continues alongside declining exchange balances, it could indicate that less XRP is immediately available for trading on centralized platforms.
XRP Whale Activity Strengthens as Binance Spread Reaches 49.5%
Another development is the widening gap between Binance’s whale-versus-retail spread and the corresponding reading across the broader centralized exchange market. On October 26, Binance’s spread reached 49.5%, compared with 29.7% across all centralized exchanges. The difference of 19.8 percentage points highlights a stronger relative concentration of whale-related withdrawal activity on Binance.
The gap was considerably smaller on July 28, when Binance registered 35.5% and the broader exchange market recorded 33%, leaving a difference of just 2.5 percentage points. Combined with the withdrawal-heavy transaction mix, the data provide a potentially constructive signal for XRP’s market structure. Sustained net exchange outflows and stronger spot demand would offer further support for this interpretation.
Fed Decision Could Provide the Next Catalyst for XRP
The Federal Reserve’s October 27–28 meeting is another important event for cryptocurrency markets. Investors are watching the interest-rate decision and policymakers’ guidance for clues about financial conditions and demand for risk-sensitive assets.
With withdrawal shares approaching August highs, the upcoming policy announcement provides a timely catalyst to watch as traders assess whether XRP’s changing exchange dynamics can translate into stronger buying momentum. If these trends persist alongside sustained net outflows, they could strengthen the case for a more favorable supply environment. Renewed spot demand following the Federal Reserve’s decision could further improve XRP price recovery prospects.

articles.title: Brazil stock market to crash today? What Lula’s surprise victory in elections means for emerging markets, - The Economic Times
articles.summary: Brazil stock market to crash today? What Lula’s surprise victory in elections means for emerging markets,  The Economic Times
articles.full_text:
Lula defeated right-wing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, Brazil’s electoral court said on Sunday. This came as a surprise as the election results defied polls, precedent and global anti-incumbent sentiment. His opponent Bolsonaro, who is the eldest son of convicted former President Jair Bolsonaro, refused to accept his defeat and said he will ask for the result to be annulled due to a Sunday ruling from a Supreme Court justice that extended voting for two hours.
Also read | Brazil election 2026: Flavio Bolsonaro refuses to concede, says he will seek annulment of vote after Lula's win
However, the markets have already begun reacting to the election outcome. Tokyo-listed Brazilian stock exchange-traded fund, the Nomura NF Ibovespa Link ETF, which is an ETF tracking Brazilian equities, tumbled as much as 16% in Japan, the most intraday since 2020. November futures for the Brazilian currency, real, were tumbled 10% in Asian hours.
The Brazilian stock market had sharply moved higher recently, anticipating a shift to the right regime since Bolsonaro unexpectedly finished first in the opening round three weeks back. Brazil’s benchmark index Ibovespa jumped 12% in the past month. The country’s currency also strengthened, with real jumping nearly 5% against the US dollar. Interest-rate futures had signalled expectations that tighter public finances by the right regime would allow borrowing costs to decline.
Why Lula's victory dampened investor sentiment?
Lula aims to present a budget surplus before interest payments of around 1.3% of gross domestic product by 2030. That would leave money to cover part of the interest bill, reducing the need for fresh borrowing. But public debt already exceeds 82% of GDP, while pensions and other legally required spending limit where savings can come from.
Also read | 'Brazil is no one's backyard': Re-elected Brazilian president Lula da Silva
The market began doubting Lula’s commitment to control the fiscal deficit in late 2024. A selloff sent the real to a record low and affected everything from stocks to local-currency debt and dollar bonds.
Will Brazil's stock market crash today?
Analysts expect Brazil’s stock market to see a sharp crash on Monday as election results went against investor expectations of a regime change and thereby a prospective fiscal overhaul. Bloomberg cited trading-desks across Sao Paulo as saying that they expect the selling to be so intense Monday morning, and the declines so severe, that circuit breakers may be triggered.
It also quoted brokerage firm Monte Bravo as estimating the benchmark Ibovespa stock index to tumble 11% in the first hour of trading after Lula’s victory. A Citigroup Inc. survey of 73 investors published Friday showed that most expected the poll outcome to send Brazil’s currency down at least 5%, with swap rates rising more than 1% point as traders scrap the bets on interest-rate cuts that they had piled into after Bolsonaro surged past Lula in the first-round vote earlier this month.
Notably, a circuit break is triggered when the Ibovespa stock index tumbles 10% or more, halting trading for 30 minutes. In case losses deepen to 15% after market resumes, it is suspended for another hour, while a 20% decline allows exchange operator B3 to determine how long trading should remain halted.
For Brazil’s derivatives market, there are no circuit breakers but trading limits that restrict such massive price moves. For swap rates, there is a 90-basis-point trading band in both directions, while currency futures can move 6% up or down. In each case, once that limit is reached, trading is virtually stopped and the exchange needs to authorise a wider band.
The last time Brazil’s stock market triggered a circuit breaker was in 2020, at the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic, when global markets suffered a massive selloff.
"We expect a sharp market reaction on Monday, with aggressive repricing, a selloff in assets and interest rate futures likely to hit their upper limit shortly after the open," Reuters quoted Luis Felipe Vital, head of macro strategy at Warren Investimentos, as saying.
Also read | Lula beats Trump-aligned Bolsonaro in Brazil Presidential election: What happens next for US ties and the Amazon
Investors want a clear and credible commitment to fiscal discipline, the report quoted Alejo Czerwonko, chief investment officer for emerging markets at UBS Global Wealth Management. "We expect the rally that followed the first round to be largely priced out, and sentiment to stay weak until a clear fiscal plan emerges."
Soybean futures crash, emerging markets in focus
Chicago soybean futures fell to a two-month low after Lula’s surprise win raised expectations to closer ties with China, which in turn can erode US share of the world’s biggest soybean import market. The most-actively traded contract on the Chicago Board of Trade dropped as much as 1.7% to the lowest since August 26 this year.
Notably, Brazil is a key emerging market and a peer to India's Dalal Street. Back home, the market continues to see a persistent FII selloff amid multiple headwinds including elevated oil prices. Sensex and Nifty today have snapped a four-session losing streak to move into the green.
Meanwhile, the global market sentiment remained muted. South Korea's Kospi and Japan's Nikkei slipped into the red. Wall Street futures are currently in the green, signalling a positive start for the American stock market later today.

articles.title: Why Bank of England Hawks Are Gaining Ground as Inflation Heads Above 4% - Yahoo Finance
articles.summary: Why Bank of England Hawks Are Gaining Ground as Inflation Heads Above 4%  Yahoo Finance
articles.full_text:
A Bloomberg Economics model shows Bank of England (BoE) officials are the most hawkish since early 2023. Markets now price a near-certain rate hike on Nov. 5.
The BoE has not tightened as the Federal Reserve (Fed) and European Central Bank (ECB) did. It held in September on a 6-3 vote, so two members switching would flip the result.
Why Are Bank of England Officials Changing Their Tone?
Bloomberg Economics built BOESPEAK, a natural language processing model that scores the tone of Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) members. Scores above zero signal hawkish sentiment, meaning a preference for higher interest rates.
The index jumped after public appearances by MPC members, including at International Monetary Fund meetings in Bangkok.
Dan Hanson, chief UK economist at Bloomberg Economics, ties the shift to energy costs.
      "The rise in the index is striking and has coincided with the ramp up in energy costs in recent months"
Hanson expects hikes in November and February. However, he concedes the committee could simply be talking tough.
Governor Andrew Bailey holds a swing vote. He says prolonged high energy prices make a hike harder to avoid.
Deputies Dave Ramsden and Clare Lombardelli have echoed that warning as the Iran war continues.
How Far Behind the Fed and ECB Is the Bank of England?
The BoE kept rates at 3.75% in September, while the Fed raised its target range to 3.75% to 4%.
Bloomberg projects UK inflation above 4% by early next year, twice the BoE's 2% target. Meanwhile, rising private-sector pay ahead of the 2027 wage talks may weaken the labor market's ability to restrain prices.
However, the committee remains split. Deputy Governor Sarah Breeden said on Oct. 15 that 2022 taught firms to absorb costs instead of raising prices. Doves Alan Taylor and Swati Dhingra, who favor looser policy, urged caution.
A November hike would put the BoE on the same path as the Fed and ECB. Japan's central bank has already moved, with its September rate hike lifting the rate to 1.25%, the highest since 1995. Investors expect at least four hikes by July, a path Chief Economist Huw Pill has questioned.
Read the Original story Why Bank of England Hawks Are Gaining Ground as Inflation Heads Above 4% by Darryn Pollock at beincrypto.com

articles.title: Oil Prices Dip but Hold Above $100 as Middle East Supply Threats Mount - Crude Oil Prices Today | OilPrice.com
articles.summary: Oil Prices Dip but Hold Above $100 as Middle East Supply Threats Mount  Crude Oil Prices Today | OilPrice.comOil Falls Amid Diplomatic Efforts to Ease U.S.-Iran Hostilities  WSJOil prices dip on Iran peace hopes, but Saudi attacks keep Brent near six-month highs  The Times of IndiaOil extends losses as Iran mediation efforts ease escalation fears By Investing.com  Investing.com IndiaOil Declines as Diplomacy Offers Hope of Mideast Deescalation  B...
articles.full_text:
Crude oil prices began trading with a dip this week but remain significantly elevated as hostilities between Yemen’s Houthis and Saudi Arabia, as well as Iranian attacks on tankers in the Persian Gulf, continue.
At the time of writing, Brent crude was trading at $114.42 per barrel, down from over $116 per barrel last week but up from around $60 per barrel at the end of 2025.
West Texas Intermediate remained above $100 per barrel, despite the dip from Friday’s close, trading at $100.97 per barrel at the time of writing, down from a 2026 high of over $112 in April, but up from less than $60 per barrel at the end of December last year.
The trend on the futures market appears to be a series of climbs, interspersed with declines, where the declines tend to be a lot more moderate than the climbs. It is a concerning trend if it extends in time, even though physical oil prices have declined from highs reached earlier in the year in the past couple of weeks.
Meanwhile, data has emerged showing a record number of tanker attacks in the Strait of Hormuz so far this month, while the Yemeni Houthis continue to attack Saudi infrastructure, including oil facilities. The latest attacks took place over the weekend, targeting oil facilities and an airport.
At least 28 vessels were attacked in Hormuz this month, the data, coming from the UK Maritime Trade Operations and the International Maritime Organization, showed, as reported by Reuters at the end of last week. The actual number is likely much higher since not all attacks get reported. Of these attacks, at least 11 targeted supertankers and damaged them. This is problematic in a world with tightening supply of very large crude carriers.

articles.title: Global Market: China's yuan hits four-year high as dollar weakens ahead of policy meetings - The Economic Times
articles.summary: Global Market: China's yuan hits four-year high as dollar weakens ahead of policy meetings  The Economic Times
articles.full_text:
The onshore yuan strengthened to 6.6682 per dollar during the session, its highest level since June 2022, before trading at 6.6691 as of 0252 GMT. If the currency holds its gains through the late-night close, it would mark an eighth consecutive session of appreciation, its longest winning streak since May.
Read more: Fed expected to pause rate hikes ahead of US midterms
The offshore yuan was last trading at 6.6688 per dollar, up around 0.01% in Asian trade.
Before the market opened, the People's Bank of China (PBOC) set the yuan's daily midpoint at 6.7162 per dollar, its strongest level since February 2, 2023. The midpoint was 471 pips weaker than a Reuters estimate of 6.6691, marking the largest deviation towards the weaker side since September 23.
China allows the onshore yuan to trade within a 2% range on either side of the daily midpoint. The central bank has gradually strengthened its official guidance this year, but the fixings have remained weaker than market expectations, indicating efforts to manage the pace of the currency's appreciation, Reuters reported.
Read more: Global Market Today: Asian shares slip as AI jitters deepen ahead of big tech earnings
Market participants are also assessing the outlook for global monetary policy, with the US Federal Reserve, Bank of Japan and European Central Bank widely expected to leave interest rates unchanged at their meetings later this week. Investors will look for signals on the future policy path, particularly as central banks balance inflation risks against slowing economic growth.
In China, attention is turning to the fifth plenum for fresh signals on economic policy and the government's approach to supporting growth and domestic demand.
Goldman Sachs analysts expect the yuan's appreciation to continue gradually, arguing that the currency's starting point of undervaluation could allow for further gains beyond current market expectations. The brokerage maintained its 12-month forecast for the yuan at 6.40 per dollar.
However, analysts cautioned that currency appreciation alone would not resolve China's economic challenges, highlighting the need for stronger domestic demand alongside a firmer exchange rate.
The yuan's recent strength reflects a mix of dollar weakness, shifting expectations about global monetary policy, and domestic currency guidance. Investors will closely monitor the PBOC's daily fixings and signals from upcoming policy meetings for clues on whether the currency's rally can be sustained.

articles.title: Yen becoming more favorable hedge against AI market shock, says Goldman Sachs - The Japan Times
articles.summary: Yen becoming more favorable hedge against AI market shock, says Goldman Sachs  The Japan Times
articles.full_text:
The yen is becoming a more effective hedge against an artificial intelligence-driven market shock as changes in Japan’s policy backdrop reduce the risk of the currency weakening sharply when global yields rise, according to Goldman Sachs.
“The yen now looks like a more attractive hedge for procyclical portfolios than it has been over recent years, despite the global backdrop still arguing for further JPY weakness,” strategists including Kamakshya Trivedi wrote in a note dated Friday.
The call comes after the yen showed renewed signs of its traditional haven characteristics during last week’s global technology stock rout. It surged 0.9% against the dollar Thursday and briefly reached its strongest level in more than a month Friday as concerns over the AI investment boom drove equities lower and sparked a sharp U.S. Treasury rally. The currency subsequently pared some of those gains as U.S. yields stabilized.
Goldman argues that the AI boom has left both U.S. equities and the dollar particularly exposed to a deterioration in the growth outlook. A shock that pushes stocks and bond yields lower at the same time would create the type of market environment that has historically been most favorable for the yen.
There are also early signs that the currency is becoming less vulnerable when global yields move higher, according to Goldman. Yen weakness in response to rising yields has been more limited recently than over the past six to seven years, which the strategists said likely reflects reduced depreciation pressure from Japan’s domestic policy settings.
That marks a contrast with 2022, when the Bank of Japan maintained yield-curve control as global borrowing costs surged. The changing relationship means the yen “should be a less painful hedge to hold, even if carry remains negative,” Goldman said.
A more constructive domestic policy backdrop, the yen’s cheap valuation and elevated risk of currency intervention are also helping limit the potential upside in dollar-yen, improving the asymmetry of holding the Japanese currency as a hedge.
In the near term, Goldman continues to favor selling the euro against the yen, saying there is little obvious domestic catalyst for significant yen appreciation and a high bar for the BOJ to surprise markets with a hawkish message at its Oct. 30 policy decision announcement.
Over a longer horizon, however, the strategists see the dollar-yen trade as the more effective protection against a deterioration in risk sentiment. “Short USD/JPY should be the most effective hedge against general growth wobbles or, specifically, a broad AI shock,” they wrote.

articles.title: European gas prices soar to four-year high over winter supply fears
articles.summary: Jump fuelled by fears of further Middle East supply disruptions amid reports of US-Israeli plans to strike Iran  European gas prices have jumped to levels not seen since 2022 as fears continue to grow around the continent’s supply this winter and the conflict in the Middle East.Wholesale gas prices hit €97 (£81) a megawatt-hour on Monday, as temperatures across Europe fell and traders priced in stronger demand for heating. Continue reading...
articles.full_text:
European gas prices have jumped to levels not seen since 2022 as fears continue to grow around the continent’s supply this winter and the conflict in the Middle East.
Wholesale gas prices hit €97 (£81) a megawatt-hour on Monday, as temperatures across Europe fell and traders priced in stronger demand for heating.
The UK’s month ahead contract also rose by 4% to 240p a therm, its highest level since December 2022 when prices were rocketing after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
The jump in gas prices comes as fears grow that there could be further supply disruptions in the Middle East, amid reports the US and Israel have drawn up plans for renewed strikes against Iran after the US midterm elections.
Those reports helped send the oil price as high as $117 a barrel on Friday. The international Brent crude benchmark retreated about 2% on Monday but remains at nearly $115 a barrel.
Europe is also facing a shortage of stored gas reserves as it heads into winter with stores at their lowest level in more than a decade owing to a slowdown in exports from Qatar and an increase in consumption in the summer to power refrigeration and cooling. European storage is now about 75% full, against a seasonal average closer to 80%.
Britain’s energy regulators have said the country is expected to pay some of the highest energy costs in Europe this winter amid a reliance on imports to ensure a steady supply. The UK has some of the smallest gas stores in Europe after decades of relying on homegrown production from the North Sea.
The UK paid a record £4bn on power imports over the year ending in August, according to figures from the Office for National Statistics, of which half was spent on electricity imported from France.
It has also made near-record payments over the past year to fire up gas plants while wind and solar farms have been paid to turn off because of bottlenecks in the grid.
Meanwhile, British households face growing energy bills, which are predicted to rise 16% in January to reach the equivalent of about £2,000 for the typical annual dual fuel bill.
European stock markets rose slightly on Monday on the weaker oil price, with the Stoxx Europe 600 – which tracks the biggest companies on the continent – up by 0.3% in early trading on Monday. The UK’s blue chip FTSE 100 rose by 0.4%.

articles.title: Should we tip on takeout? We weighed all angles and the answer is …
articles.summary: Adding gratuity doesn’t always make sense, but the obligation to has been entrenched as a societal normYou arrive at a pizza place to pick up your order. The credit-card screen asks if you would like to tip and gives some choices. It seems strange to tip the cashier, who did nothing but hand over the pizza. But it also seems a little harsh to select “no tip” instead of one of those more generous options.What’s the right thing to do? Continue reading...
articles.full_text:
You arrive at a pizza place to pick up your order. The credit-card screen asks if you would like to tip and gives some choices. It seems strange to tip the cashier, who did nothing but hand over the pizza. But it also seems a little harsh to select “no tip” instead of one of those more generous options.
What’s the right thing to do?
Start with the situations where our instincts are clearest. Tipping is normal at restaurants, in taxis or after haircuts. We don’t usually tip when we buy fast food, ride on a bus or have the plumbing fixed.
What explains the difference? One way to think about it is through economics. A server’s pay, in effect, is split in two: a salary paid by the restaurant, and a tip paid directly by you, the customer. But why do you get a say in the server’s pay when you don’t have that role in other cases?
The logic is simple: you’re in a better position than the restaurant owner to judge the quality of the service.
You know whether the server was fast or slow – so your tip rates it as baseline, above baseline or below baseline. A low tip, though, can feel confrontational: you’re delivering your verdict in front of the person you’re judging.
And it’s not just restaurants. A cab company knows how far the driver went, but not how well the car was driven. You know that, so you leave a tip. The owner of a hair salon knows how many customers were served, but not whether they were served well. Or take housekeepers at a hotel: you don’t watch them work, but you still know something the hotel doesn’t know: how big a mess you left behind.
The common thread is that you know something the employer doesn’t. And that gives you a role in deciding how much the worker gets paid.
But what about the places where we don’t tip?
You don’t tip the cashiers at a fast-food restaurant. Why? The company trains the staff to say the same things every time, then watches them. You don’t see much that the company doesn’t. And the cashier works behind a counter where the pressure to keep moving is already strong.
When you ride the crosstown bus, you don’t usually see anything important the bus company doesn’t, and the prospect of being tipped probably wouldn’t change what the driver does. So you don’t tip.
Or a company sends you a plumber. You might know whether the problem got fixed, but not whether the plumber worked efficiently or cut corners. Since you don’t know anything the boss doesn’t, there’s no reason to give you a direct role in setting the agent’s pay.
Compare this with a case where the plumber has to climb long stairs to reach you or face off against a scary dog. Here, you do know about hidden hardships – hidden from the plumber’s boss, that is – so tipping is a sensible economic gesture as well as a kind one.
Still, the theory only gets us so far. Why don’t people usually tip employees of airlines, front-desk workers at hotels or baggers at the grocery store?
Maybe it was a mistake to imagine that there’s one explanation for tipping rather than many of them – and that they change across time and place. In some cultures, there’s little or no tipping, and a tip might even be considered an insult.
In fact, our theory above was a better fit in the United States 20 years ago than it is today, because invitations to tip have become more common in places where customers know little that management doesn’t already know.
So why is the pizza place asking you for a tip in the first place?
Some people imagine that the business is trying to get out of paying its clerks what it should; it’s foisting that job on to its customers. But that’s probably the wrong way to look at it. Clerks decide whether to take jobs and keep them based on the total pay they take home, wherever it comes from. Adding tips to their pay, in the long run, will probably hold down the base salaries that they’re paid.
Look at it this way: if all tipping were banned tomorrow, you’d expect the base pay of servers to go up soon afterwards, along with prices on the menu. Otherwise the loss of tips would just be a pay cut; and if restaurants could pay less to their servers without losing them, they’d presumably (alas?) be doing it already.
More likely, the takeout place just needs to somehow raise its prices. They think you’ll react better to an invitation to tip than you would to a more expensive menu, though it comes to the same thing. You’ll use the menu to decide what to buy and won’t think about the tip. Then when tipping is invited at the end, you won’t tell yourself the cafe raised its prices. You’ll just think the culture is changing: everyone wants a tip nowadays! But in effect, the invitation to tip is just a price hike that the owner is hoping you won’t view that way.
There’s another oddity: the timing of the request. An unfamiliar invitation to tip sometimes comes early, when some of the work you’re buying hasn’t been done yet. This might give the server a chance to see your tip before performing and then retaliate on the spot with sluggish service if you seem ungenerous, or do a good job if you’ve been nice.
This order of operations isn’t very consistent with the idea that you’re tipping in order to rate the quality of the work done.
So what should you do when the screen asks you to tip?
In those new settings – bakeries, coffee shop, fast-food places – your choice can function as a kind of vote – not on the quality of service, but on tipping itself. Leaving a tip accepts the invitation to help set the pay and encourages the arrangement to continue. If you don’t tip, you’re saying that you’re against using tips as a way to divide decisions about pay in this situation.
But once tipping is customary – not auditioning for acceptance, but entrenched – then you should tip, at least usually. The obligation isn’t set by law, but you consent to it when you eat at the restaurant. The owner is saying, in effect: your obligation to pay for this meal will be a combination of laws (that make you pay the check) and norms (that make you pay the tip).
You should play by the rules that the business has set or not play at all, even if the rules might seem to defy your theory, or any theory, of when tipping serves a good purpose. But when deciding what to order or where to eat, just remember: 20% of the cost (or whatever the customary tip might be) isn’t shown on the menu.
To put this more generally: if you run into a norm that you aren’t sure you like, ask whether you’re in a position to help shape it or whether you can only decide whether to go along with it.
The bottom line: tipping for takeout doesn’t make sense as a custom. It should be resisted unless it’s entrenched, at which point it’s best viewed as part of the bargain.
Put differently, we would vote against the idea; but having lost the vote, we go along with it.
- Ward Farnsworth is a professor at the University of Texas school of law, and Saul Levmore at the University of Chicago law school. This is an edited excerpt from their new book, Should You Tip for Takeout? Solving the Puzzles of Everyday Life, out now

articles.title: Survey on the Access to Finance of Enterprises: lending conditions tightened
articles.full_text:
26 October 2026
- Firms reported a further net tightening of bank loan interest rates and other loan conditions related to price and non-price factors.
- Bank loan availability declined by more than financing needs, widening the financing gap.
- In this survey round the sample composition changed substantially, with first-time respondents accounting for the majority of the sample. This makes it more challenging to interpret the responses to the numerical questions – such as those on expectations for selling prices, input costs and inflation – at this stage.
In the most recent round of the Survey on the Access to Finance of Enterprises (SAFE) in the euro area, covering the third quarter of 2026, euro area firms widely reported a further net increase in interest rates on bank loans (net 46%, compared with 42% in the previous quarter). Large firms reported increases more often (net 55%, up from 41%) than small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) (net 38%, down from 43%). At the same time, a net 27% of firms (down from 31% in the previous quarter) reported increases in other financing costs (i.e. charges, fees and commissions) and in collateral requirements (net 14%, up from 10%) (Chart 1).
In this survey round, firms reported that the availability of bank loans had declined by more than their needs. Firms reported a decrease in the availability of bank loans in the third quarter of 2026 (-5%, compared with a net -1% in the second quarter of 2026), with both SMEs (net -5%, compared with -4%) and large firms (net -6%, down from 4%) reporting lower availability. At the same time, a net 2% of firms reported a decrease in their bank loan needs, while a net 2% reported an increase in the previous quarter. Developments in needs differed by firm size: SMEs reported broadly unchanged needs (net 1%, compared with 2%), while large firms reported a decrease (net -6%, down from 3%). As a result, the bank loan financing gap indicator, which captures the difference between changes in the need for and the availability of bank loans, was positive (net 2%, compared with 3% in the previous quarter) (Chart 2). Looking ahead, more firms expect the availability of external financing to decrease over the next three months.
Firms continued to perceive the general economic outlook as the main factor constraining the availability of external financing (net 31%, compared with 29% in the previous survey round), with large firms now more pessimistic than SMEs (net 35% and 29%, respectively). In this survey round, a net 9% of firms indicated that their firm-specific outlook, in terms of sales and profits, had a negative impact on the availability of external financing (after 10% in the previous survey round), while the impact of their capital position and creditworthiness remained positive.
The substantial change in the sample composition in this survey round, with first-time respondents accounting for the majority of the sample, makes it challenging to interpret the responses to the numerical questions at this stage. The increase in selling price expectations was contained among firms that took part in both this round and the previous one, whereas selling price expectations rose significantly in the full sample (Chart 3).
Similarly, firms’ median inflation expectations remained broadly unchanged among firms that took part in both the current and previous survey rounds, whereas they rose significantly in the full sample (Chart 4). The risk assessment for firms’ five-year-ahead inflation outlook was broadly unchanged.
The report published today presents the main results of the 40th round of the SAFE for the euro area. The survey was conducted between 26 August and 2 October 2026. In this survey round, around half of the firms were asked about changes in the period between July and September 2026. The remainder were asked about changes in the period between April and September 2026. Additionally, firms reported their expectations for euro area inflation, selling prices and other costs. The sample comprised 12,822 enterprises in the euro area, of which 11,917 (93%) had fewer than 250 employees.
For media queries, please contact: William Lelieveldt, tel.: +49 170 227 9090.
Notes
- The report on this round of the SAFE, together with the questionnaire and methodological information, is available on the ECB’s website.
- Detailed data series for the individual euro area countries and aggregate euro area results are available in the ECB Data Portal.

articles.title: Frank Elderson: Taking action for nature – investing in economic resilience and prosperity
articles.full_text:
- SPEECH
Taking action for nature – investing in economic resilience and prosperity
Keynote speech by Frank Elderson, Member of the Executive Board of the ECB and Vice-Chair of the Supervisory Board of the ECB, at COP17 Finance and Biodiversity Day
Yerewan, 26 October 2026
It is a pleasure to open the Finance and Biodiversity Day at COP17.
The theme of this COP is “Taking Action for Nature’’.
We have talked about the need for action for long enough. Now we need to act.
Four years ago, the international community adopted the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, setting out a pathway to living in harmony with nature by 2050.
The destination is set. The path is clear. But progress has remained limited. And nature has not stood still. It has continued to deteriorate. So we need to accelerate.
Tangible progress requires a shift from targets to implementation, from awareness to engagement, from ambition to investment.
COP17 must help us accelerate the journey. And finance has a central role to play. That should not come as a surprise: without investment, there can be no transition.
But we need to get the economics right. Protecting and restoring nature is not simply spending. It is investment: investment in the natural capital on which our economies depend, investment in resilience, and investment in our future prosperity.
That is why Finance and Biodiversity Day matters.
When ecosystems falter, the economy is at risk
Let me start with a fundamental question: why is nature so important to the economy?
We tend to think of roads, bridges and electricity grids as critical assets that serve as the foundation of a modern economy.
But there is another kind of infrastructure that we often take for granted: natural capital.
Nature provides services without which large parts of our economies could not function. Water keeps our factories and farms running, healthy soils sustain our food systems, forests and wetlands regulate droughts and floods, oceans absorb heat and carbon.
The World Bank estimates that as much as half of the world’s GDP relies on biodiversity, natural capital and ecosystem services.[1]
Our own analysis shows that 72% of companies in the euro area depend on at least one ecosystem service. And 75% of euro area corporate lending goes to companies that are highly dependent on at least one ecosystem service.[2]
The message is clear: nature is not peripheral to economic activity. It is fundamental to it.
But even as we speak, the foundations of our economies are being depleted at an alarming rate.[3] When ecosystems deteriorate, firms face higher costs, lower productivity and supply chain disruptions.
For far too long, we have treated nature as though it were free and inexhaustible. It is neither.
We have mistaken the depletion of natural capital for economic prosperity.
We counted the production.
We counted the income.
But we rarely – if ever – counted the soils depleted, the water systems stressed, the forests weakened or the ecosystems lost in producing it.
In economic terms, we have been consuming our capital and calling it income.
Nature is already presenting us with the bill. Depleted natural capital is already disrupting production, damaging supply chains and increasing costs. The consequences are already spreading from ecosystems to firms, from firms to balance sheets and from balance sheets into the financial system.
This is not a future tragedy on the horizon. It is an economic reality unfolding around us.
That is why taking action for nature is not only an environmental imperative.
It is an economic and financial necessity because our future prosperity directly depends on it.
The natural currency underwriting economic activity: water
Water is perhaps the clearest example of what happens when we fail to account for natural capital. For too long, we have allowed our economies to function as though reliable supplies of clean water were an unlimited production input. But an economy cannot negotiate with an empty river, a depleted aquifer or a failed ecosystem. When we withdraw water faster than it can be replenished, we are not creating prosperity. We are fooling ourselves and failing future generations by consuming the capital on which future prosperity depends.
Think about this summer’s heat-exacerbated drought conditions throughout Europe: major rivers, like the Rhine, Loire, Po and Danube, reached exceptionally low levels, forcing, among other things, the shutdown of critical nuclear power plants, while also negatively affecting hydropower and disrupting supply chains.[4]
Drought also contributed to the severity of wildfires. These are not glimpses of a distant risk. They are stark signs of ecosystems already being pushed beyond their limits, with consequences that are already being felt by people and the economy.
Unfortunately, our analysis suggests that the potential consequences could be much larger. Research involving the ECB, the London School of Economics and Oxford University has found that a 1-in-100-year drought event could put up to 24% of euro area economic output at risk.[5]
Clearly, too little water is only half of the story. Too much water can be equally problematic.
Nearly 12% of economic output in the euro area faces risks from insufficient flood protection.[6] The recent catastrophic events in Nepal and Bangkok are a stark reminder of the devastating human consequences alongside the destruction of infrastructure and economic assets.
And there is a third dimension to consider: polluted water. Take PFAS, for instance. Known as “forever chemicals”, these pollutants are in a wide range of everyday products from textiles and cookware to batteries and food packaging. As the name suggests, they last an extraordinarily long time – and when they leach into the environment, they can be extremely damaging for people’s health and for entire ecosystems, all of which also comes at substantial economic cost.
The European Commission estimates that, if current levels of PFAS pollution in Europe continue until 2050, the cost to society could reach €440 billion over that period. Treating polluted water alone could cost more than €1 trillion.[7]
The economic challenge comes from water in all its dimensions: too little, too much, too hot, too dirty.
And the effects differ across regions and sectors: agriculture here, manufacturing there and energy production somewhere else. When sufficiently widespread or persistent, the impacts can ultimately affect growth and inflation.
Nature: our first line of defence against the climate crisis
But the example of water also reveals something else: climate and nature cannot be separated.
Healthy ecosystems act as our first line of defence against global heating and related extreme weather events.
Europe is the fastest-warming continent. Temperatures have been rising by approximately 0.56 degrees Celsius per decade since the mid-1990s, more than double the global average.
This summer again brought record temperatures, following on from 2025 which was the third-warmest year on record, and 2024, the warmest ever – so far.
The interplay between temperature, the water cycle and soil quality illustrates why the climate and nature crises should be treated as a nexus.
And perhaps nowhere is this more evident than in the ocean. The ocean is one of our planet’s greatest shock absorbers. It has absorbed around 90% of the excess heat from global warming and around 30% of global carbon dioxide emissions.[8] That is an extraordinary capacity. But extraordinary does not mean unlimited.
Even the strongest buffer has its limits.
And those limits are no longer theoretical; we are already breaching them. Seven of the nine planetary boundaries have already been transgressed. We are moving increasingly outside the safe operating space on which our economies and societies depend.[9]
In other words, we are consuming the buffers that protect us from economic disruption and climate shocks at precisely the moment when those shocks are intensifying.
Nature – an investment in economic resilience and prosperity
Recognising nature as economic infrastructure has another important implication.
If degrading nature can weaken our economies, preserving and restoring it can strengthen them. This matters particularly today, when maintaining prosperity, resilience and economic security has taken centre stage in the policy debate.
Protecting nature is often framed as if it comes at the expense of competitiveness. However, that frames the problem backwards. As we seek to strengthen prosperity and economic security, nature should be seen as part of the solution rather than as part of a separate, often neglected, environmental agenda. Economic security depends on ecological security. Secure water supplies, resilient food systems, functioning ecosystems and reliable energy systems are strategic assets that reduce vulnerability to future disruptions.
We should therefore stop treating investment in nature as a competing claim on prosperity and economic resilience.[10] It is investment in the productive capacity that makes lasting prosperity possible.
There can simply be no lasting prosperity on a collapsing natural foundation.
We cannot impoverish nature and expect our economies to flourish.
Therefore, preserving and restoring nature is not simply an expenditure. It is an investment.
We can invest in preserving and restoring natural capital now. Or we can pay increasingly through disrupted production, adaptation, reconstruction and lost economic capacity later.
Nature will impose the adjustment regardless. The question is whether we manage that adjustment, or allow it to be imposed on us.
From awareness to action
So what does this mean for central banks and banking supervisors?
Nature-related risks are global and systemic. They do not stop at borders, and no single jurisdiction can address them alone, which makes international cooperation more indispensable than ever. The current geopolitical fragment
